text: It is good if TNO's research is updated. It was then about 500,000 households, of which three quarters live in rental homes, with a risk of energy poverty or living in energy poverty. I have already seen estimates where this has increased to over 1 million households, with a larger share of home homes added, especially in rural areas. It's all known. It is good that this is updated quickly. This is precisely why the coalition agreement agreed firstly to remove the landlord's tax, to ensure that performance agreements are made and to promote the phasing out of poorly isolated housing. These are properties with labels E, F and G. Secondly, the national isolation programme has been agreed. My question is whether TNO can discuss action options in its analysis to quickly reduce the risk. I would also like to ask whether the government in its appreciation of the investigation, as soon as it comes to the Chamber, can address the question of how what has been agreed could possibly be intensified or accelerated, both in the case of housing corporations and other landlords, as well as in the case of the national isolation programme. Because if the budget is not sufficient next year, then of course until 2030 the climate and transition fund still has quite a bit of a budget. I know that the Minister for Climate and Energy is going to look favourably at whether there is sufficient budget to really reduce the risk of energy poverty in the short term.

I hear a lot of different things, I must say. At the beginning, the Minister said that it is mainly a matter for the people there. Then there's some pressure put on it by D66, and then there's some more fire. I would say, above all, hold on to that, and don't be as shabby as at the beginning. The Minister now also says that they do say that it is also about clearing the case law. Then it's not just a case for there, it's a case for us as well. Minister Van Engelshoven recently said, I think a few weeks ago, in a debate: perhaps we should think about such a leading group of Member States; I am going to discuss this in the cabinet. Now I hope for a small explanation of what exactly has been the consideration following this conversation which, I presume, has actually taken place. The Minister now sees such a leading group primarily as undermining the strength of the European Commission; at least, it seems. But you can also see it as a reinforcement that we not only let the Commission take the coals out of the fire, but that we make it clear on several fronts that this is an issue for all of us. Then we can also see how we can work together with Member States, for example in Spain and Italy, to make it clear that this is a joint thing. I would like the possibility to be actively examined by this Minister for Legal Protection, including European legal protection.

The motion in part No. 785 on the SDE++ I advise against. This concerns future CO-free capacity subsidies. It is not wise to limit this and exclude it for innovation subsidies. It has not yet been used, but the motion asks me to rule everything out. I wouldn't want to do that right now. The motion in part No. 786 by Mr Van der Lee and Mr Bontenbal, and calls for the roll-out of hybrid heat pumps. That seems to me to support policy; good idea, we are going to do it. We already did.

Thank you, Mr President. A cop who can do his or her best work is indispensable to your sense of safety and is vital. Anyone who has ever needed the police to protect themselves, another or an animal knows that this is true. Then you don't want to have to look for an internet form or a so-called pop-up police station, which is a name that disappeared as suddenly as it had come, but then you seek the familiarity of the familiar face of the district agent. Then you do not want to report it at a so-called 3D declaration counter, in an abandoned building or at your municipality with very limited opening hours. Then you really want to connect with a physical person, from person to person, that reassures you, listens to you and protects you. The president of the ACP police union says: we see that the problems are acute and that there are far too few agents in the streets, in the neighbourhood and in the neighbourhood; there are also too few people in the police department to solve criminal offences, and in society the need and expectation is that they will succeed. Mr. Chairman. This isn't new. After all the cuts, the minister had to be packed in efficiency strokes, and the transformation into a log national police force, the ageing population and the huge outflow within the police and the much too limited influx into the academy for many years, no, should have foreseen this. Even now, it's sticking patches. Already, the consequences of far too few agents are fully felt in society. But what does the Minister do? To really solve the many problems within the police, 75 to 100 million is needed, among other things for 17,000 new agents. This was argued by the ACP police union in May. How far do the police and the security of our society have to sink through the ice before the minister starts investing structurally in the police? I'd like a response. Mr. Chairman. The shortage of capacity creates problems everywhere. In society, citizens try to solve the capacity problems and the disappearance of the district agent themselves and keep their neighborhood safe by setting up WhatsApp groups, deploying civilian searches and by civilian surveillance in the neighborhood, armed with just a flashlight. Such initiatives are the result of a lack of peace on the part of the police and of delays in driving, particularly in rural areas. Does the Minister consider it his responsibility to end the need for such citizens' initiatives? Does the Minister agree with me that one district agent out of 5,000 citizens is far too little and that the breeding ground for even more violent incidents in which people or groups take the law into their own hands because they do not feel heard or because they see that no action is being taken against injustice and suffering can only be taken away if the police can do their job fully again and the citizens can rely on it? Mr. Chairman. Speaking of citizen's confidence, there are still expensive 0900 forwarding numbers that appear high on the internet search "no urgency, but police" and which, unlike the free number 0900-8844, cost a lot of money. How is it possible that this is still possible? Years ago, Parliament questions were asked about it. The Authority's Consumer & Market referred to the website as "unwanted but not illegal'. Can't the Minister put an end to this? Mr. Chairman. For the police, the consequences of undercapacity are not easy either: enormous workload, hectic in roasting, disease breakdown, burn-outs, tensions within the corps, PTSD, insecurity for agents and citizens, reports and declarations that remain, animal welfare, environment and youth tasks that no longer need time because we need to maintain emergency aid with man and power, because we also need resuscitation. The basic team chiefs set priorities and the task holders no longer belong to their specialties. How can there be more attention to issues such as violence against Ibti's people when all energy is needed for emergency aid? How can more effective action be taken against child abuse, children who grow up in an unsafe home situation? How can there be more violence against animals if there is no longer time for task holders to tackle this issue? Now it is up to the Member to take over. It has been given many new tasks, while it also lacks capacity. How's the Minister gonna solve all this? Mr. Chairman. All kinds of unorthodox measures are being taken by the Minister. No proposal is really too crazy to continue to function more or less with less capacity, far too few agents. I would like to join with all the questions that have been asked about the extended powers of police and security services, about algorithms, additional camera surveillance including facial recognition, the drag law and privacy, and the civil rights of innocent citizens, which are seriously at risk. Mr. Chairman. Then the taser. We got a letter of inquiry. Does the Minister agree with me that resting agents with this taser is not a solution to the capacity problem either? You can't count on that to arrest fewer cops. At my request, the Minister took note of the advice of the UN Committee on Torture, for which he thanked. But can the Minister please go into the proportionality of the power-bulb weapon again? In the United Kingdom, 18 people have died since the arms were imported after it was used against them. Can the Minister respond to the risks clearly described in an analysis in the NRC last Saturday? There is no provision for studies to work in a controlled setting. The Minister wants to exempt weaker groups from using the taser. But how does a cop see if a woman is, for example, four months pregnant? And why aren't the elderly excluded? Mr. Chairman. We need an emergency plan for the police. Yesterday we received a letter of fire from the trade unions stating that in the very short term, now, choices must be made by this cabinet, by this minister. The only concrete plan available concerns the length of training of agents. Probably getting shorter, more practice, more on the street. Does the Minister agree with me that training is precisely the most valuable basis for a police force that has confidence in itself on the one hand and gives citizens confidence on the other? Does the Minister agree with me that the solution to the problems of capacity, the ageing population, the massive outflow of agents and the hole that creates this outflow should not be sought in the reduction of training? An organisation in charge of the monopoly of violence is in charge of the essential and not to be underestimated important task of keeping this country safe must seek the solution not in reducing training, but in investing in the educational organisation. It's already beeping and cracking in this organization, because it has to grow from 2,000 students to 2,700 students a year. Can the Minister reflect on this? Mr. Chairman. The trade unions have now decided to come up with their own contingency plan to deal with the problems. Shouldn't the minister have taken the lead here proactively? This is in view of the importance of an optimally functioning police force, for which the Minister is responsible. Instead, the Minister writes, a little ominous, that "uncomfortable choices" must be made in the coming years. What exactly does the Minister mean? Mr. Chairman. Thank you.
The next item is the VAO Climate and Energy, with Mr Van der Lee van GroenLinks as the first speaker. Welcome to the Minister.

I always think it should be as cheap as possible. If we do nothing, the coal plants will close by 2030 anyway. We don't have to spend any more money for that. Everything you do to speed up should be as cost-effective as possible. That is why I am so curious about the outcome of the discussions that the Minister is having. Thank you.

Then we don't have to rush and I can take a breath. I'd like to move on to the Secretary of State. I don't really feel like she's thinking in transitions. That's partly because of what she says in the media. Even against the corona policy, she calls people to go shopping. But also in the major processes of change I miss the decisiveness of her when it comes to accelerating the transitions. I wonder if I'm wrong about that, or if the Secretary of State can convince me that she's going for it. She has a lot of heart for SMEs. I am curious to see what it has achieved sustainably for SMEs in this cabinet period. On the important subject of digitalisation, besides sustainability, there is not for nothing the second priority, which is also at the heart of all these European packages, and I also have a number of questions that relate to the long term. In itself, I welcome the action taken by the Secretary of State, together with her French colleague, who I believe is even the Minister of digitalization. I understand from the non-verbal reactions that this is not the case, so I am apparently misinformed; then he is also Secretary of State, Mr Delors, a non-paper on the digital service act, a very important subject. There are good things in it when it comes to data sharing, data portability and data interoperability. Kees Verhoeven can say that much better than I do. However, much less is written about structural measures, such as cutting up big tech companies, the frightening five, we know all of them, which have grown by 20% in this period of corona. They were already the largest companies in the world, but they've grown another fifth. The Secretary of State had a bit of a hint in the media that cutting up companies could be an ultimatum remedium. I find that interesting. I'd like to hear more about that. When has the Secretary of State come the moment when, as a political party, we cannot, as the Netherlands alone, but in a European context, build up the enormous market power of these companies, which not only have enormous value, but also with a huge amount of services in many markets at the same time with a huge amount of information, cannot cut back a little more structuralally, by cutting them up, or by banning them from offering too many services at the same time? I would like to hear her long-term thinking about digitisation on this point. Finally, I am finished, within my speaking time, I would like to say a word of thanks to all the members of the two governments. It is an unprecedentedly difficult time, also in the area of economic affairs and climate, because of the gas extraction, because of climate change, because of corona, and later on also because of brexit. A lot of work needs to be done. I think that more colleagues would actually have wanted and should have had to be able to handle all the work. I thank them very much for all the work that has been done.

The motion in part No. 12, by Mr Van der Lee, asks the government to ensure that there is a guarantee that if the Amercentrale does not rely entirely on renewable biomass, there is a sustainable alternative. What they can be required to do is not about the Amercentrale but about the enforcement of a law will therefore never be coal, but if I may read'sustainable' as 'non-coal', then of course it is up to this operator himself. Because driving individual power stations as part of my task package really goes too far. So if I can read the motion like that, I'll leave that judgment room. Then we have the same intention.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. As indicated earlier, we need to keep the conversation going at the same time. That is why I welcome, for example, the Normandy Format, although it is at the advisory level. We must also continue to make it clear to Russia that NATO is not a threat in this respect. I am pleased to read in the Minister's letter that NATO is also willing to listen to any concerns of Russia and to engage in dialogue and so let it go that way. Mr. Chairman. Does the Minister see any possibility of restoring the links that Russia has broken between NATO and itself, without responding to all sorts of unreasonable demands of Russia? Could the Netherlands play its own role in this? I've got two seconds. That is why I am asking what is going on with our previous request for foreign gas. Think of America, Israel, Cyprus and so on. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Nice to see you here in this role. There is a lot going on in the field of climate and energy in Europe and in the Netherlands. There are a lot of issues to discuss, but I would like to limit myself to three points, on which I have motions for resolutions. [[Motion]] [[The Chamber,]] [[heard the debate,]] [[Whereas industry, built environment and mobility require large-scale electrification in the coming years in order to maintain climate targets;]] [[noting that sufficient supply of green electricity is essential for this;]] [[Whereas the supply of energy regions is much higher than the current SDE++ ceiling of 35 TWh;]] [[calls on the Government to ask an independent party for an opinion on how to deal with renewable energy on land after 2025,]] [[and goes to the order of the day.]] [[This motion was tabled by Mr Van der Lee, Mr Thijssen and Mr Boucke.]] [[She's getting No. kst-32813-845]]

I very much agree that you must support unity. Very. That is why I made a plea for the OSCE. That's the platform, that's the stage on which we need to talk. That is where European countries talk to each other about peace, democracy and security. That's where you have to get consensus. I agree that European countries should be as united as possible on a position in this regard. That is why I asked for the Germans' position to be followed, which also says: you must not deliver weapons to Ukraine, because that is oil on the fire.

Thank you, Mr President. I'm gonna let the nuance of a moment's notice work on me. I would like to begin by thanking Mr Remkes very much for his knowledge, skill and enormous energy. I got to know him as a sober Groninger with Limburg's joie de vivre. That's two things that make me, especially in combination...

I'm that mouse on that bridge that keeps pounding. It would have been much simpler with the rent allowance and then the people at the bottom would have been compensated, implicit, just for that gas disadvantage you call. I agree with you about your cause, but your solution would have been simpler in the context of your dilemma with the rent allowance instead of making up a new supplement through municipalities. Bureaucratic and individualistic.

Thank you very much, Mr President. I have two debates here today, so I hope I can keep the two well apart. If I suddenly start talking about municipal reclassifications, you will know that something is not going well, because we are indeed talking about the Housing Act now. I'm glad we're dealing with them today, not long before the summer recess. The House Act is an important law. Reference has already been made to the history of the Housing Act and to how important that law has been, even in the past. I think we do have a special construction in the Netherlands, in which we have housing corporations that really make an indispensable contribution to housing in the Netherlands. And yes, in the recent past, there has also been some error in the housing corporations. That was also reason to tackle that and to really attract the reins. But if you look all over history and keep an eye on the goal, that is of course making sure that there are affordable rentals of good quality for people who need it, who otherwise could not find a good home with them. As I said, there was reason to change the law in 2015. At that time, the activities of corporations were highly regulated. This has led the corporations to focus more on what they actually exist for, namely: housing those people who really need it. That is the most important task they have. At that time, we had seen that housing corporations had actually strayed from their core task. They had sometimes strayed so far that it was also at the expense of that core task. That's not good. It is therefore perfectly understandable that this happened at the time. There was every reason to tighten up and amend that law. At the same time, we have found that the law leaves too little room for local customisation and that it has also led to relatively high administrative burdens. What do we want to achieve with this change of law? With this change of law, we want to enable corporations to play their role better. It's just about the core of the job they have in the housing market. I am really glad to hear in the Chamber today that this is supported here too, especially when it comes to the functioning, feasibility and future stability of the law. This is seen in cases such as local customization, less administrative burden, more risk-oriented supervision by removing detailed rules............................................................................................................................................................................................. In doing so, I believe that the strength of the corporations improves, so that they are even better able to provide those affordable, sustainable and high-quality homes for those who need them, people with lower incomes. The corporations are there to build houses and manage houses, we all know that, but of course they also have a very important role to play in making homes more sustainable. They also have a very important role when it comes to the viability of the neighbourhoods in the Netherlands. You will also have noticed that the changes were not just conceived in the Ministry, but that we are really working closely together with Aedes, but also with the Housing Union, the VNG and the Authority for Housing Corporations, for example. We do that in good cooperation. Mr President, I now turn to the specific questions. First of all, a few questions about sustainability. Mrs De Boer asked whether the housing vision and performance agreements could include an obligation to set sustainability requirements for new construction. So the bill also makes it easier for housing corporations to make it more sustainable. The corporations are obliged, on the basis of popular housing priorities, set by the responsible minister every four years, to make known their intentions for sustainability in their municipal housing vision. Municipalities and also the tenants just need to know what their plans are. Next, local performance agreements are made, as we always do, so that I can ensure that the discussion about sustainability is conducted locally, and that parties include this in their performance agreements. So you can see through that route that in by far the majority of performance agreements sustainability measures are agreed between local parties. Mr Van Hattem asked whether corporations could introduce land positions in energy cooperatives. He quoted from the explanatory memorandum the possibilities for cooperation with energy cooperatives. The bill offers corporations more opportunities to invest in energy generation, but it has to be about energy generation on or on their own buildings and the underlying land, just like other property owners can do. Energy generation at unbuilt land positions of housing corporations is not included. Windmill parks, solar fields, large-scale energy generation, that is not the domain of popular housing but is the domain of energy suppliers. That is not the job of the housing corporations either. The social capacity they have is therefore not intended for this purpose either.

Mr. Chairman. Then I'll go to the source policy. Questions have been asked about this by D66, the VVD, GroenLinks, the SP; in fact, almost everyone of you has asked questions about this. A question from D66 was in which ways heaters can be further improved, next to Ecodesign. It's good to stoke and not to stoke at the wrong time. There are still varying experiences with filters at the moment. Mrs Van Eijs made specific reference to this. They can also be very expensive. In the context in which we try to keep people's energy bills from running out unnecessarily, you should also ask yourself whether the mandatory installation of a very expensive filter is proportional to the profit you make with it. But I think we should check it out. In the context of the Clean Air Agreement, we will, of course, also look at points of reference: what points do we consider to be cost-effective in achieving further improvements in air quality? TNO sets out the options for me; that report will come in the spring. I will therefore involve that knowledge again in the design of the Clean Air Agreement. Mr Ziengs asked how consultations with the industry had taken place. There have been several contacts. The industry itself has indicated that there is no problem in these trade stocks. Leaving this in effect by 2020 also means that there is another year to sell the already purchased stock under the old rules. The industry has indicated in a press release that it is also positive about this proposal. As regards minimum requirements for an existing installation: heaters that are already in use shall be replaced over time. By tightening the rules, they are replaced by cleaner heaters. Mrs Van Eijs asked whether we are also learning from neighbouring countries. Germany has a specific measure for this purpose. I will request, inform and evaluate that information to see if that would be a cost-effective measure. A number of members asked about installation requirements. That is one of the fifteen solutions that the Platform Houtstook and Health has sent to us. This is one of the solutions where I asked the platform to come up with further advice. We will then, of course, look at what it delivers, whether it is feasible and whether it is cost-effective. These are matters that must always be taken into account in each of these measures. Any adjustments should be made to the building regulations of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. So I'm gonna get some information first. After that, I may have a discussion with the Minister for Foreign Affairs. A number of parties asked whether the subsidy on small pellet stoves could not be prohibited. In the draft climate agreement, we agreed that in 2019 we will evaluate the ISDE grant on small boilers. That's what my colleague from EZK is doing. It has been indicated that the effects on air quality will also be explicitly taken into account.

Yeah, with the same warning. I'm gonna go into what the Minister says anyway. He says he's on his own, but he's not alone at all. The IAEA also says: natural gas, and basically any fossil fuel, you have to leave in the ground. So he's basically got the whole science behind him. So he doesn't have to feel alone. Doesn't that make him feel stronger?

Firstly, energy poverty is, of course, partly the result of climate policy. See, for example, the ODE, the storage of renewable energy. Since its introduction in 2013, this storage alone has led to an increase in the energy bill of hundreds of euros. Then Mrs Beckerman says: yes, but we still need to make it more sustainable. Research carried out by the PBL has just shown that this sustainability is profitable for virtually no one. It costs tens of thousands of euros per house, sometimes even a tonne per house. That is simply for no one to pay, but that money will have to be paid, left or right. That's got to come from somewhere, and as always, it comes from the ordinary people. What are you supposed to do? On the contrary, we must stop this climate policy. Then we can eliminate storage of renewable energy. We see that the energy tax on gas goes up again and again, 4 cents per cube, then 3 cents per cube, and why? To encourage people to go off the gas in the context of the climate, so to speak. But people don't do that because of the costs and then have a huge energy bill. So, in conclusion, if climate policy is to stop, then all related burdens, tax increases, can be immediately removed from the table.

I have always chosen the line, for a number of years now Mr Nijboer knows that I think there is no contradiction between the approach to tax avoidance and tax constructions and, at the same time, an attractive locational environment. I think that's a sham contradiction. I want you to do both, and companies that innovate and make money here will stay in the Netherlands as well. In that sense, I understand that you're also looking at the profit tax, but my election program didn't include that cut in profit tax. That's obvious. In fact, we want a European minimum rate, so that you may take away the economic urgency to do something about it. However, I would say to Mr Nijboer that I think that a reduction in the tax on profits is much more justifiable than the abolition of the tax on dividends. I know that Mr Nijboer agrees with me, and if I didn't know that, I saw it in his response. Mr. Chairman. The approach to tax avoidance is, in addition to making sure that next year people will receive a number of billions of relief in their wallets, the second important line of this cabinet. The coalition agreement was ambitious and this Secretary of State also fills that in very ambitious terms. That really is a trend break with the past. The Secretary of State is also praised for this, for example internationally by the OECD, the club of rich countries. That's the second red line. One of the most important measures is the withholding tax, which I would like to mention. As far as my group is concerned, the third red line is the greening of the tax system, both bread and much needed. I see that the Secretary of State is really taking steps in this Tax Plan to convert the measures of the Climate Agreement into legislation. He's the first as far as I'm concerned. As I said in the WHO, his colleagues can follow quickly, because the urgency is high and much needs to be done. Soon the CO tax for industry will come along. This is an important measure to ensure that industry also achieves 49% reduction. We will soon be talking about the flight tax, for which this Secretary of State is trying to get an international alliance. It remains bizarre that fueling a Fiat Twingo or a cup of coffee at Schiphol Airport is taxed more heavily than kerosene on an aircraft or, indeed, marine fuel. That is another area in which we must do something internationally about the tax exemptions that I do not consider to be explanatory. Mr. Chairman. From these three red lines I go to the concrete legislative proposals. The Tax Plan, the main law, contains, first of all, those tax measures that make people feel better in their pockets. We postpone the reduction in the tax on profits and in 2021 it will go down significantly less than the plan had been in the past. Tax reliefs are brought forward by the Cabinet, so we'll do them sooner. We are taking a number of measures such as the higher employment discount and a higher general tax discount. That is sensible, but there are also a number of more precise measures which I would like to consider. I believe that Mr Omtzigt has already mentioned the low VAT rate on electronic publications. It is indeed important that we see that the lower VAT rate is translated into lower prices. It's a search, but I'd still like to ask the Secretary of State what can be done there. Secondly, I welcome the answer, including in writing, to questions I asked in the legislative consultation on, for example, suppliers selling loose articles bundled. I mentioned the example of Blendle. As far as I am concerned, the written reply provided the clarity that was asked for in the sector and by me. I'm grateful to the Secretary of State for that. I'm still looking for future resilience. Is it future-proof, for example for providers who start offering things without advertising and without cookies, so you can pay the low VAT rate? The Secretary of State said if you start with that, you can. I continue to wrestle with him about providers who are not doing so now and who are going to make you pay a little more for a product without advertising, because that would not apply to the low VAT rate. I keep finding it complicated. But that a new provider with a new product without cookies and without advertising is completely covered by the low VAT rate, I have in any case cashed. I will come in the second term with a motion to continue monitoring that what we are doing here also supports future innovations in that sector and does not stand in the way. Mr. Chairman. The fact that company periodic penalty payments are no longer deductible for the tax on profits is a repair that I am very pleased with. I was here during Question Time with Minister Hoekstra, who then replaced the Secretary of State, in connection with the graphite rains from Tata in IJmuiden and Velsen. The fines they received for non-compliance were deductible, but that is now being repaired with this bill. I think that is right, because when you talk about incomprehensible to people, I found this incomprehensible to people. This bill also includes the increase in excise duty on tobacco. My group is in favour of this. We take a step towards that €10 per package, which we know will certainly make it easier for start-ups to start smoking and we can take the step towards a smoke-free generation. In the legislative consultation I asked, together with Mr Nijboer, very specifically about the treatment of the electric cigarette, the e-cigarette. It has been said that Secretary of State Blokhuis is already investigating whether it is harmful. I'll wait for that investigation. The signs that this is the case are increasing and they are not just coming from the United States. It's kind of weird that you don't burden that. That does not fit in with the current system and that is why I asked the Secretary of State if it would be harmful, he would see if, for example, you would have to make a separate consumption tax for that. The Secretary of State has now, as I understand it, promised a two-stage missile. I'd like to confirm that one more time. He awaits the investigation of Secretary of State Blokhuis. I'm okay with that. If the result is that there is health damage, which is expected to be D66, he will investigate whether a consumption tax is possible and whether something should not be done about it internationally. I believe that this is also a matter for the other Member States with which we are in the European Union. Did I get it that well? Then the trotting and racing. Mrs Lodders and I have drawn a great deal of attention to this. There are still conversations, also with NOC*NSF to make a compensation on that side. This is the only sport that we cannot compensate for at the moment for a tax measure, and I do not think that would explain this particular sport. The Secretary of State is optimistic. I would ask him to inform the Chamber as to when that solution will come. Can the Secretary of State state state state a time limit and will he undertake to inform us about it quickly? Then there's the transportation of care. We have concerns about whether enough electric vans for target transport can be put on the market in time. The Secretary of State says it's going very fast in the market and he's optimistic about it. We have another motion that was passed last year. That was from at least the four coalition parties, but I think it was widely supported. The request was to keep the finger on the wrist that we can really take that step towards electric transport and that we can offer that kind of transport. I would like to ask the Secretary of State once more whether he sees another need, and if that is possible, to do something for the first year at least. I'm telling you quite frankly, I don't know exactly how that could happen. I am still not quite sure whether it is really necessary, but I do understand the concern in the sector that the replacement will soon be blocked because the type of vans needed, including the number of people who fit in, are not available. I would like a little more clarification from the Secretary of State. Finally, in this legislative proposal, the landlord levy and, to be precise, the 10 times 100 million discount that can be applied flexibly. That money can therefore be spent earlier, for the first few years already more than 100 million, precisely in order to stimulate new construction. We have a crisis in the housing market and we need to make sure that it can be built, built and built. D66 has also said that this is a design aimed at scarcity areas. I understand that you want to be able to put down a substantial amount of money and then you want to focus on the areas where this new building is most needed, where the housing shortages are greatest. But my group also found and believes, looking at that list, that it is a difficult story for Nijmegen, Breda, Leeuwarden, Tilburg and Arnhem. What do I say to these municipalities about why they are not covered, when they are also just in those top 50 areas of cramped areas? In my view, this has been discussed extensively in the legislative consultation on Living. In the short term, I expect an amendment from at least the members of the coalition to extend it. Mr President, I see Mr Nijboer.

Protecting the Dutch coast is, of course, a very good plan. That's what we have to do. Of course, the Netherlands has been doing this for centuries. The Netherlands can do that very well. And if a delta commissioner says we're safe at least until 2050, I don't understand Mr Grinwis' panic. Mr Grinwis talks about "putting the head in the sand." Let's just look at the facts. The Netherlands is responsible for less than half a percent of total CO emissions. He blamed me... At least, it wasn't really a reproach, but he told me that I can't save the world and neither can he. But as the Netherlands, responsible for half a percent of these global emissions, we have no influence on this either. And then we're going to get houses off the gas here in the Netherlands, while households in Germany even get money if they take gas. We in the Netherlands are going to close down the few coal plants that we still have and which are by the way among the most modern and cleanest in the world, while there are plenty of coal plants being built up in Asia. And if we ignore that as if we could save the whole world in this small country with our climate policy, as Mr Grinwis does, then we will be sticking our heads in the sand.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The CDA has already argued several times for the refining route and the use of hydrogen in it. It is not hard enough for me and therefore this motion. Mr. Chairman. Finally, I would like to call on the Minister to express his uncomfortable feeling about the 90 million acceleration budget for Shell and NAM. D66 wants under 12 billion cube as soon as possible. If it is not legally different, can the minister at least appeal to companies on their moral responsibility? Thank you.

If I may, I will return to that last question in the second term. I'm just checking to see if I can actually go into that planning. When it comes to the declaration of a company, actually an industrial cluster such as Tata, that wants to make it more sustainable, there is just a lot of extra needed for wind at sea, for example. That is exactly what both the PIDI programme and the President-in-Office of the Council have always been short, but also in many other places. These are also the ideas that Mrs Minnesma recently shared with the Prime Minister and me. She says: the sustainability of industry could look like this and so much wind is needed at sea. She also put this on Mrs Hamer's table for the sake of a new cabinet. Here's the question. How much extra wind can you get at sea? How much infrastructure for hydrogen can you arrange? Within what timeframe do you want to ensure that industry can be made more sustainable? At the moment, Tata also says that he needs a lot of CCS in that transition phase. There are parties like the environmental organisations and the FNV that say: no, you can skip that if you do it in a different way. That's what they're looking at right now. An extra gigawatt is certainly what is planned. It could just be that I'm gonna be standing here more often, because we're gonna get more wind at sea.

Certainly, Mr. Chairman. I saved it for Mrs. Van der Plas. The reason for my question to her is what she said about high gas prices and the consequences for gardeners. Yeah, they're horrible. It sounded a bit like that because we have to be careful with climate policy, but maybe I misunderstood that. It would be fantastic for gardeners if they were no longer dependent on Russian gas, but on heat from their own soil. It would also be fantastic if we were to help gardeners by ensuring that the heat price is no longer linked to the gas price and that we help them to electrify without a penalty through a storage of renewable energy. When we take these steps, horticulture becomes greener, it is less dependent on Putin's expensive gas and we help not only horticulture but also the world a little further. There was some concern in the words of Mrs van der Plas. I'll share that. It also sounded a little too negative, while there are opportunities to help the horticulture further.

Mr. Chairman. Winston Churchill once wrote an essay in which he expressed his surprise that keeping animals is a cumbersome method for eventually eating meat. In 1931 he provided the opportunity to make farm meat. That is an inspiring challenge, similar to the first man on the man. Because, Chairman, for our daily flesh, we prey on the earth. If we look at the use of biomass, all that we produce on Earth, then one third of it is used as animal feed. With a growing world population, which also eats more and more meat as prosperity grows, it is a fiction that can do so with the current agricultural model. Anyone who claims that we must export this current Dutch model deserves the noble prize for fiction. It just can't be, because you need three globes to feed all people. That's why D66 is focusing on circular agriculture where we're going to use the Earth much more efficiently. Unfortunately, there is still very little of that. And then grow meat. The Minister writes that she will continue to follow developments. That can't be true with a technology with so much potential! Imagine that the CEO of Kodak had said: we continue to follow the development of digital technology with interest. Imagine if Nokia had said: interesting, that smartphone, we'll keep an eye on it. Oh, no, they said that. But those companies are bankrupt. This attitude is a bit like that of city drivers who followed the development of the car with interest and in the meantime continued to focus their policies on reducing horse manure in the streets. A minister of tomorrow shouldn't be yesterday. D66 expects not only an open attitude but also direction from the cabinet. The most difficult route for young businesses is the approval of farmed meat as novel food. The government has experience in dealing with difficult, bureaucratic organisations such as EFSA. How do you make a file? How do you ensure that the raft and with a positive result go through the procedures? Help these companies with this! Mr. Chairman. In addition, it is necessary for the government to allow experiments. So not confiscate a piece of farmed meat, but ensure that the product can be developed in such a way that the dossier can be submitted. This simply includes tastings. In Germany it is allowed. I lend myself as a volunteer, as a test subject, for the first piece of farm meat, but I honestly do not feel like finishing that tasting with a criminal record. That is not the attitude of the government that is needed. Simply make sure that experiments are allowed. This is necessary for product development. Allow the testing of farmed meat under controlled conditions. It is now becoming increasingly clear that the livestock in the Netherlands is far too large. This solution is too late for the nitrogen crisis, but in the long term, farmed meat is an excellent alternative in terms of reducing the environmental impact of livestock farming, with minimal use of water and land and minimum greenhouse gas emissions. And not to mention the avoided animal suffering. Eat meat, not animals. I'm rounding up. The Netherlands was among the first countries to see the potential of farmed meat, which led to the first patent, in 1999. China, Israel, the United States and Germany are now in a race to launch the first commercial market. The Netherlands is missing in this list. Make it an inspiring journey to the moon, to prevent the earth from going to the philistines. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr President. Coal is a highly polluting fuel to produce electricity. The present legislative proposal aims to ban this production and thus significantly reduce CO emissions and to take an important step towards meeting climate targets. The CDA Group supports this line of thinking, but the last word has not yet been said. Let me first make a general comment. I had such a suspicion, but since the recent first annual analysis by the Cabinet's Council of State of Climate Policy, I am beginning to believe it more and more: the cabinet's climate policy is incoherent. I mentioned it in the written preparation a search in which little is established. Anyone who looks at the history of the draft law before us can see that this has been the case in the past. In fact, there is even political fickleness. About ten years ago, one of the previous Cabinets advocated the construction of coal power plants to produce electricity. The idea behind this was: coal is cheap and infinitely available and the negative effects on the environment are overcome by underground CO storage. It looked like Columbus' egg. Seemed like it didn't happen. That is to say, the underground storage has never been realized, but the power stations have been built. There are three brand-new installations in our country built in 2015 or related to them, which could be produced for decades to come. But that's not the point. These coal plants, together with some older ones, must cease production because they emit too much CO. The government agreement is clear: by 2030, coal-fired power stations will no longer be available in the Netherlands. Mr. Chairman. This is, to say the least, a government zigzag policy. In ten times, there's a complete reversal. I would like a reply from the Minister and an answer to the question as to what this erratic behaviour could mean for companies' willingness to invest in the Netherlands. The Netherlands closes coal power stations. Elsewhere, for example in Germany, such power stations and even lignite power stations continue to operate. It clearly indicates relativity or, to remain in the spirit of the above, the incoherence of things. I would also like a response from the Minister on this matter.

Mr. Chairman. I'm with the European Recovery Fund. The Minister says: but things are going very well; the economy is recovering. Then, of course, the question is how prudent that is. If you look at the uncertain developments in the world market, inflation, labour market shortages, energy prices, the bitcoin bubble and the negative effects of Brexit, there is only one thing that is certain, namely that it is highly uncertain, except for Mr Van der Linden, because he knows that interest rates remain high, but that is his interpretation. Excuse me, I hear Mr van der Linden saying that inflation is high and not interest rates. Yeah, he knows more than I do, but I think it can be said across the board that it's uncertain. Then I would say: let the reform fund be implemented on the formation table as quickly as possible and make sure that there are plans for the cabinet to be able to do its bit. Mr Vendrik said it was rather special that it has not yet arrived. Well, I find it exceptional that we, as the Netherlands, have not submitted a plan. That's really not regret or no-regret. The Recovery Fund has a history. I know. The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, with Mr Van Ballekom in the back seat, have always reacted somewhat reluctantly to this whole fund and seen it as a kind of cuckoo egg in European developments. But the fund is here. Use it. I'd say look ahead. I do have a question, because from the documents I understand that there is not a starting period but a final deadline. Investment must have been made before 2026. What does that mean? Can the Minister inform us of the significance of that term? Mr. Chairman. There has been some fuss about a letter from the Minister about Brussels' demands, but I think that is a real shame. We should not lay down the issues of reform in Brussels; we should take our own decisions on this. Mr. Chairman. A number of additional investments are still needed and we all know where: in the decisions after Glasgow, in the attractiveness to become a teacher, in the staff shortages, in the housing and housing sectors, it is already mentioned in the nitrogen issue. Here, the cabinet has not taken sufficient action to use this minister's terminology, and is failing the Millions note to make a number of choices. However, we hope that this can be changed as soon as possible in a new government agreement and in a missionary cabinet. Luckily, money is reserved. Budgetary provision is made for a solution to the surcharge affair. I see the Secretary of State here and I ask her if we can come up with what she thinks is necessary. Mr. Chairman. I saw that there was an increase in expenditure on social lawyers in the budget, but I am concerned about the years after, because they are falling again. When we talk about surcharges, there is also a link between these two issues: cuts in social law and the consequences of supplements. I would like to put one final question to the Secretary of State who is also responsible for customs and to clarify the questions raised by the European Court of Auditors on the recovery and reduction that our country receives as a collector of funds under the rules of the MFF. What's going on here? Could she explain that? Mr. Chairman. Finally, the D66 Group is, of course, looking forward to the answers of the rulers.

Mr President, thank you. In Winschoten, our inhabitants are dealing with earthquakes caused by stacked mining, namely the extraction of gas from the Groningen field and the extraction of salt. First of all, I would like to ask the Minister whether, as a result of the earthquakes or a fall in soil above the salt caverns, there have also been reports of damage to Nouryon. If so, how will this damage be dealt with? The Minister has indicated that residents can go to the Temporary Committee on Mining Damage in Groningen for this stacked mining. Given the reservoir that is there, I ask the Minister how these claims are dealt with. In addition, I would like to hear from the Minister whether the monitoring of the caverns with acoustic measuring equipment has been set up by Nouryon and whether State surveillance of the Mines agrees with the planned monitoring. Are there sufficient accelerometers available in the area? If that monitoring isn't there yet, when will it be? It was supposed to be there by 2018, Mr. Chairman. To what extent is salt extracted from salt caverns at Winschoten? The SodM indicates on its website that there is no long-term solution for the abandonnering of the caverns at Heiligerlee and Zuidwending. Is the Minister prepared to discuss this with the SodM and salt extraction companies to ensure that the caverns are secured for the long term? We get the impression that it is not yet well arranged. Other colleagues also spoke about this. We all have concerns about that, Mr. Chairman. It is also necessary to prevent old pipes from leaking, as happened in Twente. To what extent does this play out here and what actions are being taken against it? Because of the big problems with the gas extraction in Groningen, residents are anything but enthusiastic about mining. This calls for more effort to involve residents in the mining companies. The CDA sees the pilot Harlingen at the salt extraction there as a good way to do this. Residents have entered into the conversation with mining companies themselves and a covenant has emerged from that. I believe that Mr Sienot referred to this as well. The question is whether this is included in the agreements made with the salt companies for their own damage protocol. The colleagues of the SP and GroenLinks have asked questions about how we continue to deal with local authorities. Are they well involved in all matters, as reported to the Chamber in the Minister's letter of December? And how does that work for residents? I should also like to point out, for example, that residents bring forward the following points. Nedmag has a shareholder: the NOM. And the NOM is again covered by EZ. And that's how you get suspicion about how salt extraction works when it's also a business case for the government itself. Mr. Chairman. I hope that the Minister will be able to contribute in a good way to the confidence that, in this case too, the people and local authorities are being treated properly. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Baudet, this is what's above it. It's taking all the costs for climate policy. I'm actually looking for the constructive tone with you, because you're right that it's going to cost a lot of money. But this state shows that we have lost less money on the cost of energy, by saving energy. Those two things keep each other pretty much in balance. That shows the PBL. All costs were included. Could you go into that again? I think it shows you wrong.

I cannot fully see Mr Klaver's proposal here. It does sound like raising taxes for business. There is a risk that we will drive companies away, which is ultimately not good for the prosperity of this country. But I want to take a serious look at the proposal he's making. What I do like about the cabinet plans, for example about the SDE, is that it is not through the energy bill, but through the general funds. I think that is a step towards what Mr Klaver wanted earlier. I'm gonna look at his proposals and take them to me. I can't do that here from the loose wrist.

I think that I still consider the motion to be a commitment of the cabinet, because I do not think that we disagree there. We simply do not want any more natural gas projects under the TEN-E. Mr Dassen is quite right: the Council has defined its position and the so-called trilogue is now in progress. It may mean that the existing projects will continue to be covered and that the new ones will no longer be covered. We must also be honest about this, because that is the current state of affairs. Projects are already allowed. We are now looking at the new regulation. That balance... In addition to what I would like to do, we must also be realistic. We are raising ten other countries in the view that gas projects should in principle no longer have a role, but I also note that natural gas projects in the list of PCI projects before us are now permitted. That is the actual situation. I would like to go on the road to ensure that that is no longer in the new regulation.

I have good news for you. I have just sat down with Mrs Arib and for the next two months you can stand in this room as often as you like. I understand your party is rich, so if your party pays for the electricity bill, it'll all be fine.
When that energy directive comes, we look at the content and scope of the proposal and then we start by unanimity. That's the cabinet's point of view.

I do not think it will help in such a process as in the relationship between two countries the charge we have just mentioned, namely elements such as doubting the intentions and placing things in the perspective of postcolonial et cetera. That makes it all complicated. Sometimes you have to maneuver around somewhere to get to the goal. In a relationship where there are only two countries in the Kingdom, one of which has a problem as a result of a natural disaster, you might be able to organise it differently. There's a couple of bonds in here, though. In fact, it also has a lot to do with the discussion we have just had about autonomy. Of course, that disaster was huge. It can't carry any land the size of Saint Martin. But in the reconstruction and the things you can do, you need a certain execution force. Let me give you an example, Saba. That's a whole different order of things. That's a public body. They were able to do so very quickly, also with the help of the Netherlands, but still, to pick it up themselves. It is a smaller island with fewer inhabitants, but it did have the knowledge and skill to do so. Sint-Maarten was just a lot more complicated. With the knowledge of that time we had made the same decision, perhaps even with the knowledge of today. Only in the pre-stage, so before the start, you might need to strengthen the conditions that a country has to meet in order to make it a success, for example that establishment agreement and ensure that you have sufficient knowledge and skills. There we may have had too much confidence, as in the greater sense with the autonomy of the countries, that if you make an appointment, they will also fill it out. Then it's not always a matter of unwillingness. Sometimes it's also a matter of powerlessness. They'll sign, but they won't be able to deliver in the end. Then you ended up cleaning up no roof and no garbage. Further to Mr Dittrich's question on reconstruction, what we have done is as follows. In particular, he asked about the schools. He doesn't think it's gonna make any sense if I put it in my own words. At present, repairs have started at three priority schools. The tender for the next three schools is under preparation. The remaining 13 schools follow after restructuring the agreement between the World Bank and Sint-Maarten. This also requires additional funding. This is an example of a project that has gone on for far too long. There was a long run and a long preparation. It was in the Ministry of VROMI. We told them to make that inventory, because that is not what the World Bank is doing. They had to make the inventory of what was damaged and had to be repaired. That's the only thing that took me a long time to get loose. That was also because the Ministry of VROMI is ultimately quite a small department, not comparable to a ministry in the Netherlands, which had to do all kinds of things. This just didn't come up as a priority. A lot of time has been lost. In the end, we have also flown in an external expert who is currently doing so. Well, now it's working. It's been way too long. Of course, we started with the shelters. We've started with the highest priorities. Schools were not quite at the top, but are of course extremely important, especially in view of any new hurricanes, which of course you can never rule out. Then I come to the third block of the four: a number of questions concerning the BES. Mr Dittrich wondered about the plans for Bonaire as a Blue Destination. Blue Destination is a wonderful concept, I think. It's really from the island. That's what they came up with; we didn't think of it for them. But then you also have to take a number of measures with regard to wastewater management and coral protection in order to achieve that asset of diving and beautiful nature in the future. You're gonna have to invest in that. Within the framework of the Envelope Region, we have released 7.2 million for the implementation of the coral recovery plan. Another part that is currently running, also with tourist organisations, is certification of destinations and tourist locations as Blue Destination destination. They are tested against a number of labels to see whether they meet sustainability and environmental requirements and whether they handle raw materials in a good way. I feel that it is still in its infancy, but I think it is a very strong concept or idea. But fair is fair, it's still too much of a concept and too little load. In discussions with the public body, I insisted on making it more concrete. Bonaire is now also working on a master plan in which they want to focus on sustainability. That goes hand in hand with wanting to grow, how many want to grow, what is needed for that. These are choices that the public body itself has to make in the first instance, but it does not hurt to use knowledge and skills from the Netherlands in that area too. That is what we have been asking for in the meantime. Once again, this is a very important element in the governance agreement. Mr Recourt, Mr Dittrich, Mr Van der Burg and Mrs Oomen asked about what is being done for the Caribbean Netherlands when it comes to the aid packages, the recovery and how it looks. What's that gonna look like after July 1st was also the question. How can we continue to support the economy there? Mutatisively, the Caribbean Netherlands is the same as the countries, namely that they are largely dependent on tourism. Only, they fall under the umbrella of the Netherlands. That's what we've been working for. I am very proud that there was broad support in the cabinet for the same arrangements as in the European Netherlands to apply to the Caribbean Netherlands. Not quite the same because the arrangements are sometimes a bit different, but at the core they are. Then you should think about the wage subsidy scheme and the subsidies for fixed charges. They've all been translated. This also applies to the expiry date of July 2021. This is the same end date as for the Netherlands. Caribbean Netherlands is also included in every decision-making by the Dutch cabinet on European Netherlands. I cannot anticipate in general terms how this is going after July, but the same principles will apply to the Caribbean and the European Netherlands. That is an important starting point, I think, because with that there is also full recognition for their position within our country. Mr Dittrich asked what the governance agreement has achieved so far. That was also an agreement that did not come about entirely without fireworks. There was broad support, but some people's explanation was that the Netherlands came to take over. That was not the case at all. This played in the period after the intervention on Sint-Eustatius. I am very pleased that we have reached a number of agreements together with the public body. There's a program manager on it. I have already mentioned a few examples that are the result of this. First of all, we looked at how to strengthen the official organisation, so more administrative power. This is important to translate the political ambitions into implementation, quite simply. That sounds very simple and self-evident, but it hasn't always been on Bonaire. A job centre has been set up together with the Ministry of SZW. That was before Corona. There, people looking for a job can get advice about their job and career opportunities. Then affordable homes; 500 social rental homes, which is really a breakthrough with the local housing corporation FCB. There are 76 ready now. I've been visiting, too. Beautiful apartments. At the moment we are working on the realization of the next phases. A bill has now been passed, also by this Chamber, on the rent committee on Bonaire. A pilot mortgage guarantee has been launched. All kinds of things that we think have added value to Bonaire, in this case, we roll out. Everything you prefer in the European Netherlands, I always say, we keep it here, because we don't have to export all the laws to the Caribbean Netherlands. There is no need for that. Only if it helps, if it adds something. Many improvements have been made around agriculture and the slaughterhouse. I went there on my last visit. There they really try to create new forms of lease local entrepreneurship, often on small pieces of land. If you get bigger, you're successful, you can farm in other places. I think it's very good to reduce dependency. The infrastructure is a big problem on Bonaire. You don't have to put thresholds there because the roads themselves already slow down the speed. But that also has disadvantages and sometimes causes dangerous situations. That is why there has been considerable investment in infrastructure, especially around schools, and that is going to happen much more. That is really starting to happen, also with knowledge from the Netherlands. Around the board, the operation of the island council, a clerk has flown in from Maassluis. He'll back up the clerk there. We really try to take people with us by coaching on the spot and train them step by step, to get the board to a higher level. Finally, and not unimportant with regard to the governance agreement, and I am very pleased that we have continued to do so, we are also looking at how to keep talent on the islands, or even sometimes to allow it to return. So these are young Bonairians who, for example, have studied in the Netherlands or in another country, and who want to come back after a number of years to work for, for example, the electricity company or for the local government. And these people do a program with each other, a talent development program. BZK supports that. We have been doing this for five years now, and that simply results in very good results, so that people also have support for each other to give an impetus to governance with modern education and backgrounds. Every time I'm there, I'd also like to invite you to do that. I'm going to talk to those young people, with those lights, because it's always very inspiring to see what people are moving to commit to their own island.

Madam President. First let's get a logistics report in advance on the distribution of the topics. The Monitor Broad Prosperity, the climate, education, Defence and security will be handled at the highest level by myself. The Minister of Finance deals with everything related to the annual reports and the budget, the reports of the Court of Auditors, infrastructure and the VWS topics and pensions. Finally, the Minister for the Interior deals with ICT and developments at the Rijksdienst. Just a few words in advance. I don't see him right now, but Mr Bruins' words touched me. He referred to D-day today. I was allowed to be in England yesterday, where the departure was commemorated on June 5th before D-day on June 6th. That was very impressive. Among the veterans still present were two Dutch veterans, who also flew along. One's gonna be 100 in three weeks. He said, "The worst thing about older people is when they get a cracker voice like that." That is not necessary. This man had such a voice that he would be able to change the behavior on the other side of the football field over the troops. You'll be almost 100. When you hear what this man has been through, I fully agree with Mr Bruins that we owe very much to those people for the fact that we can talk about the advantages and disadvantages of the Broad Prosperity Monitor in relative peace. Those weren't exactly the kind of subjects that were discussed between 1940 and 1945. Let's be incredibly grateful for that. The great anti-revolutionary statesman and Prime Minister Abraham Kuyper once said that governing is something other than administering. He was right about that. Governing is making choices in scarcity and those choices are rarely to be reduced to what you see in this debate today as a simple calculation or a ticking list. It is always about complex trade-offs between different interests. They can be material, they can be intangible and sometimes both. Politics is then about security, freedom, care, education, public finances, migration, the housing market, pensions, climate policy, burden burden, purchasing power, at home and abroad. That's all in the mix that the Cabinet and the Chamber deal with every day, so all of us. And yet it is important that we sometimes manage to ask ourselves whether we are still doing what we have agreed and whether the tax money is being spent properly and efficiently. That is why there has finally been a Day of Accountability and this Accountability debate. I think that started about 15 years ago. I remember that in 2006-2007, when I was chairman of the political group, we were going to celebrate the first real days of accountability here. There are three of us here today. This means that, for our part, we are also trying to serve the Chamber more and more widely in this debate. That is quite simply because accountability is part of democracy, but also because it is disciplining and stimulating for us as cabinet members. In that respect, I would like to thank the College of the General Court for all the work that has been done. I would also like to thank the Chamber for its contribution in the first term. Some were of course more complimentary than others; we will answer everything. And let me immediately join all the critics who point out that the cabinet still has a lot to do, because I fully agree with that. However, I cannot ignore the fact that care on some really big, far-reaching issues such as climate and retirement must now go a little above speed. You will say: that was then done, because the climate is not going very fast and pensions have lasted nine years. Nevertheless: why is that necessary? Because it is important for longer term support in politics and society to ensure that quality of content. This week there have been several debates on this type of subject, in which I was present. In a political landscape, a society and civil society with increasing fragmentation, there are no obvious majorities anymore, see also the results of the state elections and how long it takes in the various provinces to form colleges and see also the composition of the First Chamber, where the largest two parties now have twelve seats. You used to be about the fourth party, so now you're either the biggest or the second largest party in the Upper Chamber. If you add all this together, achieving major social breakthroughs on major issues such as climate and pensions requires building social coalitions. And then there's no other way than that care in this kind of subject is above speed. The facts are that the cabinet has been working for one and a half years. That is one and a half years of the four years we need to implement the coalition agreement, or at least we are talking about that period here. During that year and a half many plans were carried out or put in the scaffolding. I refer to the pension agreement, but also to a number of major decisions, such as the one on gas extraction, which has also been debated this week. The last terrible quake and the same debate this week show how important it is to speed up gas extraction to 12 billion cubic metres and then to 0 cubic metres. Important laws have been passed and filed, look at the Labour Market in Balance Act, which has also been adopted in the First Chamber and which reduces the differences between fixed work and flex work, but also look at the Intelligence and Security Services Act. Big investments are being made in the public sector, look at the extra money for elderly care, teachers, Defense and the handling of traffic jams. The relief has been mentioned here by a number of people. This is indeed one of the largest relief packages of the cabinet in this century and it is also a multi-annual political map, including in the First Chamber. The next instalments will come in January in the next two years. Several important and other measures have been taken, look at what we are doing, for example, to combat loneliness, to tackle poverty and debt, to make people grow old worthy and to fight undermining. All these results are the subject of this debate. This is also reflected in the breadth of the first term contribution of the Chamber. Madam President. In my experience, governing is mainly work in progress and every day doing what is needed. Sometimes it goes faster than planned, often it doesn't. Anyway, there is always the danger that you will be swallowed up by the delusion of the day and that there is therefore too little time left for reflection. Once again, I believe this is the strength of this debate. So I'm starting to reflect right now by going into the different subjects that I'm dealing with right now. Firstly, comments have been made on the trade-off between economic growth and well-being. That was brought in by GroenLinks. Mr Snels spoke about this. On this point in his speech, I would like to reply that the cabinet is seeking to bring together several aspects of prosperity at the same time. It's en-and. For example, we are working on an energy transition that not only contributes to a better climate and cleaner air, but also to a stronger economy, because it must lead to more jobs and more innovative power. The effects are that we live longer and healthier, but also that we get more comfortable, isolated houses. Of course, this is an economic opportunity. Another development that is taking place in the social debate, to which Mr Snels referred, is that the satisfaction of leisure is decreasing. There's more stress and less directing about one's own life. I agree with him that working in itself in certain circumstances can lead to stress, but can I point out that unemployment and poverty lead to much more stress? So we will have to balance society more and more. This immediately brings me to the theme of the Monitor Brede Prosperity. Several questions have been asked, including by Mr Snels. Without repeating his questions, I'm trying to answer them. This monitor helps with information about the recent past in mapping the situation and the challenge for the Netherlands. The monitor does this by providing a very broad, objective overview of the prosperity, with the various indicators that the report provides for and which the report is rich in. That information feeds the debate. Policy objectives are formulated in the cabinet formation and, if necessary, adjusted if topicality so requires. This makes the monitor itself a useful source of information for the cabinet formation, but also for discussing the state of play every year here. However, it is less appropriate to look ahead, such as predicting how much budget is needed to improve the outcome of certain indicators. Changes may occur as a result of other developments, such as the economic situation. There is coherence between different welfare aspects. In some cases, there is indeed an en- and. That energy transition is indeed a good example, but of course you can also see it on other major themes. Look at pensions, which must also be balanced: we need to ensure a good pension, but also that people can get that pension in a healthy way. There are several aspects that play a role in this. Then, of course, there are things where choices have to be made in the scarcity, because the budget is always limited. The formulation of concrete policy objectives and accountability is difficult. We have to be honest about that. It would be interesting, however, if I could come a little bit closer to Mr Snel's report to see if it would be possible to give more direction to the interpretation of the indicators in the monitor. At the moment, trends in the monitor are positive if they lead to higher broad prosperity and are positive when we belong to the best countries in the European Union. That's actually how it works now. I would suggest that we explore the possibility of using the monitor more in the policy cycle itself, considering reporting on results in the monitor with the question of whether and how policies have contributed to it. The question that follows is then what policy options exist to influence the results. This is extremely complex for several indicators in the monitor. So that reconnaissance will take time, but if we do, I think we're gonna take the monitor one step further. That is the beginning of a response to Mr Sneller's question, from the circle of D66. He asks how we can integrate budget figures more into the monitor. Again, the budgetary figures themselves are mainly about input: how much money do we spend on all these different policy areas? This is how the output is realized. Those are the government instruments and arrangements that we all have. This ultimately leads to a result, the outcome. Of course this is in connection with what is happening in the private sector and abroad. The Monitor Brede Prosperity describes that outcome. So it's not just possible to integrate it, but again, I think it's interesting to do an exploration to see how you can use the monitor for a more predictive value for the future. This will enable us to integrate him more into the policy cycle. I think this is a response to Mr Snels and Mr Snelter's contribution.

If the coalition supports the package, I can jump high or low, but that's gonna make it. I indicated last time in my first term that I like the cabinet's commitment, but that I would like to see where improvements are possible. I believe that both you and I, as well as the cabinet, agree that it is an improvement. Only, the question is about feasibility. If the IRS couldn't have done it, I would have said we shouldn't. Because I don't want to destroy the IRS. We really need to rebuild it with each other over the next few years. But I feel a little less sorry for the energy suppliers. Personally, I've noticed the following the last time. My energy supplier went bankrupt. After that, when I switched, they had the financial statements together like this. They had renewed it again as well when it turned out there was another mistake in it. Then I think: it's such a generic, easy measure. I would very much appreciate it if the cabinet would give the motion judgment Chamber. Then I'd take a more positive look at that. But that is without prejudice to the fact that I am very happy with everything we are doing right now to support low incomes and middle incomes.

The subject is now the examination of the legislative proposal 35283, Amendment of the Electricity Act 1998 and Gas Act (implementation amendment of the Gas Directive and a number of regulations in the field of electricity and gas). I would like to welcome the Minister for Economic Affairs and Climate Policy to the First Chamber. I inform Members that in the event of a motion, you should read the text yourself, and then put it on your right side of the table next to the speaker's seat. The Courtesy will collect and distribute the motion after your contribution.

Mr. Chairman. I'd like to close with three questions to the Prime Minister. My first question is: are you prepared to postpone all priceless measures in the Climate Agreement, such as removing gas from homes, until the corona crisis is over? My second question is: are you prepared to temporarily stop all immigration until the housing shortage in the Netherlands is resolved? My third question is: are you prepared to suspend all the commitments you made in Brussels in July to support other countries, under the guise of corona, until the Netherlands recovers its own finances from the corona crisis? In other words, public debt has been reduced to below 60% of gross national product. By the way, I would also like to ask: when is the government planning to pay off the debts we are going to incur? I do not need a precise date, but I would like to know if we will pay the extra debt before or after the Netherlands is CO2-neutral. What's the government's priority? Mr. Chairman. So these are four questions about policy priorities.

First of all, there is the reduction in the energy tax that benefits everyone and then, relatively speaking, especially those with a narrow scholarship and middle incomes. That's the good news. The slide, where gas becomes a little more expensive and electricity a little cheaper, turns out to be largely Modo neutral. From there, you do have to go to work. If you're gonna trade, you're gonna win money. Mr Asscher is right to ask: what if you do not have that perspective of action? Then we need to look at where we have that perspective of action. A few examples: where do we start first? Which corporations can get to work first? I would say: start in those some vulnerable neighbourhoods, where people do not have that choice and where there are poorly isolated houses.
