We have that freedom of choice and that conversations we can make with housing corporations. I would also like to say that on many pages of the agreement we have a hand-to-the-crane formulation or a finger-to-the-pulse. This also requires a great deal of work and we are going to talk about this. I think it is a legitimate concern: what do you do with the people who have no choice? I think you should take care of it first and serve the first. That will always be my benchmark.

Mr. Chairman. Then there are the other questions. I'm gonna go through that a little faster. Mr Kops asked what happened to these acceleration measures. He's not here, but I'm sure he wants an answer anyway. We have already talked about the construction impulse and the construction agreement. I think we've seen some really nice results. Of course, that's still on a relatively small scale, but of course that building impulse worked with how to do that contracting of contractors and how to set up the business office so that you make it a priority that the residents can go there, that they can just have a conversation with someone there. We have that building agreement with those 75 contractors registered in that open building pool. We have the trajectory owner chooses builder. At 40 addresses, it's started now. There are still notifications from contractors who want to do so. The same applies to residents who are interested in organising these work cases through this route, through that route owner chooses builder. That acceleration package also includes the typology approach, which has now received a positive opinion. Another element is this practical approach, where residents have the possibility to have the whole process, from inclusion to execution, carried out by one contractor. This practical approach is carried out by the Business Bureau Bouwimpuls. These are all really important pathways that have produced concrete results for people, but also for the organisation, for the NCG, a lot of lessons that they are using in the implementation of the reinforcement operation in the coming period. There are other examples, but I'll skip them. From the Heft in our own hands we have of course also learned a lot of lessons, namely that it is really important to be in very good contact with owners, with a delegation of owners, to pick up early uncertainties, so that you can really improve that program by discussing experiences and questions of residents with them all the time. In the end, you can do what those residents want. What comes back from the questions asked to the people in that residents contact group is that that intensive contact is very much appreciated by them and that they also consider that very important. The NCG has the experience from that program involved in their other program and also in the communication they are doing with residents. The explanation of the cost methodology, the role and responsibility of construction guidance, the explanation of the lead times and that kind of thing, very concretely, are actually coming from this project. We've already talked about Opwierde, Appingedam, I think. Then there is the capacity for construction and also for young people. That's a well-known point. Mr Van Otterloo just brought that up. I have the capacity problems in the construction industry very strongly on the retina, which is why we have that construction agreement. That gives a lot of space to some smaller and also local companies. By the way, it is fantastic in corona time that it has really succeeded in just working on it. It is true that young people need to be trained for this and they need to be interested in working in construction. That is why we have invested, together with the region, in additional jobs for young people in construction, for example in Delfzijl-Noord. The construction is, of course, wider than just the building you see in front of you. It is also about the energy transition and all kinds of opportunities there. I had already answered the question about monumental buildings. Can residents give their own input about the state of the home at an inspection, Mrs Beckerman asked. The recording of a house is done by a structural inspector. So that is an expert, who is there to carry out that recording objectively and competently with his or her expertise. Of course, the resident can at that time report to the inspector matters concerning the state of the home, so that they can be involved in that inspection. Then Mr Sienot said... uh, no, let me do it last; I actually liked that question. Just a few concrete points. How can the recording be faster and more easily accessible on request was a question from Mrs Mulder. That trajectory started in March last year. 632 applications have been received at that point of contact. At 417 addresses such a recording has taken place or is carried out. There were also addresses where an engineering firm had already prepared a recording advisory report. The owners will receive a decision in the coming weeks. It has indeed been a bit difficult to get started. One of the reasons for this was corona. So that start-up phase was really tough, but I think that more experience has been gained and that it is now progressing better, so that we can better inform the residents and we can indeed speed it up. But I've been reported that there are still limitations due to corona at the recording. This is also understandable from the perspective of the residents.

Now, Mr. Otten, that's as follows. I have also implicitly said this to Mr Vendrik. I believe in an energy mix. So if Mr Vendrik says we need gas on offshore wind farms, I don't believe in that. I do not think that we can make very much progress. Of course, the technology is moving forward, but also the profitability, or the less eligible of wind farms, has changed dramatically over the past ten years. And that's how it goes on. But still, no matter how far the technique goes, I don't think it's gonna work, and it's also unwise to put all kinds of eggs in one basket. That is why we have called for the widest possible energy base, so that the economy in the Netherlands is not affected.

Mr Azarkan does not want to talk about what we are doing this year. He says, "There is, and from now on we have to look further." That makes sense in itself, but with that we have reduced the energy tax by €400 per household and the fact that we have allocated €800 to people with a vulnerable income position, plus all the other things I mentioned earlier, off the table. I think it would be fair to keep that on the table and then to establish that it is wise to look at what is more structuralally necessary for lower and middle incomes from 2023 onwards. There is therefore an opening to do something for the group that gets €800.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. When I went shopping a few weeks ago in the district in Rotterdam-West, in Spangen, I think there was a line of up to two hours. It was a pretty hot Saturday. I don't know if anyone remembers it. People then lined up in front of the energy box, where you can save about €15 a month. Those rows have been in all the neighbourhoods of Rotterdam since then and I think in many other municipalities, but I haven't seen them literally there. We also remember the rows in Groningen. We were right to do that, because we couldn't. The rows for the energy box that I see every day now, for that €15 in the month, are hugely long. They're rows of people who are in trouble every day. There is another example, also in Rotterdam. There's a philanthropic institution up there, not the government. That philanthropic institution has said: city of Rotterdam, government, if you do not increase the compensation for a larger group, to 140% of the social minimum, then we are going to do it. We make working people in the Netherlands just beggars. That's what you do when you let philanthropic institutions settle the debts of hardworking people. It's not just about Rotterdam, because I'm standing here in front of the whole of the Netherlands. Over 2.5 million households are facing financial difficulties. That's what Nibud warns of. People can't pay the bills anymore. The little bit of savings that there was, of course, isn't there anymore. The Social and Cultural Planning Bureau also demonstrates in its stress test that more than a million people are in financial difficulties due to high energy prices. Families see the accounts double or sometimes even triple. Every day the question with them is: can I eat hot tonight? Do I have enough to pay the rent and the bills? And now it's still warm, isn't it? It's a super-beautiful summer day. But you're gonna have to figure out what it's like to be in the winter when that stove has to be turned back on. The concerns about this are already enormous. So something really needs to be done to prevent us from ending up in a tsunami of debt and misery. Lowering VAT on energy and the one-off energy surcharge are really not enough, no matter how beautiful the gesture is. It's totally inadequate. Much more needs to be done to help people who are in serious trouble. Mr. Chairman. There's just too little happening to those people's needs right now. €800 is not enough to cover the increasing costs. The target group is far and far too small. People are sinking through the ice. The lowest incomes but also the middle incomes cannot pay the bills anymore. The Labour Party finds it incomprehensible that this cabinet has chosen for the limited target group of people who earn 120% of the social minimum. Again, a philanthropic institution sees it and says: no, 120% is too little, so please do it up to 140%, otherwise those people will die. So that's gotta be wider. So come up with an extra energy surcharge for this autumn, possibly via those €500, as the PvdA and GroenLinks have already indicated. We know that this will not happen, but increase the target audience for the energy surcharge to 130%. My question to the Minister is therefore quite simply: is she prepared to do so? Mr. Chairman. There are countless poignant stories of students living in drafty homes. Students are wearing four sweaters if it's not as hot as today. They have to make additional debts to pay the energy bill, which has just risen enormously. We are talking about hundreds of euros. In the case of questions concerning the student energy allowance, the Minister refers to the individual special assistance. But apart from the fact that this doesn't make it any easier, it is also priceless for student cities to help that group of students in this way. For the city of Utrecht alone, this amounts to about 25 million euros extra. What do municipalities have to pay for that? Should they be cutting back on social services? Is that a good plan? On top of that, the exclusion of students for the energy surcharge, according to lawyers, is simply unlawful. I would therefore like to ask the Minister what justification there is for excluding students as a group. Students should be entitled to the energy surcharge as a group. This can be done via municipalities or through DUO. I'm asking the Minister to find a solution. It doesn't matter who or how it is paid out, but make sure that students aren't literally in the cold again in winter. Mr. Chairman. The rising costs of groceries, electricity and gas cause problems for people. I told you, they're getting into trouble financially. They can't pay all the bills anymore and knock on the door for debt relief. Is this Minister going to take additional measures to counter these debts? Is the Minister prepared to agree with energy companies on buying up debts? We are also getting signals that municipalities still impose all kinds of additional requirements on people for the energy surcharge. People are asked whether the energy surcharge is refused due to savings. If you are going to address these municipalities, I ask the Minister through the President. Municipalities which do receive the money for the energy surcharge but provide this supplement to a smaller target group should also be called upon. Are you willing to share an overview with the Chamber which municipalities pay the energy surcharge for which target group? I would also like to ask the Minister how she can support young people under 21 who live on their own. They cannot use the energy surcharge, but they also simply have to do with high energy prices. Their parents often can't afford this either. Mr President, concluding. Needs are high. It's gonna take more than that. Action must now be taken to keep all these families out of the water.

I can quote from one lawyer another who says it does not harm. It is the opinion of the Cabinet, as stated by many legal scholars, that it does not infringe the right and the judicial position of governments to conduct, implement and make adjustments in the public interest, for public health and so on, including the energy transition.

They must all be assessed against the criteria. Some of these six points are more obvious than others. I'm not embracing proposals right now, and I'm not rejecting anything. We come up with the criteria and then Mr Van der Lee and I can, together with that paper in front of us, try to estimate what will or will not be covered. I do not rule out anything, other than that we already know, because that has already been communicated, that it cannot be about structural or regular expenditure. There was another lesson and it is also important, because there is in a way a small distance from how we have done it so far. We realise that a greater role of government is needed, including in the direction. When managing a transition across sectors alone, the main role of the parties going through this transition is the government. Technology is also becoming more important. Other countries, continents and power blocks are shielding their technology more. That also leads us to think differently about our technology. Spatial integration is becoming a major issue. There, too, more government direction is obvious. So there's more government in the soup we're about to eat, including in the field of investment. We have to recognize, fundamentally, that in the coming decades the government will have to do more to address a number of things that we have always found public interests, but with a smaller budget, such as knowledge building and the development of research. That could also be in all kinds of new types of infrastructure. The role of a government is necessarily increasing, not because we choose ideologically, but because we see that this is necessary. I will go over these six themes in a moment, but before I get to that, perhaps a few words about that investment fund. That is not part of this debate. In the first quarter, I will try to send a letter on this with the Minister of Finance, which makes it clear how projects and investment proposals are selected, how they are judged, who they are judged and what timelines they contain. It is also important that we are already trying to honour a number of important major proposals in this cabinet period, but only if they are very good proposals. Because in all honesty: the number of proposals that have been put forward here, which I quickly added to 80 billion, shows that there is a great deal of interest. The mailbox is filling up. This means that if something is being accepted, it must also be a very good proposal; not only a good idea, but also its effect must be good. We need to set up a standard setup. We shouldn't be FES. A question has been asked about it and I will answer it separately later, but we should not fall into traps from the past. Well, that means I'm not gonna honor any projects right now, but I'm not gonna reject them either. And, of course, what this is not really about, and that is why I will not be able to answer all the questions later either: the whole discussion about the growth strategy and the discussion about the fund are not intended for today's political questions. Today's political questions must be resolved by the government, in consultation with Parliament. You can all be satisfied or not satisfied with that, but we must do so now. That's regular policy. We are now working for the generation of the next 30 years. That's about these six things, but not about some things that are going on right now. And they are no less important, they must be done now, but that is not what this debate and this letter are about. A number of questions have been asked on the six points. With that, I got myself a rather administrative job, because I wanted to pass them by at a point, and then bring up the questions that have been asked. I designed a whole flap system for it while you were talking. Look, the basis of all prosperity is knowledge, and the basis of knowledge is foundational education. That's number one for a reason. Everything starts with that. And that is not only very important for prosperity, but it is also an extremely moving thing, in which we help the youngest Dutch people get on the road in the world and prepare them to also contribute to our existence. And the quality of education in the Netherlands is good, but it is no longer top. We're going down the ladders. We have to worry about this, because if we want to be more than average wealthy, more than average stable, enjoyable, clean and so on, then we must have more than average good education; then we must have top education. All these little Dutchmen deserve that. Mr Futselaar has other ideas about this. He says, "These ideas don't add up at all." Well, these are the ideas the Cabinet is putting on, but not exclusively. There are all kinds of things in the regular policy. There are all kinds of discussions, which I do not want to serve up at all, but which were not par excellence in the econometric inventory for the next 30 years, but are therefore no less important. But that's not what this letter is about. In any case, the further development of these ideas must be carried out by the Minister of State. But it is important that there is also more tailor-made work for children in a digital learning environment. Children are used to it at home, but even less at school, and that can change. To Mr Verhoeven's question whether we are dealing with delays: more tailor-made work is one of the ways to tackle backlogs. Moreover, I think Mr Verhoeven knows that the Netherlands can be proud that it is one of the countries where the delays are being dealt with relatively well. That's the piece of talent. We need to do something about that. Without that, without a strong upgrading of it, we will not be able to achieve a higher earning capacity. Developing talent is just as important. My plumber complains that he only works with people who can install resumes, while the heat pump is still a secret. I recognise that education budgets mainly flow to those who have the longest education and that it is all concentrated at the beginning of the career. We see this has to be better. That's what we've been seeing for over ten years. Every cabinet has done things about it, including this cabinet, but a bigger step is needed. We see that very large parts of the secondary education system need more regular training in order to meet all kinds of new challenges. It's necessary. That is an economic issue. We have to take care of that. I've heard the subject come along a lot. Many economists say: we have heard you, but here we need a bigger step. Period. The third theme concerns part-time work. Mr Bruins has spoken a few harsh words about this. But in his direction: no one is being put to work by the government. As long as you don't have social security, you're on your own. But working is an extremely valuable part of life. It takes care of the usual portion with back-up and setbacks. It's a contribution that makes you matter. You gain acquaintances and knowledge. But we're in a part-time culture. That would also be okay if we would all accept the consequences of that and be happy with that position, but research shows that this is not the case. Many people who work part-time do not choose to do so and would prefer to do so differently. Those people don't do that for all kinds of reasons. Many of these reasons also have to do with childcare. That is what we must do. But once again, in the end, that's up to everyone. No additional questions have been asked about this. Oh, I do.

I certainly give you this time and I hope that in two years' time we will be able to have the debate with each other on the basis that I suggested. I hope we're gonna get that confidence together. In addition, there is the content. I also spent a lot of time on Tuesday to make industry more sustainable. In that context, I have two motions aimed at hydrogen. [[Motion]] [[The Chamber,]] [[heard the debate,]] [[noting that hydrogen contributes to meeting the climate objectives, the energy transition and strengthening the Dutch earning capacity;]] [[Whereas consideration should be given in good time to the market organisation of the hydrogen market and to safeguarding the public interest;]] [[calls on the Government to involve external experts in an investigation into the intended market organisation for the hydrogen chain;]] [[calls on the Government to inform the Court in spring 2022 of the intended market organisation for the hydrogen chain,]] [[and goes to the order of the day.]] [[This motion was tabled by Mr Erkens, Mr Boucke and Mr Bontenbal.]] [[She's getting No. kst-35925-XIII-26]]

The discussion or discussion about clear rules for purple hydrogen is also ongoing in other EU Member States, so it is useful to do so together. The purple hydrogen that we may be producing at a new Dutch nuclear power plant may also cross the border to the Belgian or German industry, so you have to agree on this internationally. Mr. Chairman. In my view, I have also answered the second-term questions. I thank the Chamber for the input.

It's a bit of a rerun of moves. I said: legal sustainability, strong guarantees I cannot give either. But unlike the PAS, there are now concrete goals that you must maintain. Unlike the PAS, the Minister then acted very well and responded to the recommendations of the Council of State. That gives us sufficient confidence that this whole package is sufficient to continue it. Mr. Chairman. I was at the quick buy-up of the peak chargers and what possibilities that gives. I have said before that the system in which you earn space before you can spend it is very appealing to us, also in the context of legal sustainability. At the same time, however, we do not want the problem of nitrogen to stop or propose other necessary activities, such as housing, infrastructure and energy transition, to make it impossible for industry to be greened. And there's tension. On my questions, the Minister states in the preliminary report that, for example, she cannot guarantee that all housing plans can continue in the coastal provinces. We are very concerned about this, because it is precisely there that it is necessary to build these houses, where the need for housing is greatest and there too we are very dependent on external sea influences. You say that you cannot guarantee that, but then there are some additional measures to be taken. Would you care to comment on that? Because we all say it in this campaign: we have to build, build, build. Mr. Chairman. If I see correctly, the development space of 20 moles per hectare must also be earned by the source measures. This means that a generic reduction of 100 to 120 moles per hectare is needed over the next 9 years to meet the 50% target. That's where the development room comes in. Can the Minister state exactly how she intends to achieve this and how big the buy-in and buy-out programme is going to be in order to achieve these objectives without the economy closing down? How does the Minister estimate that emissions are falling very slowly due to internal and external netting? It's possible. Mr. Chairman. D66 would like the commitment that economic activities aimed at the energy transition and greening of the industry that we previously approved in the Energy Agreement and the Climate Agreement will not be delayed by the nitrogen problems. The nitrogen bank should be filled in such a way that these activities can go unhindered. I'd like a response and a commitment. Finally, a few brief questions. There is no solution for microdepositions yet. The plans for a microdeposition bank can wait a while. Is it possible to work up to that time with a threshold of, for example, 0.5 mole per hectare? The court ruling on PAS also destroyed a number of land use plans. That is not, of course, on your plate, but I assume that the cabinet will think about how things are getting back on track, as this is also needed in the case of housing development, for example. Mr. Chairman. With this legislation, the Minister has started to reduce nitrogen. Moreover, a great deal of money has been allocated to strengthening nature, and that is another compliment. But to achieve the objectives, there is still a great deal to be done, and I do not think this is the last time we will talk about this dossier. I think it will be discussed again at the formation. We would like to await the Minister's reply.

I've already made clear exactly what I want. We have a legal problem. We in the Netherlands have agreed far too strict rules. The PAS would soften some of that, but it's now dead. So we need to relax those rules. We need to find a solution not in bullying farmers or in driving them away, but in relaxing the rules. You yourself come up with a proposal for a threshold, as Germany does. Fine! That's the solution. Surely we do not need a Remkes committee to come forward with worthless proposals after six months? That should have happened! The government could have done that by now. We must not let Brussels and our own beautiful sector drive us out of the country, but we must stand up for ourselves. As with fishermen, we should not be belittled by Brussels. Mr. Chairman. I'm rounding up. I'm gonna have to get a little cynical now. For it is precisely those small and medium-sized family businesses that are affected by the strict environmental rules. On the contrary, they are often close to the many Natura 2000 sites we have. They still have relatively small numbers of cattle and do not have the millions to invest in hermetically sealed industrial megassages with air scrubbers. I now show the article in The Financial Daily about the opening of the first Remkesproof stable. I believe it contains 33,000 pigs. I'll show the article to the Minister, too. It's all hermetically sealed, and it's huge numbers. This is really some kind of industry. This is bio-industry! This is Remkesproof. And this is what we get. I don't know who wants this, but we don't want this. We have a small, beautiful sector with family businesses. We don't need $20 million worth of gas that has been sealed down, with all the chance of a stable fire. Mr. Chairman. We want to support these small and medium-sized entrepreneurs. They are now so valuable to our country and our landscape, Mr. De Groot. They can maintain those beautiful wood walls and bloom all those beautiful flowery fields. This policy will once again lead to a further increase in scale. This is bad for entrepreneurs, bad for young farmers, bad for our landscape and bad for animal welfare. Mr. Chairman. I ask the cabinet to stop this poldering with the environmental fundamentalists and the people who want to talk to us about flesh shame and not listen to D66 and GroenLinks. I ask the cabinet to relax the rules on nitrogen. The Netherlands does not need to have the strictest rules in Europe. We do not need to be stricter than Germany and Belgium. We need to stand by our entrepreneurs. We really need to stand behind our farmers and cut off the excessive rules that are breaking so much. It is only when you do that that you can rightly say: we are proud of our farmers. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Mr President. It was 2017. Kraft Heinz climbed the balls at Unilever; PPG banged on the doors of Akzo from Mexico and previously América Móvil sailed like a Viking dinghy to what once was the Royal PTT. The barbarians came no further than the gate, but several established names on the AEX had a near-take-over experience. Mr. Chairman. D66 stands for progressive capitalism. Most shareholders have just as much interest in long-term value creation as companies themselves, and the purpose of a law like this should therefore not, as far as we are concerned, be to curb or dismiss shareholders as locusts. Because acquisitions can be good, through consolidation that combines knowledge, streamlines production and thus provides a better, cheaper product for the consumer. Imagine if takeovers were impossible. It can make established companies sleepy. Successful companies also need to renew, because as the world changes, the market also changes. For example, towards sustainability. A company that continues to adhere to a fossil earning model depends on a dying market, with all its risks. Shareholders often force change. I am thinking of Follow This, Shell's green shareholders, who, together with institutional investors, forced climate ambitions at Shell. But, Mr President, there is another side. Acquisitions can also create uncertainty, about maintaining jobs, about controlling vital infrastructure, but also about the possibility of restricting free competition. Sometimes this serves only the short-term interest of certain shareholders, which prevails above that of longer-term value creation. This can happen with activist parties who think they can achieve fast profits by cutting up or repairing, without an eye for the future. Isn't the Netherlands, as an open economy, too easy to prey on a continent where each country still has its own unique economic structure? And where in other European countries it is often not so easy to take over a company, by loyalty shares, by family ownership or simply by political pressure? That is why we believe it is right for the cabinet to recognise that the corona crisis also increases the chances of activist shareholders being interested. After all, recession often means consolidation. The reflection period, the cooldown period of 250 days, a product of the debate we had in 2017, may come in handy. But for most stock exchange companies it will not be necessary at all, because in a new stock exchange a company often takes up a foundation's preferred shares in the construct, as KPN also wagered against América Móvil. A recent example is CureVac, the German vaccine producer on course to produce an important corona vaccine. Donald Trump offered the company a billion dollars to go to America. And now that they're going to the stock market, they're trying to prevent the vulnerability to an opportunistic hostile takeover. This could not be done in Germany, but in the Netherlands, and so CureVac has now formally become a Dutch company with a foundation preferred shares and the reflection period in the statutes. Rather the same was true for Ferrari and Campari, a few beautiful Italian companies that have also come here, but with the construction of loyalty shares. In other words, my group is looking for a new balance here, because it is very good that CureVac can continue the work on a corona vaccine unhindered by this construction, but at the same time it cannot be the intention to build up protection structures. The reflection period comes primarily because some companies have never been able to include a protection foundation at all, or any other structure, and specifically those companies are therefore vulnerable. But the Netherlands must retain its character as an open economy. That is why the question: does the cabinet see the risk that a stacking could make the Netherlands a kind of protection paradise in Europe, in which companies choose the Netherlands because they can incorporate in statutes a mix of protection structures that make a takeover virtually unthinkable? The amendment tabled by the VVD is also in favour of this, and we will support it. In the end, we are dealing with a single internal market, and like shopping with tax rates, labour law or environmental frameworks ultimately means that most countries are worse off, as far as we are concerned. With more new companies going public in many European countries in recent years, we see the point of avoiding a race to the bottom. So my question is this: does the Minister want to prevent the Netherlands from becoming a protection paradise? Does he think it is right or not if there are more similar rules for this in the internal market? And is he also prepared to open the discussion on European business protection frameworks, even outside the vital sectors?

I would also like to ask Mr Erkens whether, in order to avoid any misunderstandings in the coming period, he realizes that after having decided to introduce this production restriction in the Netherlands because we do not make it to Urgendavonnis, Germany has launched a very ambitious Kohleausstieg programme, with a large-scale farewell to coal, including brown coal. On the basis of a court ruling, Germany has recently increased its climate ambitions to 65% CO reduction in 2030. So that fear of that wrong energy from the east is really an out-of-date station.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. I think the Minister is missing an important ethical point here. He says he's not involved in this deal because he wasn't involved in the negotiations and not in the decision. But in business and in the rest of the world, perhaps outside this minister's experience, things are very different. There's someone called the "dealmaker" or "the oil guy." He usually asks for a commission for that or a bill fairy. That's instrumental for making the deal. So the idea that you stay out of this whole deal because you weren't at the table when the signature was signed is ethically untenable. Of course, Mrs Agema had a fantastic point there. My first question to the Minister is therefore the following. 17 million Dutch people are looking at this. They think: "Well, that minister was just involved, because he was the dealmaker and without him he wouldn't have done it." Can the Minister imagine 17 million people thinking that?

I certainly didn't want to dispute that right either. I was just trying to explain what considerations the cabinet has made and what elements have been relevant to it, which we have involved. It is indeed a weighting for the students; that is correct. That is a substantive weighting, but it is actually a technical implementation. We have often talked about this with the municipalities, especially with the municipalities that have students. They very much want to be able to implement this arrangement, just for the minimums, and said: when that group grows big and when we have to check all kinds of things, for example whether they are living or living at home, it means that the execution is such that it really gets complicated. Hence the route of individual special assistance. I keep emphasising that. But you have every right... you don't, Mr. Chairman. Yes, you too, Mr President, but I mean Mr Kox has every right to make proposals here to see what else is possible. I give our reflection on that. Let's see. That was Mr Kox's question. I also referred to Mr Koffeman's question, which also asked about the students on this point. Then there was a question from Mr Crone. He asked: will there be another window for people with liquidity problems? You're on the wrong side, Mr. Crone, but I'm glad you're spreading your wings wide; let's leave it there. In general, I recognize a great deal in Mr Crone's speech, including the liquidity problems of households. We also see that group getting bigger. It's on multiple levels, I think. As has been said, for those who get into trouble very directly, there is the way to individual special assistance, but I think the question here is wider: what do you do if the energy bill is really not affordable anymore and there is a high bill at the end of the year? I am currently having this conversation with Mr Jetten and also with energy suppliers. We are looking at how we can make sure that we can meet people who are in trouble. This can be done, for example, by means of payment schemes or by means of debt relief. We are also trying to put all kinds of unorthodox measures on the table. Eventually we have to weigh things up after that, but we see the problem that it may increase by the end of the year. That process is still under way, so I will, of course, inform you as soon as we have more insight into it. Mr. Chairman. Then I come to the questions about the IO-AOW. A number of your Members, including Mr Crone and Mr Van Rooijen, have asked questions about this. I have noted that... Mr Van Rooijen is already coming forward before I have given the answer.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. When the minister just got off the plane, yes, the plane had gotten off when he came back from the Madrid climate summit, he said: "What have households been getting in their pockets for the last 20 years? Almost nothing." At the same time, however, it is the same minister of the same VVD who keeps burdening citizens with towering energy bills. Today we have a debate on climate and energy exploration. That's the name of the report. Which of the people who are sitting at home watching this debate gets better, will that help? What people really care about is affordability, or rather the pricelessness of their energy. But what do we read in the report? The evolution of the average household energy account is not included in this KEV. That is easy, while energy poverty in the Netherlands is a fact. More than 650,000 households can barely pay the energy bill to no longer. This number is likely to rise to 1.5 million households by 2030. But the minister said it wasn't so bad. Yesterday, in response to Parliamentary questions from the PVV, he wrote that "The Netherlands scores relatively well on affordability of the energy bill in a European perspective and has relatively little energy poverty." 650,000 households living in energy poverty, doesn't the Minister think so? In the climate and energy exploration is really something else. In this we see that the prices of electricity in Germany are much higher than in other European countries and in France much lower. And what's that all about? Quite simply: Germany is currently experiencing a disastrous energy turnout with windmills, solar panels and the Atomausstieg, while the French have plenty of nuclear power. Mr. Chairman. Energy is a basic requirement, but this cabinet has made it a very expensive luxury product with its very expensive energy transition and CO-obsession according to German example. Yes, Chairman, a CO-obsession. And what do we read about it in the climate and energy exploration? These CO targets are not even met, despite the many billions wasted on them. 49% in 2030 was the intention, but it is not going to work. 14% of renewable energy by 2020 was also intended, but it is not going to succeed. Expensive amateurism, that's it. But in spite of this climate change policy and the billions wasted on it, it must all be worse and even faster. See that horrible European Green Deal of climate hippie Timmermans. By 2050, the whole EU must be climate neutral. There will be a European climate law. Loading posts must be placed, trees must be planted, CO emissions must eventually go to zero and name it all. This ultimately costs EUR 260 billion per year; EUR 260 billion per year. Then the question is: how is the Minister going to prevent the energy bill of households or any other account from rising by one cent as a result of this madness at EU level? Mr. Chairman. So the climate and energy exploration, the report we are discussing today, can actually go straight through the shredder. Because all this EU climate policy, thanks to Mr Timmermans, is going to be fine. If you think that with that terrible climate agreement of Mr Nijpels and co you have had everything, well, not so. The Timmermans of this world like to do a little more on top. Mr. Chairman. There is only one conclusion that can be drawn: we must get rid of this terrible climate policy as quickly as possible. Thank you.

Exactly. This is exactly why you did not hear me say much yesterday about developing those emergency scenarios. That's the homework you have to do anyway. But what's even more important than that is that we do everything we can to prevent that, and that starts with boosters. It has to do with stepping up testing policy, it also has to do with the measures you could take as a precaution in case it comes to that. I'm gonna talk about the care capacity later. I would actually like to go further with the measures that we have to take. Maybe I should go into education briefly first. I have heard the critical sounds, and I would like to put a number of things aside. Let's look back to September and see what developments that virus has been going through, see at what time the epidemiological situation was at issue and what measures we had to take at that time, advised by the OMT, weighted and decided by the Cabinet and endorsed by the Chamber. Then I think at those moments we have taken the measures that were needed at that time, where there was one time that the measures afterwards turned out to be insufficient to actually bring the R back under 1. That was the November 12 package. It took a long time for actual results to become visible. That has brought us, as it turns out, just under one. At the time when we took stock of the question at the end of November, "is this going to be hard enough?', We didn't think it was hard enough. That is why we got past the 24 November package. This has led to a reduction in all figures. In the test streets this is most visible, but fortunately there is also a serious decrease in the number of hospitalisations and even in the occupation. That's the game against delta. We have taken measures in a number of steps when it was necessary. Had it been the case that there was no omikron variant, we would have just been in a decline that would have brought us back below the limit value in the first half of January, as we agreed with each other: the 25 ic intakes per day and 100 hospitalizations per day. Depending on the actual R-value, this would be at the beginning of January or mid-January. That was the cabinet's commitment. In this context, the advice given by the OMT in recent weeks has also been included. It was not until mid November that the Omikron variant was first detected on Dutch soil. In fact, it is only since last week that we are actually beginning to see, perhaps a week earlier, what this will mean in the European context and in the UK. That means that you have to weigh today's figures in a different way. If you didn't know about Omikron, you'd think, "Good, the figures show a decrease, so the measures have an effect. That is exactly what we wanted, because that brings us back below the limit we had set for ourselves." But we do know about omikron. We know of the potential risk of a much faster spread. We don't know so much about the disease-making ability of the virus yet, but we do know about the much faster spread, which has a lot to do with the decreasing vaccine effectiveness. This means that we need to give gas, in particular, to that point. I'm about to explain. However, it also makes it necessary to avoid that there is a catalyst for that new variant somewhere in society. Of course there is also that story about delta and about the very short connection of school week to Christmas dinner. Of course, that has also been an important point of consideration. However, the decisive point in the recital on whether or not schools are closed has been the information that has come to us over the past week and last weekend about the much faster spread. Because every brake you can apply in the introduction of Omikron, slowing down the introduction of Omikron, is probably lowering the wave we're about to face, because it gives us time to actually complete the booster campaign. That is the decisive argument. That also means that I can't go along with the question of whether you should have closed the restaurant two weeks ago, because you wouldn't have to close the schools now. I'm not going along with that, because I don't think you can think about it in that contrast. If we had closed the catering industry two weeks ago, even during the day until 5 p.m., it would not have posed any other problem at the moment with regard to education. By the way, the catering industry is already insanely limited. I think it's one of the most limited sectors during the whole corona crisis. If we had closed the Efteling, non-essential services or all those other places at the moment or in the last few weeks, it would not have allowed us any more room for consideration of education. Those were all decisions with an impact on the delta variant and we are winning that race. It's all going too slowly and the pressure on care is still very high, but we're winning that game. What we need to do is slow down the introduction of the omikron variant. We need to slow that introduction down to lower the wave of later. That is the decisive reason for education.

The Minister is right to point out that SWIFT exclusion has and can have a major impact on both Russia and Europe. Here's the thing. Mr President, thank you. I would also like to thank Mr Koffeman for his supplementary motion. Let me be honest: common consent on the one hand but also appropriate resistance on the other hand compete here in me. I will try to explain to you in as short a time as possible, one minute, why this cabinet finds that biomass restraint is in place but why I am going to discourage this motion. Biomass is inevitably part of the mix. I do not find that specific as a private opinion. That is what the IPCC and the International Energy Agency think, the parties we need to explain to the rest of the population that we need to do something about the climate. Biomass is an inevitable part of that. What is important is that that biomass is really sustainable and not, to put it bluntly, fake. If we're gonna throw primeval forests into a coal power plant, everyone understands that it's fake and not real. It is also appropriate to focus on air quality. I agree with critics, but when we talk about wood pallets in coal power stations, they are not primeval forests. Wood pallets are a very limited part of the SDE anyway. The high numbers in this motion, I can't bring home. As a biomass, we use the residual flows of the traditional timber production that has been going on for centuries. That is thinning wood, pruning waste and waste from the wood industry. That is what the Dutch sustainability framework says. So there are no primordial forests in coal power stations. We'll do the rest streams. As far as the implementation of the motion is concerned, the judgment depends on how you read it. If I read 'a proposed grant as soon as possible' in such a way that the decisions already issued should no longer be complied with and therefore we will have to stop the decisions already issued, then I must advise against the motion because this will lead to major damages claims and failure to comply with the sustainability rules. If it says here that we do not issue any new grant decisions for wood-burning in coal-fired power stations, then I will leave this motion for a resolution to the House. Bon! We are not going to issue new decisions on wood-burning in coal-fired power stations. Here's to it. With that explanation, I'll leave the motion to judge Chamber.

Mr Koerhuis talks about the fact that we have to drop strange sustainability requirements, because otherwise there will be no affordable construction. But I wonder how Mr Koerhuis looks at the affordability for the resident, who ultimately has to live in that house and who has to cough up the energy costs of a poorly isolated house.

Let me look up that piece on the independent counsel. It says, in response to the internet consultation: "The independent counsel is only competent for old damages and reinforcements, not for new damages under this law." So that's pretty clear in there. It is precisely the social parties who are very concerned about this. I think that's right. We would all like it to be superfluous here. That is absolutely not the case at the moment, no matter how much we like to believe that all these promises will come true at some point. Mr. Chairman. At present, the damage protocol annexed to the Mining Damage Decision regulates what is entitled to be harmed. It won't be in the law anymore. The Minister points to the independence of the new institute as an argument for this. But it does not harm independence in any way when we simply say that the current protocol must be the lower limit and when the new institute has all the room to change it when it benefits the injured? Then the old damage. In recent years, a lot of Groningers haven't gotten what they're entitled to. The NAM has paid thousands of Groningers far too little compensation. And now we're finally putting the NAM out of the damage settlement. But that doesn't give people who haven't been compensated enough for what they're entitled to. Finally, a small start was made in compensating for old damages. Through the temporary committee there is a hardness clause which sometimes also compensates for old damages and there would be a window for the people with old damages who had not received enough at the NAM. But from the new law that hardness clause has disappeared and the counter at the province shows, according to the GBB, an empty shell. Only a small group can go there. They have to produce evidence themselves, and the NAM is still judging. That's not a real solution. We would prefer to see all those who were underpaid by the NAM to be compensated. Each time we hear the argument that that would be too much work for too few damage experts, but actually that remains very harsh. Whatever 417 billion can be made as a State, but then can get away with the non-indemnification of all the doomed. We will support the amendments to bring the hardness clause back into the law, but the question is: how will this be implemented? Which groups will this apply to? Will this also apply, for example, to the people from the former outskirts with a Witteveen+Bo report? Mr. Chairman. Some legal aspects. Degraded Groningers have had to fight unfairly and unequally against the NAM, Shell, Exxon and the State in recent years, as I have said before. Several times this law is justified: recognizes that the position of the injured in relation to the State is unequal. In order to ensure that victims are quickly properly compensated, several lawyers and the Council propose that the case-law be given the opportunity not only to refer questions to the Supreme Administrative Court but also to the Supreme Court. Is the Minister prepared to take care of that? Mr. Chairman. Then the position of the NAM. Duplicitous people no longer have to fight the NAM, Shell and Exxon, but what about the government? The NAM cannot appeal against individual decisions, but against the tax imposed on it by the State. What are the chances they're gonna do the same? Why does NAM not have to contribute to the costs of members' remuneration and housing costs? According to the Minister, this would damage the Institute's independence. But the institute is also independent of the government, isn't it? And he'll pay the costs. How logical is it now for the whole of the Netherlands to pay for this, while the NAM is still partly responsible for the damage caused? Pay, not determine, as far as we're concerned. Why does the Institute actually fall under the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate? That is precisely the Ministry that has failed so badly in supporting the Groningers, the Ministry that time and time again thought about the economy, but not about the people and our security. Mr. Chairman. Then the position of us as representatives of the people. What about the position of us as representatives of the people and other governments? We're the controlling power, but we can't control anything too often now. Examples. For months now, the Minister has promised to give us insight into the reinforcements. We still don't have a real insight. In the past, we were shown every quarter how much money came to the victims and how much overhead was. And when the percentage that did not reach the victims reached 67%, the information was stopped. How's it going later? Do we get insights per week, per month, quarterly, and through whom? Mr. Chairman. Finally, the reinforcements. 2020 will be the year of truth. We are not having the real discussion today, but it is yet to come. This discussion has been pushed forward again, while the SodM called upon the regulator to adopt a crisis approach after the last earthquake. Damage handling and reinforcement had to be merged, they claimed. Of course, that call wasn't new at all. The United Nations has already hit the Netherlands twice. In 2015 and 2017 the Research Council for Security ruled hard on the role of both the NAM and the State. And in 2017 their call was already clear: make sure that one body is responsible for damage, for reinforcement, but also for intangible damage and loss of value. That's exactly what's not happening now. Today we talk about the damages, the law on strengthening comes later. The concept of that law is once again being judged harshly. The regulator itself reiterates that a crisis approach is not chosen. Acceleration of reinforcements is not in the law. The Gasberaad concludes that the strengthening law ruins Groningen's last chance. Residents don't get the initiative themselves. Thus the restoration of trust is abandoned, they argue. The Groninger Soil Movement is also harsh in its judgment. There are again too many parties involved, which means that there is a high risk of delay. It is deeply sad that we are not talking today about damage recovery and reinforcement. It's deeply sad that the law on reinforcements is so bad. This way, the restoration of trust will never happen. In this way a social disruption can be increased. That cannot and must not become the truth of 2020. Mr. Chairman. I'll leave it at that.

Mr. Chairman. Let me begin by thanking Mr Tjeenk Willink for his work as an informant. It is a good practice, it seems, that as soon as chaos arises in politics in The Hague, he is called upon. That is never in vain, not even this time, for which I am very grateful. The election took place seven weeks ago today. Immediately after that election, I made clear the commitment of the Labour Party. As far as we are concerned, it was and is necessary to speak first of the information for a new cabinet about the major tasks that the Netherlands is facing, about the everyday concerns of all Dutch people. This would, of course, include the fact that we are expected to do so in response to these major problems and to formulate solutions to these concerns. Seven weeks later, we have to conclude that we have actually barely gotten there. The formation is degenerate into chaos and almost came to a standstill. Trust in the Prime Minister was abandoned by the entire opposition after his role in reconnaissance. The great waiting for the radical ideas of the VVD leader to do it differently, so far is quite... What shall I say... We have been waiting a long time. Meanwhile, the Dutch are waiting for us to really do something about these everyday problems, until there really are solutions to the problems caused by the corona crisis, which have been exposed and deepened by the corona crisis. The big workload in care. Every day we ask more of the employees in the care. The great sadness that has hit our country, now that so many people are confronted with serious illness or a great loss, when they have lost people. We have seen that cooperation in healthcare works better than market forces and competition. We see the concerns of entrepreneurs, of self-employed people, of the arts and culture sector, who are in the water's mouth. The inequality is growing, and that is what it should be about now. It should also be about Dutch people who are excluded by discrimination, by institutional racism, about people who are faced with a government that is opposed to them, rather than protecting them, such as the parents who were victims of the childcare allowance scandal and the people in Groningen, who are still waiting for recovery. Are we a government that is there for them and that protects them, instead of a government that turns against them? It must also address the major issues facing the Netherlands in the coming years when it comes to correcting the great inequality. The outgoing informant proposes to do so now and also makes a number of concrete proposals, such as, as I mentioned, the restoration after corona and the strengthening of the democratic rule of law. That can count on the support of the Labour Party. But there is also a need for other issues to be addressed. The security of work and income for all people in the Netherlands. It has to be possible to find an affordable house all over the country. All children must receive good education. Loving care must be available without the people in care constantly having to work overtime. We want a viable planet with protection for our nature and a clean energy supply, and a strong position of the Netherlands in Europe and in the world. And we do want to have a new governance culture, as it is called, but what I would just like to call: a fairer and better Netherlands, where, for example, all people have access to the law. We talked about that before. Mr. Chairman. It is time for the series to end, so that we can deal less with ourselves and especially with the Netherlands, with the problems of people. It is now up to a new informant to carry out and report on a substantive review. That's what we're waiting for. Thank you.

Haste rush is rarely good! Certainly not when it comes to spending as much as EUR 20 billion, with a fundamental form of state capitalism being launched in the Netherlands. Apparently, many parties have an interest in getting to work with this EUR 20 billion green grabbelton as soon as possible. The National Growth Fund therefore seems more like a National Graai Fund, and taxpayers are again paying for it. Mr. Chairman. As every Dutchman knows, you can only spend your money once. It is precisely in this unprecedented global economic crisis, as a result of the coronavirus, that this money should have been spent on structural relief for middle-income and hard-working Dutch people in particular. More and more people are no longer able to make ends meet in the Netherlands, but we spend 20 billion on vague sustainability projects without a return target. "The hardworking Dutchman is ours," I heard a VVD senator shout in this Upper House yesterday. But forget it. The VVD gives the hard-earned tax money of the hard-working VVD-voting Dutchman to a number of old boys and former politicians, to fund their pet projects and GroenLinkse sustainability dreams. Mr. Chairman. There is much to do about the name of this fund. Is it the Wiebes fund, the Wopke-Wiebes fund, or the Wiepke fund? There is, in fact, almost more discussion about the name than about the content and the objectives. As far as our group is concerned, we should call this fund the McKinsey Fund, a theoretical study room solution, conceived on the drawing board by two former McKinsey consultants, namely Mr Wiebes and Mr Hoekstra. One of them even made it a partner at this illustrious consultancy firm. The other was the architect of the fees-wretched as Secretary of State for Finance. As Minister of Economic Affairs, he is the man who wants us off the gas and concluded an expensive Climate Agreement, for which the hard-working, tax-paying Dutchman can take the fall again. Such a consultant-student room solution is now reflected in the design of this National Growth Fund. We see a consultant approach that looks nice on paper, but the question remains as to what will become of it in practice. The consultants Wiebes and Hoekstra come with a roaring presentation and big plans; others are allowed to carry out the plans. Our group has repeatedly warned of the risks of this chosen approach. Mr. Chairman. We were pleased in that, and not by the least. Former Finance Minister Onno Ruding, also CDA member of Minister Hoekstra's party, said in Het Financieele Dagblad: "If you think it's important to spend money on something, you have to include it in the budget. Then you get a fair balance: how much priority is it really? Such a fund soon becomes a big grabbyton. When someone suddenly comes running in with a big bucket of money, everyone comes in like locusts. That's the way it is in politics." But also Sweer van Wijnbergen, former secretary-general of the Ministry of Economic Affairs of Minister Wiebes, and professor of economics at the UvA, warned extensively in an article in NRC Handelsblad with the ominous headline: "Don't let them throw away 20 billion." I quote Sweer van Wijnbergen on the Wopke-Wiebes fund. "The (...) name arose as a result of a childish quarrel over who first put forward this bright idea. Whoever came up with it, we don't know, but we know it's an exceptionally bad plan." Thus top economist Van Wijnbergen. Van Wijnbergen, like our group, is also very concerned about the selection of investment projects. I quote: "The only further test after lobbying companies arrive with projects is (...) a typical polder advisory committee (...) full of more or less large names but without relevant expertise............................................................................................................................................................................................................................................. These are not my words; those are the words of Mr Wiebes' former Secretary-General of the Ministry of Economic Affairs, Mr Van Wijnbergen. Our group shares this sharp analysis of the former Secretary-General. Mr. Chairman. Last year, we held a wide-ranging debate in the First Chamber on the 2.5 billion euros that the cabinet made available to a similar investment fund of former Finance Minister Wouter Bos. This fund is called Invest-NL. Mr Van Ballekom also referred to it. I looked back this morning on my first term of the debate on Invest-NL, on 12 November 2019. Many of the objections I raised there against Invest-NL apply mutatis mutandis and to a greater extent to the National Growth Fund. Only the National Growth Fund is ten times bigger. Invest-NL was launched big, under the motto: impact investment. The impact is limited, as far as we can see now, especially to creating a large staff of 50 people and a lot of overhead. My question to both ministers is therefore: what has the Invest-NL investment fund invested in over the past year? What activities and amounts are involved? Invest-NL was sold to us to solve market failures. The Ministers were not able to explain to us exactly how they were supposed to do this at the time. The National Growth Fund is now going to do so on a ten-fold scale. It invests in such things as "knowledge developments, research, development and innovation, and infrastructure." Of course, all this happens with efficient CO pricing and to increase our earning capacity. My question to both ministers is: how is that earning capacity measured before you invest these billions? Such decisions are surrounded by enormous uncertainty. My question to the rulers is: how is it dealt with in concrete terms? How can the cabinet ensure that the billions here do not disappear like snow before the sun in the pockets of sustainability illusionists, who naturally preach the managers of the billions of dollars that the taxpayer has coughed up to eat out of the billion-dollar dungeon? Mr. Chairman. I'm rounding up. It is clear that we do not see this National Growth Fund in its present form and fear that it will eventually end in a walhalla for consultants and sustainability illusionists, and in a tear trap for future generations. We therefore want an emergency brake to be added to this National Growth Fund, as with the 750 billion EU Restoration Fund. But that must be an emergency brake which, unlike the emergency brake of the EU Restoration Fund, actually works. That is why we are tabling the next motion. I've already said it might not have been necessary for me to have a law, but that's where it is now. If that's what's needed and if that's comforting, then that's fine. With this prospect, everyone can now concentrate on these new municipalities and on all the challenges and tasks ahead of them. We all know, also from other reclassifications, that at first there will be some energy in merging. It is necessary to be able to look ahead, to see the dot on the horizon, and I am confident that it will succeed.

The law is about energy prices, and that's what I was talking about. I also want to go back to September last year. Then there was also a report, from TNO, that mapped out what at that time was the group of people in the Netherlands who already had to do with energy poverty. This showed that this group is concentrated among the people who have either a welfare or a bald AOW benefit. In fact, 80% of the 550,000 people were in the picture at the time. Seventy-five percent of them were hired. What happened next is that on Prinsjesdag a compensation package was agreed by the coalition, with much of it going back to people with often higher incomes. That was then repeated in March, in the package we are discussing today. Last Monday, with the CPB, we reviewed his report on the scenarios for the future. It looks ahead, while TNO looked back at what was the situation at the time. In this we see that the problems are really concentrated in the group that I and TNO mentioned earlier, the group up to 120% wml of the group between 120% and modal and a part of the group from modal to one and a half modes. The people up there can take care of themselves. They have sufficient income or sufficient reserves. Yet, in two packages, unfocused, 6 billion has been spent. This money comes to a large extent from the people who earn more than one and a half times the average. That's really problematic. I therefore hope that, in the future of the debate on the Spring Paper, it will become three times the charm. We have missed twice the opportunity to target large amounts of money, so let's do it once again, this year, to really meet the people who have the hardest. I understand that the VVD would like to have the assurance that companies will fully pass on their VAT and excise duty reductions to citizens, but of course they will not get them. That's where money leaks; we know that. It is not just the energy producers who make windfall profits. We see high inflation and rising prices everywhere that companies pass on more than necessary prices to citizens. Suppose it is not technically possible to set up a solidarity levy. Yesterday, the Secretary of State said a number of things about this: you will soon find yourself in discussions on state aid. He specifically talked about the mining tax, whether compared to England or not, because then you have more to do with locational climate. If all that is going on, I am not thinking of increasing the Vpb a little bit, to ensure that we can give a sum in hard euros this year to at least the people who are going to be able to get around this year.

Following on from Mr Schalk's question, I would like to ask an almost similar question. On the one hand, it concerns the high-quality biomass needed for the glass industry. On the other hand, we are talking about 30% of coal plants where there is probably no need to add high-quality biomass. That's two different things, isn't it? Surely one cannot lift or compensate the other?

Mr. Chairman, I'm coming to my next motion. It's about geothermals. We believe that this is very important, and we also want to speed it up. The problem is at another point. I would also like to ask the cabinet what is the situation with regard to this basic readiness if, for example, we get that question about Hormuz. Can we send a ship at all? Is a ship basic, but also mission-ready? For example, can they handle a place as dangerous as Hormuz? If we ever get that question again, for example from Europe, can we send a ship at all? In fact, I do not see anything in the budget about the development on the Russian side. Why is nothing written about the Russian side, when the Russian side has invested greatly and is also getting much stronger? Mr. Chairman. NATO expects the allies to have a national plan to reach 2% by 2024. The Netherlands, through the Prime Minister, has also submitted such a plan. A good first start has been made with the Spring Paper. There's gonna be money for nine F-35s, special forces, cyber and personnel. But that's not nearly enough. NATO is asking for much more: for more firepower at sea, on land and in the air. On 4 December there will be a NATO summit in London on the occasion of the 70th anniversary of the alliance. What is our cabinet going to say there to show that we also want to get that 2%? After all, we say in the budget that we are not achieving that 2%, but there is no justification for that. It doesn't say that we're actually not okay with that either, or how we're gonna do it eventually. The CDA calls on the cabinet to shape that national plan and would like to see how we are working on it, also towards the re-evaluation of next year. I say this all the more so now that serious problems are being exposed. For example, at the moment, defence has not allocated funds for the implementation of the operational energy strategy. The financial consequences are yet to be seen, with a budget under pressure. Even more worrying is the state of the real estate. I really want to make that a very important point. It hangs like a millstone around the neck of Defense, because after years of austerity, I also say to Mr Öztürk, we have neglected maintenance. A huge catch-up is necessary. The CDA saw in the staff note that there is a deficit of about 6 billion euros in the coming years. Is this true? 'Cause that's quite a corpse out of the closet, you'd say. Already, the Department of Defense is forced to take money away from equipment to close the worst gaps. For example, the LC fregates have been postponed for no less than five years. That's not good for our Navy industry again. The CDA sees a further balding of the equipment in the prospect. We find this extremely undesirable. I'd like to have a reaction to that. What is the government's view of the climate funds, which it pays out every year, about 300 million; exactly what we lack every year, to spend as much as possible in the state real estate? After all, the aim of the climate funds was to make the state real estate more sustainable. That's what we want. That is an objective of all of us. If we can solve a major problem in the Defense Department directly by making state real estate sustainable, isn't that a solution to the problem? If the cabinet feels strengthened when we as a Chamber make a ruling on this matter, then I am prepared to table a motion for this plan in the second instance. Mr. Chairman. The CDA is concerned about delays in major projects, first of all ICT. That's not gonna make any sense. They're gonna ask for a reprieve for that again. We fully understand good research, but we do need ICT and it will not be cheaper. How much longer do we have to wait for that? The decision on the Marine barracks has been made. But when can we expect implementation? When will that decision be implemented? Flessingen waits, but also Doorn waits, because they also want to go through. The decision on the submarines is not taken either. This also takes longer and longer. Because these frigates have also been delayed for five years, it is becoming increasingly difficult to maintain an independent, self-developing, autonomous naval construction in the Netherlands. Because we can't just do that with those four frigates that we can build, while we postpone everything else. That's a real danger to me. The discussion is not only that we want the best boat for the best price, but also how we maintain the naval construction in the Netherlands. My supporter Hanke Bruins Slot has always been very clear about that. She has tabled motions for resolutions on this matter. We want speed at that point. When can we make that choice? How much information does the cabinet want to ask for at all? And what are they missing from information that doesn't make it possible to make a decision yet? Parties that will be disappointed because they are not allowed to do so will continue to be disappointed if we wait for the message of postponement. However, the delay will weaken the winner of the tender, as he will have to wait longer and longer with the investment. Let's see. I've got a few more minutes, so I'm gonna end up with this. The recalibrate is very important. We are very much looking forward to that, because that is where we will have to show what Defence is really worth to us. If the armed forces are worth anything to us, if security is worth anything to us, and if the protection of our homeland is worth anything to us, then we will have to make that choice. Whatever choice we make, there's gonna have to be money. I would ask the parties to take this into account in their programmes for the next elections. We cannot allow this basic task of the government to be lost for €1.75 a day. Finally. Last sentence, Chairman. The CDA Group Chamber was once a ministerial chamber in the last century, where weekly cabinet meetings were held. That was the reason that above the four doors the four main tasks of the government were painted and written out: spiritual development, physical development, legislation and, Mr. Chairman,... Defence.

I honestly don't know. My first impression would be... There has been a debate in Europe about the ESF and the European Globalisation Fund, the EGF, where there is additional scope for labour market transitions. Think about the energy transition and that sort of thing. A demographic transition could also be part of that. But I'm gonna check this out for you for the second term, because I don't have this ready.

However, I have not yet received an answer to my question. You can blame me for anything, and you can do it. But if, after that introduction, you answer my question, we will get on with it. What are you doing with the coal fund? What are you doing with that shift from the ODE? What are you doing with the energy tax cut? What are you gonna do with that? Are you going to vote for it or are you going to vote against it?

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Given the time, I'm filing two motions immediately.
