Mr. Chairman. I say to the cabinet: do not lose sight of business. Because the reduction in corporate tax is being postponed. Construction and earthmoving companies struggle with unworkable pfas policies. Why didn't the Department of Control stop this? Then I'm talking about the Ministry of Economic Affairs. Companies in the food industry and greenhouse horticulture are facing enormous burdens by increasing energy taxes. In short, where is the government's commitment to our business? Because it's still the case: no jobs without companies. Mr. Chairman. Many companies have to deal with procurement policies. Very often unreasonable conditions are imposed or procedures are not properly followed. Most procurement services do have a complaint counter, but that very often does not work well. Many entrepreneurs do not dare to complain because they are afraid to miss follow-up assignments. If they do, there is a good chance that they will not respond until the tender has been completed. Businesses argue for better legal protection in the form of a procurement authority, for example under the wings of the competition authority ACM. The Secretary of State has not yet given any thought to this, but I would ask her to move on in this area. Mr. Chairman. As I have just said, the SGP is concerned about the impact of energy taxes on companies. I note that the burden increases are mainly on the shoulders of greenhouse farms and other non-industrial large consumers, and on the shoulders of smaller industrial companies. I tabled an amendment to the Tax Plan last week. Unfortunately that was only supported by the PVV, but who knows there will be new insights. The Dutch food industry, for example, pays five times more ODE tax per tonne of CO than I call a company called Shell's refinery. Large industrial companies are exempt from energy taxation through voluntary agreements; the smaller ones are not. The cabinet is now shielding with extra money from the SDE++ for industry, but what are the chances that large industrial companies will run away with the money? Where is the previously promised SME test under the Climate Agreement? My question to the Minister is whether he is prepared to identify what all these increases mean for the different sectors. The real question is: is there still fair burden-sharing? Mr. Chairman. From local authorities we get a lot of signals that the speed with which regional energy strategies are nurtured will be at the expense of gaining support and at the expense of democratic decision-making. I indicated that in the event of an interruption towards the VVD. At least there's no time for residents' meetings. That while it has a huge impact on people's living environment. The expression is still: runners are killers. I would like to say: care above speed. Mr. Chairman. The municipality of Groningen is at the forefront of the designation of natural gas-free districts. I can imagine that there, too. But the municipality is now putting plans in the refrigerator because it lacks 3 million euros for its implementation capacity. If you calculate that on the back of a beer skin, you'd say we're talking roughly 1 billion, which is 3 million times 355 municipalities. I admit that this is a very rough calculation. In the Municipal Fund, EUR 70 million have now been made available once for the RES route and the natural gas-free neighbourhoods. According to the Climate Agreement, the municipality should receive at least 150 million. My question is: how about that? And above all: how is the cabinet going to ensure that municipalities are able to fulfil their heroic role? Mr. Chairman. Then there is the energy saving. As a SGP, we have been committed to this for years. I note that the RES pathways focus on renewable energy production. Of course, that is very good in itself, but energy saving remains rather underexposed, while I think there is a lot of potential in it. Several regions are struggling with these sustainable energy challenges. I would say: give them room to use extra energy savings instead of extra wind farms. In the built environment, so-called Energy Service Companies, in plain Dutch, can play an important role, not only for households but also for entrepreneurs. But there is one problem: the lack of proper guarantee schemes. My question to the Minister is whether he cannot ensure that these energy service providers can also use the SME guarantee credit. Mr. Chairman. I can see the Minister's eyes. He's thinking, "When's he gonna come up with it?" But it's coming. The electricity grid is under great pressure. Several renewable energy projects cannot be connected while we are only at the beginning of the energy transition. Network management tariffs will increase significantly in this respect. And here he comes, here he comes: we have argued earlier for the stress tests for the energy system. My question is: when are they really coming? Look! I made the Minister happy. Now he can formulate a very sharp answer to that. Mr. Chairman. The cabinet also struggles with nitrogen and CO. That's what we're struggling with all over the country. In this respect, unorthodox measures are not shy. I think so, too. But I would like to add one more, namely to reduce the number of Sunday shopping days. More and more municipalities allow shopkeepers the free rein, at the expense of Sunday rest, small shopkeepers and employees. Emissions of an estimated 1 megaton of CO and nitrogen are also at the expense of the environment. Mr. Chairman. I say, let Sunday be a day of reflection and family instead of a day of commerce. As my colleague Mr Bruins said earlier, the beautiful gift of free Sunday is in several respects very good for everyone in our society. My question to the Minister is therefore whether he will at least look at what the possible elimination of Sunday shopping could bring in environmental gains. If you want to take the remaining Urgenda quote of 2 megatons of CO seriously, look at these kinds of measures. Mr. Chairman. I'm a little disappointed by my colleague from D66, who's gone now. Last year he talked a lot about the Sunday shop opening obligation. Anyway, we tabled a fine motion on that at the time. I'm actually waiting a lot for the law against mandatory shopping on Sundays. My question to the Secretary of State is when that law comes to the Chamber. Mr. Chairman. Finally, climate ambitions. I'm gonna go over my time with that, but I'm not gonna do a second term tomorrow, so I'm gonna use that last minute. The SGP believes that the cabinet is too distracted by all kinds of predictions and climate objectives. Yeah, I really do. There will be a new set of measures to reach exactly 25% next year instead of 23% CO reduction. The cabinet also wants extra action because we are about to miss 14% of renewable energy production by 2020. The Minister also writes that the cabinet is determined.I understand that in order to achieve the 49% CO2 reduction by 2030, and also that the challenges of the Climate Agreement will have to be increased if market fluctuations are to change estimates. I fear that this mop policy will be at the expense of consistency and support. So I would say less strife and more realism. 'Cause you better have one sunboiler in the attic than ten on paper. Thank you.

Yeah, I think so, too. Kind of exciting, but I'm sure it's gonna be okay. Mr. Chairman. We're in the National Climate Week. We just had Climate Day. Monday was the day of the Climate Agreement. The international climate summit in Glasgow is going on. You can't open a newspaper, you can't turn on a transmitter, and it's about climate. Climate is the subject of our time, and I think quite rightly. We have all seen the misery that the people of Limburg have suffered from the floods and the terrible consequences, with deaths, for our neighbouring countries. Science is clear: climate change is going extremely fast and man is clearly the cause. In addition, the heavy rainfall that caused those floods last summer has become more likely due to this climate change. By taking responsibility now, we can ensure that we leave our country and the planet in a good way for generations after us, so that we have not only increased the risks. Several Members of Parliament who said that climate change does not end at our borders and that only a change in the Netherlands will not make a global difference are, of course, quite right. For example, Mr Eerdmans talked about China's emissions, compared to what we are doing here in the Netherlands. I understand these comments very well. Although a country such as China can and must do much more in this context, the fact that China has recently set stricter climate targets and plans not to co-finance coal plants abroad is a step in the right direction. I will go to Glasgow myself on Monday and I am encouraged by Mr Eerdmans and, of course, colleagues to continue calling on other countries to provide their fair share. The only way to get the rest of the world is to join forces with our neighbours, in our case Europe, as a small country. The way to get our neighbours, Europe, to join us is by showing ourselves that we are willing to do what is necessary. Luckily, we can do that. We see a common target of 55% in Europe, but we also see good cooperation between the countries. In this context, Mr Erkens had a question. He asked about the possibilities for joint hydrogen production in the North Sea with our neighbouring countries. I think Mr Erkens has a very good point. In the future, energy production in the North Sea will be strongly interlinked internationally. We are already working with the surrounding countries. This year, for example, Germany and Denmark are looking at the intentions for cooperation. The cabinet, together with Denmark, is investigating what an energy hub between several countries can look like. Hydrogen production is also part of this research. I expect this to be completed in December, and then, of course, the Chamber will be informed. That is what I am saying to Mr Erkens and to those Members who had questions about it. As promised earlier, I will also send a letter to your Chamber in December on the government's hydrogen plans, in which I will also address my vision for the market organisation for hydrogen. So that's what's coming. I will also deal with the way in which public interests are protected; that was also a question from Mr Erkens.

The Hermans motion also included 500 million for a lower energy bill. This concerns 375 million for an increase in the tax relief energy tax and a reduction in the ODE on electricity in the first disc, and 125 million for a reduction in the ODE on electricity in the second and third discs. That's literally in the motion. If more needs to be done in the short term, I am very curious about how the cabinet is dealing with this, because at the moment the cabinet is looking closely at how the energy price is developing. The problem seems to be getting bigger and worse from day to day. This is, of course, due to a geopolitical cause at the moment, namely that Putin is holding the gas tap very well and not opening it wide. Whether this is a structural or a short-term issue, we need to look at it. Looks like a short-term issue. Then it also seems logical to me that the government should look in the short term to see if another step is needed for the energy bill. Structurally, this Chamber decided two weeks ago to lower the energy bill, especially via the electricity route. This is not only good for dampening the huge rise in energy prices, but also an incentive to electrify.

By making use of what we all sometimes find very complicated, namely that there are 19 groups in the Chamber. But the strength of Dutch democracy is also that there are nineteen groups in the Chamber which will all bring aspects of this policy and its impact on people into the discussion. It is then up to the government to make a proper weighting and try to achieve a parliamentary majority. Because there must indeed be a future for farmers in the Netherlands. There must be a future for people not to live in the shadow of a windmill. It is inevitable that there will be windmills, but you must do so in such a way that there is as much support for this as possible; I discussed this with Mr Eerdmans earlier today. So it's a smart energy mix. All these decisions will have to be taken in the coming years, but what is very helpful is that we do so in a strong economy, with a favourable economic boom. I think that's what's really gonna make us suffer with each other.

When I hear the minister talk like that, I think: did the new reality get through to him? Putin even threatened to shut down the gas tap this afternoon. So we're in a completely different world in which these plans and this beautiful weather planning were conceived. Build two nuclear power stations, I hear the Minister say. Then I ask the Minister when he thinks that if he gives extra gas there, then gas on the nuclear power stations is not electricity coming from those nuclear power stations. Then we're at least ten years away, optimistic. We are now in a very different situation in the short term. I still miss the sense of urgency to do something about it quickly. Those coal plants are state-of-the-art. These were built at the time at the request of your party colleague Brinkhorst.

Then you say very bravely "ten minutes" and then there turns out to be quite a shitty pile of motions. Fortunately, they were all meant as encouragement, so that makes it easier. Here I go. The motion in part No. 1008 is about no compulsion in natural gas-free. This encouragement I must advise against. I have explained that there is ultimately a trade-off between sustainability, freedom of choice and efficiency in the use of public money. You can't promise at the end of the day that you can do it without coercion. Of course, that's not the starting point, but I said that you can't just wait for the last car. That's just the way it is. So I'm not suggesting this motion. Then the motion to part No. 1009, which asks the government to give priority to Dutch manufacturers when granting subsidies for sunshine on rooftops. This is contrary to European regulations, so I advise against it. Then the motion to part No. 1010. That is a fairly similar motion, namely no compulsion in the case of natural gas-free. I advise against it for the same reason I have just mentioned. Then the motion to part No. 1011 to immediately stop the Natural Gas Free Neighbourhoods Programme. Well, we're not gonna do that. We will of course continue to develop, because we want to move towards a district-oriented approach within the Acceleration Sustainability programme built environment. Everything we already do in the Natural Gas Free Districts Programme is really going into that. I explained that. I dissuade this motion for that reason. Then the motion to part No. 1012 to investigate the place construction stored carbon has in the policy for the sustainability of the built environment. I would like to leave this to the House, provided that you come up with a Dutch word for construction stored carbon. I think Mrs van der Plas would agree with that.

Here too, I am actually saying that we should talk about everything, including the proposals which I appreciate come only from the Labour Party. That's no problem at all. The only warning I give is that as a Chamber, not just Mr Asscher, we should be careful with the ease with which we say 'we charge companies and we give them to citizens', because that is the reality that what we levy at companies often falls down on citizens and that the people who actually pay that high energy bill now have to have jobs. It also makes no sense to reduce the energy bill by a tenner if people have then lost their jobs. That's the choice we have to make.

Mr. Chairman. The VVD and this Prime Minister have actually been held hostage by GroenLinks from today or yesterday; I said that in an interruption. I was once this Prime Minister's mentor. I sincerely wonder: when did it ever go wrong with that man? He was someone Wilder's mentor, and now he's in bed with GroenLinks. That can't be good, Mr. Chairman. All madness on a stick, of course, it has to be quite different. We must stop lying and cheating and promising things to the voters just before the elections, when it is completely unclear whether, when and how it is being observed. We must not let these climate plans, which cost a lot and cost a lot of energy, continue. And all those billions that cost those plans, we have to spend on other things, such as care and tax cuts. And we need to get rid of this cabinet. Let me summarize my second term. I put all that in motion, too. Mr. Chairman. The world is on fire, literally in all places, as a result of the climate crisis, but also of politics. Look at Chile, Lebanon, Iraq, Hong Kong and France, but also the teachers in our own country. Tens of millions of people worldwide are on their feet to raise their voices, for freedom and human rights and against exploitation, inequality, corrupt elites and neoliberalism, which has been breaking down achievements for decades for the benefit of an ever smaller cabal of super rich people. We must not allow ourselves to be infected by authoritarian, oppressive leaders such as Bolsonaro, Bin Salman, Erdogan, Putin, Maduro and Al-Sisi to embrace and legitimize. Or by blindly chasing Trump or NATO. More of the same is not the solution, the fight for universal human rights and the strengthening of democracy, the democratization of the economy and the fight against inequality all the more. The solution will come from the bottom up, through the joint fight for social justice, for everyone, worldwide, through the fight for democracy, for socialism, for a policy that works for many, not for some. Mr. Chairman. In Chile, millions of people are opposed to neoliberal policies and repression by the state apparatus. What does the Minister think of this development? Last Sunday evening we saw the most horrible images from Bolivia. That's where President Morales was forced to leave by military forces. A coup was committed, after which horrific violence was used by opposition militias, army and police. Is the Minister judging this? Since October, more than 300 demonstrators have been killed in Iraq and 15,000 have been injured. It is brutal repression of a population that rightly criticises a government that is not functioning, a government that is making billions of dollars in oil exports and supported by the West. The population is also tired of the foreign interference of anyone. Amnesty International calls it excessive violence "a massacre." I ask the Minister to condemn this violence against demonstrators in clear language and to call for independent investigation. Is that what he wants to do? Mr. Chairman. The West did not want to prevent Turkey's long-announced illegal military intervention in northern Syria. Worse still, even after President Trump and President Erdogan made an equally dirty and treacherous deal after which the war broke out, serious measures were not taken. It is extremely painful and it reveals that interests take precedence over important values and exalted principles that the West claims to represent. Meanwhile, Syrians are driven out of their homes and killed by Turkey and their Islamic militias. It's the world upside down. What values are we talking about again? Why was an arms embargo imposed on Turkey not long before Syria was invaded? Why has this Minister put our proposals aside over and over again? Money had to be made. Turkey is a big spear and still an important NATO ally, we heard the Prime Minister say. Now there is an arms embargo, sort of. Not from the EU, because it was too divided, but from a number of EU countries, including the Netherlands. Of course that's very good. It would also be too absurd for words if weapons could still be sold to Turkey today. That is why I ask the Minister to assure us that no Dutch weapon will be delivered to Turkey as long as Northern Syria is occupied. I also ask the Minister to look back at all those times when calls for arms embargoes were not recommended. Without having the illusion that history would necessarily have gone very differently, I would ask the Minister what he thinks of that. An arms embargo, even for existing contracts, is actually just a beginning of a reaction. It's gonna take a lot more than that. To this end, Parliament has been called upon to do so, reminding the Marijnis motion which calls on the government to seek personalised economic and diplomatic sanctions with like-minded other EU countries. In the debate on this subject, it was stressed that the cabinet cannot hide behind a lack of unanimity within the EU. Can the Minister explain how he is carrying out this motion? Are there countries with which the Netherlands is in line and with which a set of sanctions can be agreed? I would like to receive a response from the Minister, a response in which he does not directly shoot into the 'can not' reflex, which was rightly criticised by the coalition last month. Mr. Chairman. Turkey has announced that it will send IS fighters to the countries of origin. The Syrian Democratic Forces in Northeast Syria want to send the children to the countries of origin, with the mothers with them. My question to the Minister is: what are the facts? And above all, what are the Minister's plans now? Is the Minister also prepared to hold talks with the Syrian Democratic Council in northern Syria? Mr. Chairman. The invasion of NATO alliance Turkey in Syria is yet another proof that NATO is in crisis. NATO does not appear to be able to call a member to order and force himself to abide by supposed principles of the alliance, such as the non-performance of an act of aggression. This is in addition to NATO's attitude in the conflict with Russia, which, through continuous expansion and militarisation of the border area itself, also contributes to escalation. Another crisis phenomenon is the NATO war in Afghanistan, where a lost battle has been sustained for eighteen years, in my view only to prevent loss of face. And then I have not even mentioned the demand that as much as 2% of our income be spent on war, while our teachers cannot even count on a decent wage. And what about the nuclear weapon file? Instead of disarmament, it is aimed at a billion euros of devouring modernisation, which makes it even easier to use nuclear weapons precisely. And then there are the statements made by the French President Macron. After Trump had previously called NATO "unneeded," Macron now calls the alliance "brain death." In his view, European countries can no longer rely on NATO and the United States for their security. That's true, of course, although he comes to this insight very late. I do not rule out the fact that future historians will have to establish that NATO and the US have not worked in the interests of our security since the fall of the Wall exactly 30 years ago. Of course, the list of crises is much longer, but I think my point is clear. I ask the Minister to reflect on the NATO crisis. Does he see the gravity of the case? Does he recognize there's been a crisis? Does the Minister see any possibility of investigating alternatives to NATO? What are the possibilities of creating a new security architecture capable of defending Europe but not itself contributing to greater insecurity? Or does the Minister accept the status quo? I thought that Mr Koopmans now feels that this is a natural moment to ask a question.

I agree from A to Z with what Mrs Kröger says about the impact that such words have on her, on me, on all of us. I understand the words, too. I'd be done with it myself if I lived there and it went this way. We all have to feel responsible for that, and I'm sure of it. There's no discussion about that. That falls into three parts. I told you, that backup needs to go faster. The damage repair is fairly steamy, I think. And the gas production has to go back to zero. That seemed pretty steamy. There is now a very nasty kink in the cable, which means that from a extraction level you may end up at more than 3 on more than 7. This is due to two factors. That's because of the nitrogen plant that's coming off too slow. I think that is a statement that I can explain to Groningers. It can happen, also due to corona and licensing issues, that such a thing can take longer. That can happen on its own. It's awfully miserable when that happens, with all the mistrust that's already there, but I still think that's explainable. Of course, that German contract is in my throat too. We're looking at what we can do about it.

What the Minister is saying here, I would like to make a slight adjustment. First of all, on the climate agreement. It says that 800,000 people are about to switch to a heat grid. This is indeed intended as an alternative to gas, in addition to the heat pump, for all those people who do not have a suitable home to prepare for a heat pump. So it is meant as a way of getting rid of the gas.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The new Secretary of State for Finance has indicated in general consultation that it may be wise not to always have the right of veto on the table if you want to achieve something and if you want to move forward with international measures. This applies in this case to energy taxation, but I think that also applies to tax avoidance. I think that's progress. I would like to commend the Secretary of State for doing so. I also hope that the coalition will allow him the opportunity to live up to that with his European international experience, and that we will not soon be able to get him to be flogged back in a converging fashion, I fear, frankly, and that he will not be able to go any further. I hope that we will be able to act in those discussions on taxing polluting behaviour, but also on tax avoidance and taxing large multinationals such as Europe and not just as the Netherlands. Thank you.

Mr. Chairman. We started the general consultation from the Christian Union with the observation that it is good news that the gas tap is closing faster than expected, in 2022, and that we are already going to 12 billion cubic metres next year. Fantastic. At the same time, there are many concerns with the people in Groningen. Will the backup still go on? How's the security of my apartment? I am therefore pleased to hear that the Minister has made a firm commitment to continue the programme. I would like him to repeat that again in plenary today. Mr. Chairman. I don't have any motions of my own today. However, I have co-signed a number of motions, including those by Mr Nijboer on the characteristic image-defining buildings. My group has been lobbying for this for a long time to allow Groningen to be Groningen. I would like to make two comments, first of all on the 90 million compensation. A lot has already been said about this by other people. My group, too, finds itself extremely unhappy and then I still express myself mildly. At the same time, the importance of the people in Groningen is paramount, as is their safety. If that amount is needed, I think this is a step that needs to be taken. Anyway, it's extremely uncomfortable. The other point is the news that came out today about a report of a consultation between the Ministry, the National Coordinator and the NAM. If the coverage is correct, there seems to have been blackmail. I look forward very much to the Minister's letter. I also welcome the fact that a hearing has been requested so that we, as a Chamber, can have more insight into how these talks are being conducted. This cannot and must not happen in this way. Talks are still taking place, even towards the future, and I really hope that we can send out a strong signal with each other that this will not be accepted. Thank you.

I agree with Mr Van Strien that energy poverty in the Netherlands is a very big problem and that families affected by it have not been helped sufficiently in recent years. Why is that? We have not had enough climate and energy policy in recent years. If you want the green transition and the social transition to coincide, we should of course have been working for a long time in those poor rental homes, to make them sustainable, to isolate them, to provide solar panels, so that people don't live in a drafty home, but in a pleasant house with a lower energy bill. So I think it is also our duty to ensure that the green transition is a social transition. Then it's just helping to speed things up.

So I understand that these are all new studies, that the previous studies are unnecessary or not included in this respect, or that at least they are not enough to say that we are going to put these subsidies into real renewable energy.

Apart from the question of whether I should act as a passing-through door, I think that we should monitor, including as regards scientific insights. I said in an earlier debate, and I underline what Mr Futselaar said: we must base ourselves on the views of the scientific institutes, but science can sometimes be sidelined or new insights. Scientifically proven that the extraction of gas in Groningen could happen safely and at some point that scientific insight has changed a bit. I very much agree with Mr Graus that we should continue to monitor developments and that we should also seek dialogue with those who have other insights.

Very often the word 'crisis approach' falls because it was also used by the Ombudsman, I believe, and rather by the Court of Auditors. Part of the crisis approach is to strengthen and bring damage politically into one hand. That is what has happened, namely in the hands of this Secretary of State. A second important part of the crisis approach is what I mentioned earlier, that one-house-one-plan idea. I'm just gonna walk by. Mrs Beckerman asked about people who have not been compensated by the NAM. I've asked the IMG to allow the re-evaluation. They're working on that now, and as soon as I have concrete data, I'll report it to you. I've discussed the contours. Mr Van Wijngaarden asked about damage to dungeons. The IMG compensates for damage to manure cellars as of September 2021 and has started a special scheme. The IMG determines its own course of action and has obtained expert advice. On the basis of this information, the follow-up damage to farmers will be reimbursed. I will check on Mr Van Wijngaarden's signal on my next visit to Groningen to see if that goes well. Mr Nijboer asked a rather fundamental question, which again has to do with the one-stop shop: is it not because it is two different organisations? Yeah, I think so. I think that's part of the problem. But I'm also afraid that if I try hard now to merge two organizations with a totally different corporate culture, anyone who's been with the organisations will recognize that, we'll be running late. I am going to try to put something over it with this one-stop-shop idea and so on, so that you still function as one organisation. Mrs Beckerman referred to a deadline of 15 months. The letter to IMG states a maximum time limit. In practice, IMG's aim is to do so within six months. That works in the majority of cases. I agree with Mrs Beckerman that it should not be the case that IMG imposes more time limits on itself than it allows residents. I mentioned communication. I just said I'd come back to the suspicion of evidence when I come back to Grab Church. Then I'll take Norg with me right away. Mr Van Wijngaarden asked about the housing improvement subsidy. I am going to say something about this explicitly later. Exactly: the subsidy with the rows. He asked: can you make sure that there could be an extra year for those three years? I'll report that to the SNN that's running it for us. I actually agree with that. I'm gonna try to do that. Let me answer that. We talked about the 41 million. Last thing on this block, I have to say something about... no, I have more, I'm sorry. I wrote in the letter that I will work more closely with civil society organisations, the Gas Council and the Soil Movement. When I was in Groningen, I got the impression from those two organizations that they were more or less pushed out of processes and reflections what they were in before. I have been in contact with the two Presidents and I have said that I am going to fix it. That is the concrete implementation. I understand my officials are already in Groningen tomorrow to talk about that. That brings me to the subsidy scheme. It has been said many times in different ways and I have just said it in my own introduction: that must never happen again. The SNN is willing to do the next batch, but before it starts to see who is entitled to the next 250 million in this scheme, it's going to handle the first 25,000 that have been done properly. I think that's wise. Secondly, the SNN is still evaluating what went wrong with the digital process. There too, all sorts of things have gone wrong. A relative of mine lives there in the area. He was standing at the top of the queue, turning around to get coffee and then stood at the bottom of the queue. Oh, that's terrible. That's what the SNN's looking at. Then it would be the thought that in April there would be a plan for that last batch, in which we could distribute the 250 million. That could be completed before the summer.

Mr. Chairman. For understandable reasons, Mr Snels mentioned the name of Secretary of State Keijzer, but I would just like to say that she was here on my behalf. Her name should in no way be associated with this file. So you're really gonna have to do it with me. Many households are uncomfortablely surprised by the energy tariffs for 2019. The cabinet has indeed made a ruling on this earlier, but let me be clear about it immediately. Yes, the cabinet has based itself on the estimates that are always used, of the Planning Office for the Environment, the NEV. However, in all honesty, the cabinet should not have been so sure, knowing that the NEV predictions were already more than a year old at the time and that apparently other parties in the market would have anticipated that for the following year other energy tariffs could not be applied but the following year. So that determination was unjustified. One of the things that needs to be done right away, I started some time ago, is this huge cacaphony of different communications about the energy bill. It confuses a lot of people. So it is important to update that estimate of the NEV 2017 that we are currently working with. I asked the Planning Bureau for the Environment two weeks ago, but I also had a conversation with parties like the Nibud, the CBS and the Association Eigen Huis. We all use other things and the Empire always assumes the NEV, but it is clear that it is useful to make that more compatible. As far as purchasing power is concerned, I can't say yet. I know this. An inflation forecast was assumed by the CPB. That inflation forecast still seems to be in line with that. This would mean that although energy has increased more strongly, other things less, but in all honesty, let us not anticipate that. Let me leave that certainty aside for a moment. Whether it really is, we need to look at the CPB figures for next month. Then I also hope to have the update of the Energy Bill of the Plan Bureau for the Environment. So then we have both one picture of the development of the energy account and the latest inflation rates and thus the latest purchasing power figures. So we can answer Mr Snels' questions. Again, that's all wonderful, but that doesn't help people at home. For the time being, people have an energy bill and energy tariffs that have fallen out higher than they thought. In all honesty, I shall say: even higher than the cabinet thought on the basis of the PBL estimates.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. While Dutch people can't make it anymore, can't refuel normally, can't pay rent, can't do groceries and can't pay the energy bill, it's true that the political choice here today has been made to not really tackle the terrible consequences of inflation. While this can be done, EUR 100 billion in climate and nitrogen policy, a huge amount, should be returned in part to all those people who are suffering so badly at the moment. This is on purpose not being done. All I get is "no" in answer, whether I ask my question to the coalition or to the minister. This is a serious scandal, because it is causing more and more people to fall into poverty and more and more people to face major financial problems. We can't do that to people. Mr. Chairman. As you know, we have tabled a number of amendments. Next week, a number of these amendments will also come back to the Spring paper. I want to get an amendment out of it now. That is Mr Wilders' amendment to substantially increase the energy surcharge, which we were actually talking about today, by €400 so that it totals €1,200. I sincerely hope that this very realistic proposal can count on broad support from the Chamber, because then we will really show all of us that we care about those people and that we really want to help them not to get into trouble. Thank you.

Right. Mrs Van Dijk, among others, asked about the Caribbean Netherlands. We'll make $5 million available for that. Mr Van Rij continues to discuss the impact of this package. So much for the block of energy surcharge. Let me now turn to the set of other questions. Among other things, it has been asked whether the increase in the statutory minimum wage cannot be brought forward and whether we can further increase it. Of course, the coalition agreement is based on 7.5%. In addition, there is also the minimum hourly wage, that 36-hour and 40-hour working week. That's really helping, too. What we need to be aware of for a moment is that the minimum wage continues to work in all social schemes. In this context, I would like to mention taxation and surcharges. That makes it quite complex. This means that the introduction takes time. So we can't increase that by 1 July of this year. That's just really impossible. It is, of course, important that we do this quickly, because the increase in the wml is going to help the groups that just deserve the wml. Let me also take a look at the debate on vulnerable groups. We need to make them less vulnerable. I will come back to you before the summer with information on the precise impact of this increase in the minimum wage and the legislative process. I would also point out that in the coalition agreement we have embraced the initiative legislative proposal on the introduction of the minimum hourly wage of the PvdA and GroenLinks. That bill aims to ensure that every minimum wage earner earns the same amount per hour. That really means a significant increase for a number of people. Then there were questions about the earning limits in the Participation Act.

That might be possible, but of course we do not want to do something that we do not need in the end. If we had now done a lot of studies on CCS for Tata, Tata would have said at this point: well, I don't need to; I want to make the battle for green steel straight away, via green hydrogen and green steam.

Basically, we're already using a lot of hydrogen. That's right. Well, in that case, it's fossilly cheerful. Blue hydrogen naturally means that you use CO storage to produce what is now called "grey hydrogen." We already have one. In the meantime, we collect the CO in order to achieve more CO reduction. In addition, we're going to scale up the green hydrogen with each other. The "Fit for 55" package from Europe also sets out objectives for this. The question is whether they are feasible or not. But we're also just tied to obligations that make us scale up that green hydrogen. I think that's just gonna happen. We only have a different view of how quickly that can happen.

You know what I can't explain to you? I find it truly complicated that we all say that everyone needs to move towards renewable energy, while helping big business with its fossil production. That's where billions more go, including electrification. But when it comes to renewable energy, households have to figure it out for themselves. I think that's really weird. I'm noticing that. It's en-and-and when it comes to the subsidies they get, but that doesn't apply to the residents. They are told: put on a warm sweater and turn off the lights, because then we will make it. I don't think that's it. I think it would be very stupid to continue with CO storage, because it does not reduce CO emissions. You put the CO underground, when we don't know if all of that can be safe in the future. You're not reducing emissions either. There is no reduction because emissions are not taxed. That doesn't mean there's gonna be any reduction. In the past, the SP has helped many companies to improve in the context of the environment and emissions, without destroying them. We did that by standardizing them. You should take a look at what happened, for example, to all kinds of industry in the port of Rotterdam. During the 1980s this was forced by employees of the factories together with the SP. It didn't break them, but it made them better. I really think that as long as we let them get away with untaxed CO2 in the air, the big extortionists in business have no need to invest in a turnaround. That is what we have seen in the case of very large polluters.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I would like to turn my attention immediately, because I would like to begin by congratulating the chairman on her birthday. I think there's nothing more fun than having a debate on the Digital Government Act on your birthday, especially with this committee. Mr. Chairman. The Digital Government Act regulates that electronic services by municipalities, implementation organisations such as UWV, SVB and the Tax Administration and organisations such as health and education institutions are safe and reliable. Specifically, these are safe and reliable means of logging in. This is very important in terms of access to patient data and the application for a permit, benefit or supplement. The law provides that public and private parties providing logging resources may only process personal data in order to allow secure logging in and that any other use of personal data, such as the trading of personal data or the logging in behaviour, is excluded. It is important to note that this law does not oblige citizens to do digital business with the government, but gives citizens and businesses the right to do digital business with the government. This is then done safely, reliably and user-friendly. Citizens can then opt for public logins, such as DigiD, or private, i.e. market-based logins. Public authorities have a duty to accept authorised logging resources, provided that they meet strict admission requirements. There has already been a detailed examination of this bill. The reason we are talking about it again today is the novelle that is the result of the debate on the bill in the First Chamber. The draft law before us makes three improvements, namely in the areas of privacy by design, the ban on trade in personal data and the better development of the concept of "open source." My group has six questions. The first question is the following. The explanatory memorandum to the legislative proposal states: "When assessing the application for recognition, the current state of the art is leading: it is considered whether the design according to the state of the art and other reasonably available possibilities provides sufficient data protection at the time of application." Further on, it says: "The proposed amendment to the seventh paragraph of Article 9 provides that an approval may be amended, suspended or withdrawn if the design of an identifier or the enabling service does not (longer) comply with the state of the art and other reasonably available data protection options. A holder of an approval shall be deemed to implement any new techniques and processes and apply for a modification of the recognition for that purpose. If this is not the case, the approval may be withdrawn." The question then is, of course, how it will be maintained. Will there still be regular checks on whether services still comply with the current state of the art? So what's this gonna look like in practice? The second point is the following. The starting point of the law is "open source, unless." Where open source software can reasonably be used, it should be used. Where this open source software is not available, it shall be weighted as to whether it is reasonable to disclose the source code of the developed solution. The CDA Group wonders whether too much control over the use of open source software can also have an opposite effect, namely that new providers can have too easy access to the software needed to create the login resources. Doesn't this development also attract all kinds of shady providers with all the vulnerabilities that this entails? My third question is this. The Council of State and the Minister differ on an important point of view. In short, the Minister believes that technology independence should be guaranteed in the law and therefore only the functional requirements of the generic digital infrastructure should be adequately described in the law and the technology-dependent effect should be left to lower regulation. But the Council of State believes that the law should contain key elements of the regulation because otherwise the law becomes too abstract and too vague and it is no longer clear what we as a Chamber are now agreeing to. I have to quote one sentence from the reaction of the venerable Council of State, and Mrs Leijten has already done so: 'The law must call man and horse and not leave it with a general indication that mammals are involved'. The Minister replicates this: "The naming of concepts such as DigiD or MyGovernment in law does not lead to a better framing of the provisions. On the contrary, by not naming these concepts, the law itself must describe the function of these provisions, which guarantees a greater guarantee for the maintenance of such a function." Can the Minister explain again why it ignores this point in the opinion of the Council of State? I believe that this is one of the major points of the debate: why include it in the law or not? The Council of State is critical of this. So I think it would be a good idea to explain that again. The fourth point. The CDA Group raised the question of the possibilities for the Minister to refuse, in the interests of national security or other risks related to privacy or cybersecurity, new providers or to deprive them of the accreditation they have previously received. My group would like to ask this question again, in the light of the rapidly changing world situation. For too long, we have been naive in, for example, our dependence on energy and raw materials from Russia and China. We are right to refer again to the need for strategic autonomy. In this context, should we not also ask which companies we would like to exclude from providing this kind of digital service? Point five. As mentioned above, the Digital Government Act does not oblige citizens to do business with the government along the digital road. My group would like to continue to stress the need for public authorities to remain open to everyone in society. Sorry, Mrs Rajkowski, I'm making this point too. It may be somewhat out of order, but I will finish this point. Human contact and human measure must always be possible, especially for vulnerable people or people with disabilities. How does the Minister ensure that this is always possible? My colleague, Mr Van der Molen, tabled an amendment at the time to also focus the proposed review of the law on less digital literate people, so that we can see if people are excluded. Finally, my sixth point. For companies, there is currently no public means of logging in as there is for citizens. I quote the Secretary of State for the Interior from the previous cabinet period, who said: "In the position on the role of the government, there seems to be a shift in this Chamber, but also beyond, as indicated by the Cyber Security Council, for example. Safe logging in is increasingly seen as a useful function, and the government is expected to play a greater role in all social movements." So that's a quote from the previous Secretary of State for the Interior. My question is: how does this minister view these statements? For example, should there also be a public login for companies? That's it, Mr. Chairman.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. It'll be shorter than the time before me. We're talking about a growth fund. This gives the impression that growth, growth and growth are necessary. Growth, growth, growth, however, leads, as we have noticed, to gray, gray, gray. We're grabbing the planet empty, and that's been through to this government by now. In order to continue adoring growth, growth and growth, the greenwashing word has now been invented. I quote the Minister: 'The key to uniting economic activity and climate neutrality is decoupling economic activity and greenhouse gas emissions'. Decoupling is now the magic word. And we swear by green innovations like methadone for our growth addiction. But does decoupling work? Isn't it just a magic word, but also a bedtime fairy tale? Two years ago, the European Environment Agency published a comprehensive study to uncover the fairy tale. I quote, and it's a long quote, because it's important that we get it right. The quote is thus: "Given what is at stake, careful assessment is needed to determine whether the scientific bases behind this decoupling hypothesis are robust or not. This report provides an overview of the empirical and theoretical literature to assess the validity of this hypothesis. The conclusions are both overwhelmingly clear and sobering. Not only is there no empirical evidence of the existence of the decoupling of economic growth and environmental impact on a scale that is close to the scale needed to cope with environmental degradation, but also, and perhaps even more importantly, such decoupling does not seem to happen in the future." So there's no decoupling. And again the Minister's quote: "The key to uniting economic activity and climate neutrality is decoupling." The key! Mr. Chairman. Is the Minister wiser than the scientists to whom the European Environment Agency refers? On what scientific reports does the government's story support that we can continue to grow as we innovate? I'd like a response from the Minister. Mr. Chairman. The next question follows on from questions that I also came across implicitly or explicitly in the stories of previous speakers' contributions to the debate. Why are only projects eligible to increase earning capacity? Why should projects that lead to sustainability, but not directly to economic growth, fall outside the scope of this Growth Fund? Mr. Chairman. Take the interventions in the agricultural sector that have now been presented by the cabinet. Does that increase earning power? No, it's not like that at first sight. Is it a project that leads to an economic, social and environmentally friendly sustainable future for the earth and for present and future generations? Right? I quoted here part of the legal definition of sustainable earning in the bill. What does the Minister think? Would an investigation into the need for the intervention now proposed in the agricultural sector fall within the scope of the Growth Fund? I'd like a response from the Minister. Mr. Chairman. Everything is related to how the definition of "sustainable earning capacity" is to be read in the law. From the Minister's answers, I understand that a time horizon is maintained for up to 30 years. Does this mean that projects that lead to less earning capacity in the short term, but which are needed to guarantee a viable Netherlands in the long term of 30 years, fall within the definition of "sustainable earning capacity"? Here it becomes important how the definition should be read in the law. "A gross domestic product that the Netherlands can generate on a long-term structural basis," the legal definition begins. But this definition continues with the following: "in view of an economic, social and environmentally sustainable future for the earth and for present and future generations." "With an eye for it," my question is how the government explains this. Should we read this as "subject to that"? As an administrative lawyer, I note that the legislative text requires at least that account be taken of the importance of an economic, social and environmental sustainable future for the earth and for present and future generations. This interest must therefore be taken into account. Is this true? If so, is the Minister prepared to give that explanation to the Advisory Committee and to implement it in further rules as referred to in Article 8? So "with the eye for" should be read as "subject to that." Mr. Chairman. We're going to invest with the Growth Fund. The starting point is that we get something in return. According to the Minister's replies, the fund has no revolver and no return target. What we get in return is on another plane. With the increase in our national income, the Minister sees the debt as also increasing the tax revenue for the government. In response to questions from our group, the Minister points out the following. "Growth contributes to the financing of public services, and the energy and climate transition also requires large investments," said the Minister. Mr. Chairman. In order to free up funds for financing public services and transition investments, it is necessary that our gross national product continues to increase. Is it not possible to achieve the same result without growth, but with a fairer tax distribution? Mr. Chairman. The number of super rich is increasing. Oxfam calculated that 62 new billionaires in the food sector were added to the pandemic world-wide, while 263 million people fell into poverty. I would like to hear from the Minister or without the growth of national income, but with a fairer burden-sharing, it is not possible to achieve comparable revenues for public services and investment. Mr. Chairman. The greener the technology, the more it uses essential scarce minerals. In the foreseeable future, demand will be higher than supply. Does the Growth Fund take that into account? My group asked this question in the written round but did not receive a satisfactory answer. That is why I ask the Minister again. I'm just gonna build on those scarce minerals. In December 2021, the Chamber adopted the Prast motion, which calls on the Government to ensure that Invest International takes only initiatives, which are clearly established that no use is made of cobalt mined in Congo. Is the Minister prepared to give the same condition as binding in the case of funding from the National Growth Fund? Mr President, I am coming to the end. I'm joining the advisory committee. Mr Otten has already asked questions about it. The members have a great power. I note from the reply that the starting point is that the cabinet does not accept proposals that have received a negative opinion from the advisory committee. I would almost like to say to Mr Otten: if that is the starting point, then it seems that these ministers are not even involved anymore. But what about when a positive advice has been given? On what grounds can the cabinet decide not to honour the proposal? I'd like a response from the Minister. The members of the advisory committee often have a background in business, as I understood from the Minister's answers. This raises the question of how to prevent conflicts of interest. I do not read in Article 9 of the legislative proposal that there should be binding rules on conflicts of interest. Isn't that strange, I ask the Minister? In the answer to Question 29, Mr Otten also quoted in that reply that there is a kind of procedure, in order to exclude members with interests from taking part in an assessment. Who made those rules? Is the Minister prepared to submit a draft regulation to the Chamber on this issue? Can the Minister undertake to do this? I'd like a response. I come to my last question. The members of the advisory committee have a major influence on the selection of projects. This means, in my view, that they should be appointed on the basis of a pre-established and approved profile by Parliament. The Chamber should be able to check whether a desired mix of expertise and experience can be guaranteed from a social point of view. Is the Minister prepared to admit this? I look forward to the Minister's answers. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Thank you also to Mr and Mrs Minister for answering the questions, although some answers have been moved to the second term. So I am still very curious about the final answer to the questions. The Minister states that the reason for the creation of Invest International lies in improving the competitiveness of Dutch business. That is a very nice objective and of course the VVD fully agrees with that. The second objective, the resolution of international issues, is, of course, also to be found in the VVD's objective. The third reason was that the commercial banks withdrew. That will be the case, but I would say: keep the commercial banks on board through FMO's shareholdership, because then they would be better able to serve their client base by saying: we still have a company that we are a shareholder of, so they could help you in this case, and we can also participate in part of the loan or part of the risk. A fourth issue is, of course, always a bit strange: yes, but other countries also have such an institution, and that is why we must have one. Yeah, but those other banks, like Kfw, are real banks and not funds. Moreover, they have a 70- or 80-year experience and a huge network of offices in third countries. This fund does not have that, so all the more reason for another construction to be reviewed once again. I was triggered by the fact that the Minister said in his reply: there is a substantial pipeline of potential projects. Could the Minister provide more insight into this substantial pipeline, so that we have an idea that there is more meat on the bone than in Invest-NL, so to speak? But with the loss of a derogation, there is an acute problem. The Minister is now working for a derogation for this current year. The manure season has been on steam for three months. I very much share that. That has a number of components. The component you mention: if you have to make a political assessment that does not really require epidemiological or medical consideration, then we have to do our own work. We shouldn't, because we find it complicated, give the decision out of our hands, to the OMT. That requires discipline on the part of politics. I think there's something else that requires discipline on the political side. That's that you need to leave medical scientists, or even scientists, space for moving insight. That is precisely what scientists live on. That's actually the essence of medical science: that you discover new things, that you learn new things, and that given the facts and circumstances of a given moment, you come to a conclusion for that moment, but also that a week later you might come to a different view. This is very difficult to handle in the political context, because we are inclined to justify, for example, the issue of consistency. It was precisely the science that had to be free to have moving insight. That is why it is right to separate the political-administrative domain, of which we are, and the medical-scientific domain, of which they are. Don't sit on each other's seats, it's great. Then test it, Mr. Chairman. I mentioned Mrs Marijnissen, but several Members have asked the question when the test capacity is in order. And then they asked about the role of quick tests. I tasted the impatience in that, which I do recognize. But first, the PCR tests, because with that offer, we have to do it right now. Last week, 40,000 covid tests were taken at GGDs and hospitals together, a day. From next Friday we can take 49,500 covid tests, at GGD's and hospitals together. And as of next Monday, there should be 56,500. So yeah, it's growing, yeah, it's rising. That is a good thing, because we also see that the waiting times have risen considerably and we have to get rid of them, because the testing has to work quickly, at least within the two 24 hours we have talked to the Chamber about before, so within 24 hours after making a test session and again 24 hours until the result. If you look closely at the figures of this moment, we are on average almost double, so it should at least return very quickly to those two times 24 hours. That's the first win we have to make. To this end, everything we discussed last week has been done very extensively with regard to the expansion of laboratory capacity and supplies for the materials currently in the laboratories. In addition, we have concluded contracts with a number of German labs. There is also a Belgian lab with a great opportunity to test a lot more. That's how I hope we're at 70,000 tests by the end of October, where we're at the beginning of October, so early next week, at 56,500 tests. It should be possible, but keep me in good shape, if we scale up at this rate, if we manage to keep this pace and if we do not have any other setbacks along the way, you will hear me make all the comments that could be done anyway to sit over the 100,000 tests in November/December. That is actually the capacity we would not have given until February the scaling-up line we saw before. We're trying to get that done a lot sooner. On the PCR tests, I say. To be honest, what I have put much more hope on in the end is the rapid tests. We're gonna have to do it with the PCR tests for now. That will only always be an actual process, and always have to do with serious lead times. Eventually you want even faster lead times, even faster than those two times 24 hours. What could help us with that? Those are the rapid tests, which are now under development. I'd like to give you an outline of some of the promising things that are going on right now. At the same time, I would like to make a commitment that, in the next progress letter, not next week but next week, I will give a more detailed outline of what is currently going on in the field of rapid tests. If I hadn't had a chamber debate, I'd open a pilot today with the LAMP test. We commissioned TNO and a number of other partners in February. That's a highly simplified PCR test that can be taken much faster, with 45 minutes until you get the results. That's a huge acceleration. Coming weeks will be tested and validated to ensure that it is as reliable and useful as the regular PCR test. That could be a great help. For example, you could provide the rapid test streets that are now being developed at the GGDs. If we are a few weeks away, I hope to be able to say something about its reliability. Then we're going to scale it up and roll it out as soon as possible. We asked TNO to make a plan to do so as soon as possible. That's one. The second is the breath test. It'll be validated in the next few weeks. I have already given orders to buy everything that could be bought, because it is reasonably viable, especially in the area of negative results. This is, of course, very likely to accelerate the testing process in the test street further. If you could pick out all the negatives before they hit the test street and only the positives would then have a PCR test done, it would save a lot of capacity. With that, you can greatly increase the capacity. So that's very likely. There are a number of other quick tests, but I'm gonna leave them for a while. Those were the innovative test methods, which come to a result much faster. In addition, we are currently doing antigen tests. Five are currently in a pilot. Everything for sale, we've already bought or we're buying. In part, it is not for sale yet and then we have bought an option. Those five are also validated in livesettings, in addition to PCR, to see what reliability is compared to PCR. At the same time, parallel scenarios are currently being developed for whom and in which setting they can be of added value, as they cannot replace the PCR test; the reliability is not that high. But you can certainly use them in a number of settings, where the reliability may be a little less important. That's a very logistical process. I hope that at the end of October I have made up my mind about the use of these rapid tests and antigen tests. From the beginning of November, we could use it gradually. The fastest one, if it goes well in validation, is the LAMP test. There's a lot of energy in it to make sure we pull it out of the ground as soon as possible. In short, everything is happening, but for the time being we will have to do it with the PCR tests in the next few weeks. Fortunately, there we see a considerable increase in capacity. I think I've done all the tests in one go.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Many people in debt do not dare to speak out or seek help. Post will not be opened at any time and letters will be discarded. On average, debt holders only ask for help with a municipality after five years. As a result, debts become unnecessary and small late payments quickly become problematic debts. Mr. Chairman. The importance of prevention cannot be underestimated. That was an important issue in previous debates. We want to help people who have problematic debts to get out and stay out of it. That is why it is important to help people take responsibility for debt relief processes where necessary, so that they can take control of their lives. For example, we tabled a motion to examine whether people in Wsnp routes and people in a clean-up process can be supported to handle their accounting properly. I also referred to the early warning, which can also contribute to prevention by pointing out which households are affected by debt. Early warning will prevent small late payments from resulting in heavy debts, requiring friendly or legal pathways, with creditors seeing only a small part of their money back. And that's what the bill is about. This allows signals of payment problems to be shared with a municipality without the GDPR creating all kinds of barriers. As a result, municipalities can have an early conversation with people and that is absolutely good. The bill makes debt relief more effective and ensures that more people are reached earlier, which can help to avoid costly aid in the future. For example, signals about late payment in the rental of the house or in the case of gas, water and light. It is also good that municipalities are given room to experiment with any other signals. I would also like the Chamber to be kept informed of these experiments. We get an update on that every now and then, I ask the Secretary of State. Mr. Chairman. The VVD is positive about the broad debt approach. The Secretary of State is actively involved in rolling out the measures in this approach. This bill is one of them. Congratulations on progress and on concrete steps being taken to improve the functioning of debt relief. We would also like to pay another compliment. During the budgetary procedure we also talked about entrepreneurs in debt and the fact that they are also entitled to help from municipalities. Some municipalities still have a blind spot. This bill makes it clear once again thatzzp'ers and entrepreneurs must be able to contact municipalities. That can't be said often enough. So thank you for the clarification in the explanatory statement. But of course there are some questions to ask. The first concerns the storage of personal data. This is reported to municipalities. These are stored for as long as necessary. In practice, it is expected that this will be up to six months. But how are we gonna keep an eye on that? I think it would be useful to check at some point whether municipalities are actually destroying this data in time. What does the Secretary of State think about this? Rent disadvantages can be an important signal for households with financial problems. It's very good that landlords get involved in that early warning. In the country there are also some pilots and the results sound good, but this is mainly about corporations. Does reporting of a late payment of the rent continue to be limited to those corporations or is it intended to apply to private landlords as well? And if so, does that go in broad for every landlord, or not? Furthermore, more early warning could put financial pressure on municipalities that are given more work to choose. The note following the report states that the structural financial consequences will be neutral on balance, as early warning will also yield a return. That seems to me to be a justified point. But I also think it would be wise to keep an eye on the pulse, because municipalities will have to be able to make the necessary investments. How's the Secretary of State gonna keep an eye on this? Then there's another subject. At least not so much a different subject on this law, but the point that Mr Van Dijk has just raised was it not that I see anyone walking to the microphone. I think it might be useful to wait.

Maybe you could take a look... It is not just a question of electricity networks, where the arguments you put forward apply, but also of certain things relating to congestion, for example, which batch of batteries may invest in certain places. You might be able to put that under the same question. Maybe it'll get a little more interesting.

Yeah, the working arms. Almost all spokesmen this morning addressed the issue of working poverty. The fact that not everyone benefits from the economic backwind is also reflected in the SCP report on the working poor, which is also on the agenda for this debate. That report shows that work, or actually more hours of work, is the main cause of poverty. That is of course good, but at the same time the report shows that not everyone with a job has an income above the poverty line, and you certainly don't have that if you have a job with few hours. That is why, as a cabinet, we deliberately reduced taxes for people who work and have low incomes on 1 January. So people just have more left in their wallet, so it pays more to work. A broader discussion will also emerge from this. Mr Kuzu said this also in an interruption debate with Mr Wiersma. We must, of course, continue to finance education, care and infrastructure. That means you have a different mix in your taxes. The cabinet has therefore chosen to increase taxes on consumption and energy consumption, and then use that money to reduce the burden on labour and on work, precisely so that you have more left in your wallet when you go to work. On balance, 96% of the Dutch have a positive purchasing power picture for 2019. This is not only according to my own budget figures, but also according to last Friday's Nibud figures. And yes, there are things that are becoming more expensive: the care premium, the energy bill and the VAT. On the other hand, however, there is a very substantial reduction in the burden on work: a higher labour cut, a higher general tax cut and a lower rate in the first disc. They are also aimed at making work pay more.
