Mr President, I shall continue. In the further reply, we also read that the Minister is now engaged in discussions with neighbouring countries on the cross-border approach to the problem of nitrogen. Model calculations seen by the fraction of the VVD show that we export more nitrogen than we import, both the NOs and ammonia. If that is the case, we ask the Minister. And if that is the case, what effect has this given in relation to the talks with neighbouring countries on our own stated objectives? After all, they see a reduction in the internal nitrogen deposition. And how are these talks going, we ask the Minister, because if we also have to reduce our exports, then should our national emissions not go down any further than is now in the law, or do we see that wrong? Our final point on effectiveness concerns a recent study by Mr Jan Willem Erisman, professor at the University of Leiden. I think I heard Mr Koffeman mention that name. Together with Gispoint, he developed the Nitrogen Deposition Contribution Card for effective emission reduction from agriculture. The starting point is that there are many sources that contribute to the nitrogen surplus in the protected Natura 2000 sites. And nature and agricultural areas are scattered around the Netherlands like a patchwork. For this research, the map of the Netherlands has been divided into compartments of one kilometre, and for each box it has been calculated where nitrogen emissions come from that box. And what's the outcome? That areas with a relatively high deposition effect appear to lie mainly in the Gelderse Valley and on the sandy soils in Brabant, Overijssel, Gelderland and Drenthe. These areas have two other things in common: they are mainly areas with a central location, allowing nitrogen to spread easily to all surrounding nature areas; and these areas also have more worrying aspects, such as poor soil quality and high nutrient leaching nitrate and phosphate to groundwater. The research shows that with the same reduction in nitrogen emissions but with more focus on a more limited number of sites, you will have a much greater impact on Natura 2000 sites than with the present approach. And then you're still talking about area-oriented policies, about generic policies, but more territorially applied. So it's not necessarily about forced buying up, but more about focusing on a number of areas. How could you possibly have a relationship here with the National Programme of Rural Areas, we ask the Minister. And then I'll be at the heading of feasibility. Under this heading the VVD Group focuses on two points: the registration and monitoring system and the relationship with other urgently desired spatial developments. The VVD Group has already asked questions about the nitrogen registration system and the storage functions for those spare nitrogen spaces. How can we find a good balance between not spilling nitrogen space on the one hand and a complicated administrative system on the other, so that the feasibility remains feasible for everyone and the paper results are as close to the truth as possible, we ask the Minister. It is not easy to intervene in our current, often long-term use of space and in the management of farms, including farms. The VVD Group is well aware of this. However, there is no choice. The way out is complex, but intervention in the current course of events is inevitable. An extensive measurement and monitoring system allows us to keep the finger on the nitrogen pulse. However, it is essential for the support base to be trusted in the systems and models used. There's still a point. That also came out a lot more often. Of course, the VVD Group is not deaf or blind to the many alarm messages that have been sent to us, especially from the agricultural sector. For example about the calculation tool AERIUS, which is filled on the basis of old maps and assumptions. And that while companies are paid for 0.05 moles. Mr. Chairman. I have to add that, just before we started again, I was given an app that there are many hexagons that count in this AERIUS system, but that are completely outside the Natura 2000 sites. How is the Minister going to bring these two worlds closer together? A knowledge programme is being set up to improve measurement and calculation systems. That's good. But as far as the AERIUS system is concerned, this is really a bloody situation. How is the Minister going to ensure that the highest possible pace is used in the promised improvement of AERIUS? I would like to hear a commitment from the Minister on this. I have also heard Mrs Prins and Mr Pijlman say something about this. Mr. Chairman. The present bill deals with nitrogen reduction and environmental improvement, but in the view of the VVD Group, it can only be optimally implemented if a link is established with other necessary spatial plans. Last year, the Planning Office for the Environment identified four current, important societal themes, expressed as a relationship between specific, desired, necessary developments. Then you are talking about the relationship between urban and rural areas, in which natural housing, recreational opportunities and mobility come to the fore. You're talking about nature versus agriculture. We are talking about nitrogen problems, but also about food supply, biodiversity, animal welfare, health and drought. Then you also talk about climate change, with the adaptation on the one hand and the energy transition, so the mitigation, on the other hand, and the circular economy. A common denominator for these four themes is that they all have a relationship with space fittings and thus with spatial design. In other words, they all compete among themselves for the limited space available in our densely populated delta. For a sustainable, long-term, effective solution, one should approach several aspects in their coherence, for example, combining the redesign of nature areas in the context of restoring nitrogen irreversibility with the prevention of dehydration, by taking groundwater measures at the same time. And so many more potentially successful combinations are worth investigating. The Study Group on Spatial Planning Rural Areas has been commissioned to develop policy options for spatial choices. This will also involve a change in land use. So it's a spatial transformation. The government suggests the possibility to look at the results of this process in the light of the suggestion of the Advisory Committee on Nitrogen Problems to start thinking in green, orange and red areas and to do so within the National Programme on Rural Areas. When this becomes clearer, we ask the Minister. How does the government see such a path? Mr. Chairman. The VVD Group supports the recommendation of the Advisory Committee on Nitrogen Problems that everyone should contribute proportionally to the solution and that structural solutions should be found for a sustainable restoration of the relationship between nature and economic development. This is clearly more difficult in a densely populated country like the Netherlands than in Sweden, for example. But now to make well-thought-out decisions and implement them carefully and at the right pace is the only way for the VVD Group to move towards a developing economy, forward-looking agriculture, both intensively and extensively, and towards a realistic nature policy. The planned periods of five, ten and fifteen years from now seem to us to be a more than serious start. It's about dividing up scarce space. This law is a first step. However, there is or is the feasibility of the goals with smart and above all fair monitoring, whereby government and both Chambers should be prepared to adjust the sails if necessary, running the route. Previous speakers have already mentioned this in all kinds of different terms. What is the Minister's view of this process of any necessary change of direction and possible additional regulation? Mr. Chairman. As has been said, solving the nitrogen problem is not an isolated process, but part of a collaboration with other desired developments that require space. As an introduction to our last question, I have three quotes. The Advisory Committee on Nitrogen Problems gave its final report the title "Not everything can be done everywhere." We would like to say that not everything can go anywhere. A second quote comes from an interview with the new president of VNO-NCW, Ingrid Thijssen, in the Gelderlander. She says: "There's always a lot of looking at the financial space, but it's the nitrogen space, stupid!" In Trouw of 31 January, there was an article by Caspar van den Berg, Professor of Public Administration at the University of Groningen, and Annemarie Kok, independent researcher, entitled "The regions are often treated as difficult children." This document focuses on the problems that addressing climate change and energy transition, including issues from that PBL list that I mentioned earlier. It is no longer the technical and financial aspects that cause stagnation, but questions of a spatial and also administrative nature. And that means that the space-demanding solutions to be found for residents of the metropolitan Netherlands mean something different than for the inhabitants of the rural, somewhat thinner populated area. Political wishes and spatial sacrifices vary geographically, according to the mentioned Trouw-article. The same applies to the problem of nitrogen. Mr. Chairman. The VVD is convinced that the proposed policy can gain strength as part of a more comprehensive spatial vision. And there is, because that's the NOVI. How is the government going to ensure that the spatial conditions of the proposed policy are really approached through the Novi line? Because sticking a nitrogen patch alone is not enough for the long term. We would also like to receive a convincing commitment from the Minister on this. And as always, we are very interested in the government's response. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Thank you also to the Minister for answering the questions we asked. All of our neighbouring countries are moving towards natural gas and we are abandoning it because we were too stupefied to find a good technical solution. You probably don't understand it, but there's a scenario where you keep up the pressure in the field and start producing in a normal way, with a low depletion rate. Then it's all possible.

Thank you. Mr. Chairman. It is good to be able to continue the oral consultation with each other today. I would like to speak a few introductory sentences and then comment on the motions that have been tabled and on a single question that has been asked. Let me begin with the beginning that I also chose in the answer in the oral consultation, namely Mr Otten's statement: if it ain't broke, don't fix it. That is a wise word, which should perhaps be repeated a little more often here in The Hague. But in this case, I don't think it's going to work. At least I would never dare the thesis: it ain't broken. With 26 laws, 60 AMvBs and 75 regulations, we have created a very dark forest with each other throughout environmental law. Procedures take a long time, too long. An important reason for the slow development of the area is precisely the complexity and ambiguity that we have organised with each other. That has also been the view of a very broad majority here in this house when adopting the Environment Act. Only two groups voted against at that time and voted in favour of a very large majority. That was also the view when we voted on the introduction law. There was also a large majority of 53 seats in 2020. So "Whether or not the Environment Act?" is a question that has already been dealt with, which has been answered by a large majority in several instances. What we are talking about here is whether it is wise to introduce the law on 1 January next. I understand that, because it is a big law, a big law, in the context that the municipalities already have an incredible amount of work to do and the implementation process is proving to be tough, especially as regards ICT development. That has been the reason for a number of delays, so I understand that not only does the First Chamber want to check the quality of legislation, it still has one of the most important tasks of the First Chamber, and you have done so, but you also want to check the implementation side. I understand that you say: we have to be absolutely sure before we say "go." At the same time, I would also like to say that clarity is actually part of that care towards implementation practice. That has to do with all the work that has yet to be done. Municipalities need to know where they're headed. That is why I have outlined a timetable following the oral consultation I had with you and what I myself intend to do. This is actually divided into two key concepts. The first is clarity. We really need to clarify the implementation practice that the introduction will take place on 1 January. If you are alderman in the spatial domain and you want, for example, to guide your new empty regulation through the board, it is nice if you know what date that is for at all. If you are project leader and are in charge of implementing the Environment Act, and you need to excite and motivate your club and keep the good people at work and fill vacancies with the best people in this field, then it is wise that you know what date you are working towards. Leading a complicated implementation without a clear end date is really unwise. It's not going well. You'll lose the energy. Then you lose the power needed to properly appear on the start line on January 1st. That's one. Two is careful. What should be going well on 1 January anyway? That is the urgent development of the area; it must be done well in any case. The second is everything citizens and businesses will have to deal with from 1 January: licensing. Everything related to licensing must work, because otherwise the services of the municipality in the spatial domain are no longer in order, and that is not good. No one's really worried about that last one. You do see flaws in beauty and you can still see work processes that have to be settled in municipalities, but the whole chain, including the functioning of DSO, the national ICT supply Digital System Environment Act, combined with what local software developers have built for co-governments, is just working well on the licensing side. AcICT does not comment on this either. There is still work to be done on the development of areas. You can see that one is farther than the other. There are software providers that are already fully ready and there are software providers that are not quite ready yet. But that is precisely what we have developed the temporary alternative measures for. The care we need to take towards autumn is a to give clarity and b to go through the steps needed to ensure at a good time that no more accidents can happen. We certainly know that because we have done everything necessary to support municipalities and provinces and because it appears that the temporary alternative measures for those municipalities that are not yet sufficiently ready are actually working. The temporary measure IMPRO is a bit of a technique, excuse for that, is about the data standard with which the environmental plans are to be made. It helps and works................................................................................................................................................................................................... I assume that some of the municipalities will indeed choose to do so. This makes it possible for the municipalities that opt for this phased growth, because they can also make the environmental plan for the new period with the data standard they used to work with in recent years. What we have to do is support the competent authorities and keep the finger on the wrist. What I have to do in your direction is to deliver you by October: the progress reports on connecting to the DSO, the final report of Deloitte on the follow-up to AcICT's opinions, and a survey of the experiences of the competent authorities with their implementation statements. It'll follow in September. What can I deliver in October? These are: the results of the integrated chain tests on phase one in July and then phase two in October, the policy response to the findings of AcICT, and a progress letter in which I fully inform you about the implementation and the DSO. I will send it to you in October, which will enable us to hold a debate in October. And let us be clear: I think we should be clear about implementation practice and I think we should be careful. I said that at the committee meeting. The best way to be careful is to provide that clarity today. And the very best way to provide that clarity would have been, as far as the cabinet is concerned, to beat the KB and to accord by the First Chamber that the cabinet that KB was going to beat. You have considered: no, we prefer to do so at a later date, if we have more progress information to make sure that that is a correct decision. I respect that, but it is precisely for this reason that it is very important to say very clearly to the co-governments and the market players, who are asking for this, that the date of introduction should be 1 January. That is what I said in the committee debate. That brings me to the motions that have been tabled. For that reason, I advise against the motion of the Member Otten. That is why I leave the judgment to the Chamber on the motion with the letters DZ, the motion Rietkerk et al., with a whole list of signatories. So I am doing so because this motion states that the entry into force of the Environment Act on 1 January is and will continue to be the starting point, because it is so important to clarify. I think that is the most important element. At the same time, I understand that you say that we want to have a meaningful debate in October on whether that is really certain. That is a 'yes, if', as Mr Rietkerk put it. I want to respond to the 'provided' as well as possible by doing everything and delivering everything I have just outlined. Mr. Chairman. Which brings me to the next motion. That is Mr Janssen's motion. The motion says, "Don't make those sentences out of that decision note public." I would like to explain again why I do not. I've been hesitant about that for a while. When you read those sentences, you're like, "Oh, come on, just say that; it's not that exciting, is it? That's what I'm saying, homey. And yet I won't. It is about the impact of conversations that have been there. That means that it is about the political process leading up to such a chamber debate. It is important to be able to conduct the political process in a confidential manner in the run-up to a parliamentary debate. That makes sense, otherwise we would keep all our conversations out in the open. That's not true. It's never like that. I believe that this political process is worth protecting. And so, in appealing to the interest of the State, which is an appropriate provision not to meet an information request, I am not releasing the sentences that stand here, although you might say: what is that about; it is only about the political process leading up to this debate? And yet I think it would be wise not to set a precedent. That means that I cannot comply with this request and also that I reject this motion.

Those frameworks remain in front of us. If you're asking for a 100% guarantee, I can't give it right now. Mr Omtzigt also knows that the spring decision-making process is really the main decision-making moment on which the cabinet can see what the windfalls and also the setbacks are. A lot of the facts just don't add up. Business is taxed. The EU ETS stands somewhere between €55 and €60 per tonne. I largely agree with Mr Eerdmans. We have a small country, which is fully built. If there are windmills on land, it must be well secured and they must be at a distance from those living nearby. We are in favour of this, and that is why we are in favour of this motion. We await the conclusion of that. But you also have choices in this. We have the North Sea, which is a lot bigger than the land surface. There are other interests that we must safeguard there, such as, of course, fishing. But the North Sea is also a lot more logical, because there it blows a lot more. Mr. Chairman. Politics seems a bit cynical sometimes. People need to grab media moments, catch flies, debit firmities. That is why, at least, I hope, it is a good thing that we are talking about Europe here today. Here we don't have to do it for publicity, because usually everyone outside this room misses what we discuss on these occasions. This is an important prerequisite for a more nuanced political debate, namely that exchange of arguments should not suffer from the need to score. That being so, I would like to dwell on the word'sovereignty'. That keeps popping up like a kind of catch in the debate on Europe. Usually it's about surrendering sovereignty versus retaining sovereignty or getting it back. "Take back control," as the Brexiters called it. If you dig something, you'll soon find out that no one actually knows exactly what it is. Being sovereign is like being the boss of yourself. Because each country wants to determine the course of things for itself, you can say that every country wants to be sovereign as much as possible, but the other way around it is with countries like with people: you cannot live on your own. So to be sovereign, you have to do things together and pool sovereignty. That's when all the confusion begins. 'Cause take the Netherlands from before the war. That was a neutral country without alliances. How sovereign can you actually have it in the world, you'd say. But that same side country had to do all kinds of things again and again that the sovereign didn't really feel like doing, because it wasn't that sovereign. We had to censor the media, for example, because we didn't want to annoy a neighboring foreign head of state, listening to the name Adolf Hitler. We couldn't afford that luxury as a small country without allies. We had to turn in the gold standard so cherished by us, otherwise we threatened to go bankrupt. 'Should', I say, because the outside world was going to use new monetary rules that we didn't really like at all. We had to negotiate trade quotas with abroad. Sovereign as we were, we actually didn't feel anything for that, but we had to, because we wanted to have food and stove. I would just like to say that sovereignty is an elusive concept, especially in our country, which, as few other countries in the world, is so intertwined with foreign affairs. In my view, a country's sovereignty is linked to its capacity to act. Is a country capable of acting, influencing and concluding the corresponding compromises, with the aim of promoting the prosperity and well-being of its own population as much as possible? In today's world, capacity for action is the practical core of everyday sovereignty. Also well-understood self-interest therefore relates the pursuit of being boss in his own home. Mr. Chairman. It is our firm belief that our country's ability to act is best served in the European arena. There we find sufficient scale and equalism to protect and promote our interests and values in the world. Here are our allies, and here we have influence. The threats to our way of life in this part of Europe do not need to be outlined in detail here. They are well known. Whether it is the economic, political advance of China, Russian revanchism, the struggle for raw materials, the security of supply of products, the struggle for spheres of influence in Africa, the instability of that continent or the dependence of Silicon Valley, all over the world there are forces that seriously violate our way of life. Everywhere it is about forces that are too great for us alone to face them. People want protection from this, and we cannot offer it alone. That is a kind of protection that we should not be fooling our citizens into believing that we can deliver it on our own. Mr. Chairman. Sometimes people are enthusiastic about Switzerland's paradise independence. I remember how PVV leader Wilders enthusiastically tweeted about the outcome of a Swiss referendum in February 2014. A narrow majority of Swiss citizens did not want immigrants to work in Switzerland in that referendum. No more immigrants. And do you know what happened to the outcome of that referendum? The answer is unheard of, namely nothing. Nothing at all. In order to be able to survive, Switzerland has more than 100 agreements with the European Union and, logically, this includes the obligation not to shop unilaterally in that package, because the guillotine falls on all the thousands of agreements. Let me give another example: Norway. There the Nobel Prize Committee decided ten years ago to award the Nobel Peace Prize to the Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo. China was angry and Norway was punished. Suddenly Norwegian salmon was banned from China for veterinary reasons and further chicanes followed. The sequel is significant. First, we saw Norway's voting behaviour in the United Nations becoming more friendly to China. Norway subsequently supported Chinese observer status at the Arctic Council. Norwegian politicians solemnly and neatly promised not to receive the Dalai Lama and they promised not to take any more action against the one-China policy. That may be understandable opportunism, but it is also something that happens to you earlier when you are alone as a small country. Mr. Chairman. In order to keep this part of the world democratic and stable, efforts by countries such as Germany and France are of particular importance. We will certainly not always agree with them on what they want and do, but as soon as they join forces, this weight will be on the scale, with Germany in particular having the means and France in particular having the reflexes to manifest themselves. Their support is crucial when the European Commission comes up with plans to protect investment, take climate action, rebut China, intervene in Africa, introduce a trade boycott or build something that looks like a start of a common defence. This requires a constructive role of Dutch diplomacy. Do we want to realize that? Do we want to have that ambition and share it with our citizens? To avoid misunderstandings, there are enough things in the European Union to be extremely critical about. Italy's budgetary policy is a tragedy, although it is worth noting that every Dutchman earns €1.516 a year from the EU and every Italian barely half, says Bertelsmann Stiftung.
A lot of people live in energy poverty. This cabinet has promised that everyone would improve.

Mr Erkens is beginning to be very promising. He says: sustainability and economic growth must go hand in hand. I couldn't agree more. But then he said, "It's got to be smart." Then I'll have some questions. You are a member of the largest party, my old party: the VVD. I'd like to tell you a few things. There are billions going to the climate. I wonder if that's as clever as you say. We're gonna make houses gasless, which is bad for the environment in the short term. We have subsidised biomass plants with billions. That's bad for the environment. We put agricultural land, which we might even be able to build, full of solar panels, while 90% of the roofs have no solar panels yet. Now we're moving on to CCS, Carbon Capture and Storage, while net CO2 emissions are higher than what we capture. Recently, from Japanese research, I come to my question, hear that we are better able to continue in combustion cars than to switch immediately to Tesla's. Don't you agree with me that all these things aren't so smart, and that we should be doing smart things?

Perhaps I have an addition to Mr Stoffer and perhaps he can agree with it. Well, then, as far as I'm concerned, it's enough. I'll be sure to. I can already say that, when it comes to disasters, we have a great deal of experience with the International Red Cross in Saint Martin. I have also recently made a contribution to equipment for the firefighters on St.Maarten in order to do good things in case of hurricanes. That's an occasional benefit. I will also answer your question in the second term. Then I'll get to the second block, Mr. Chairman. It sounds a little disrespectful, but it's about poverty. I think poverty is one of the biggest challenges for the Caribbean parts of the Kingdom. As I said before, I've seen what people are going through up close. Often they are at age and have worked their whole lives. I met a 71-year-old painter who said, "I've worked my whole life and now I have to think every day if I'm gonna make it through the day and if I have enough food." That man burst into tears and said, "What can you offer me perspective?" For example, there are a lot of people who have used the food packages. I'm sure you've made the same visit. I have to say, you don't forget those impressions easily. I believe that as politicians here, but also on the other side of the ocean, we have an expensive duty to do everything in our power to combat poverty and inequality, which is also there. The inequality is enormous. Speaking of solidarity: in a civilised country, attention should be paid to these groups. We have initially committed the 85 million for emergency aid, we have created a support and recovery package for the Caribbean Netherlands, similar to that for the European Netherlands, and we have helped entrepreneurs to get through the crisis. But that's not enough. Ultimately, the best perspective that these people can have is that there will be economic development, that there will be less dependence on tourism, that they will be better able to take any blows. The board needs to get organized. The taxes must be collected; I will say something about this in a moment. 'Cause sometimes the money's on the street, but they don't pick it up. Then there is no money to finance education and care. I believe that one of the lessons and assignments within the Kingdom should be that we should address each other, but not just that: we should also help each other, to prevent these people from getting into this situation. [[Sentence could not be parsed: Want als je 71 jaar]] I mean, you've worked your whole life, you've got a not-too-best health, and there's more in a cabin than that. You don't have to ask yourself, who's taking care of me, who's taking care of me? You don't expect that in the Kingdom at first. That's what you expect in other parts of the world, but not in the Kingdom. I think we all have an assignment in that. Mr Kuzu and others have drawn attention to the fact that people in the Caribbean Netherlands are also faced with higher burdens and that incomes are lagging behind accordingly. This is partly due to the small scale of the islands, which makes them particularly vulnerable, but you can see that since 10-10-10 they have not worked on this at full speed; let me put it this way. That also led me to go to the islands with Secretary of State Van Ark at the time and show her what was going on. I have said it before and I say it again: compliments for her, for how she picked it up and for what she did with it. In the various debates in the Chamber, which were constantly working on this, she said that we want to make the minimum standard of living better step by step, to raise the social minimum and to raise incomes. That's important. If that perspective exists for people who cannot work and who do have to provide for their livelihood, then you can make sure that deep poverty can disappear. You saw that poverty when you were visiting with the IPKO. Mrs Kuik rightly mentioned this in her contribution. You have to make those improvements step by step. Steps have therefore been taken: the disability allowance has been increased to the statutory minimum wage, a supplement has been introduced for AOW beneficiaries with an income below the statutory minimum wage, and family allowances have been increased to almost double compared to 2018. Steps have also been taken in the fields of employment and debt relief. Moreover, in order to further improve the income position of workers, the legal minimum wage in the Caribbean Netherlands has been gradually increased. In doing so, the AOV, the AWW and the state-of-the-art benefits have been increased proportionately. There has also been an improvement in the purchasing power of the islands, thanks to the measures aimed at reducing the cost of living. It's not just about income. If you don't pay the bills anymore, because they rise every day, that's not gonna help you with your purchasing power. As a cabinet, we have invested 3 million euros in expanding the range of social housing. A temporary subsidy has also been granted to reduce the rents of social minima in the private rental sector and the landlord's subsidy in the social rental sector has been increased. The pilot mortgage guarantee that started this year also makes the sales market more attractive for people with lower incomes. It is currently examining how food costs can be reduced. It is therefore a question of improving purchasing power among all types of households and income groups. Raising incomes cannot be separated from reducing the cost of living. It is clear that this will take some time. Let it also be clear that the balance between revenue and expenditure is very fragile. Additional cost increases hit the people on the small islands extra hard. Mr. Chairman. The motion adopted on the island councils of Bonaire and Saba is very understandable. This motion calls on the new government to set a social minimum for Bonaire, Saint-Eustatius and Saba as soon as possible, on the basis of the real cost of living and equivalent to that of the European part. However, the cabinet does not want to take the real costs as a starting point for the social minimum. In setting the benchmark, the cabinet deliberately did not choose to do so, because that would mean taking the too high costs for granted and focusing only on that revenue. That would create an unbalanced situation. So there is all the more reason to do something about these costs. After all, it cannot be the case that the inhabitants of the Caribbean Netherlands with a smaller wallet will not improve anything. At the same time, I would like to say to the Minister for Social Affairs, and now the Secretary of State for Social Affairs after the event, it is important that the social minimum is set in step and in view of the regional context, the capacity of the economy and the competitiveness of the islands. These are things that you may not immediately think about when you look at the income position, but it does do something about employment and competitiveness in relation to the nearby islands. The most important thing is that we not only focus on the tourism sector, but that there is a diversified economy where income can be generated on multiple fronts. This has been the subject of many debates here in the Chamber. I sympathise with the speeches made by several Members to increase the minimum wage and related benefits as from 1 January 2022. Such a step is also in line with the approach taken by the government in 2010 to the social minimum benchmark. It is also in line with the Kralendijk Agreement concluded at Bonaire with the social partners. Members De Vries, Van den Berg and Kikken asked if this cabinet will take steps by 2022. In the debate we had before the summer on the social minimum benchmark, in which Minister Koolmees was still present at the time, this was also discussed with him and he explained that in view of the missionary status of the cabinet, it is not obvious that the cabinet would now take that step on its own. At that time that was based on the idea that the formation would not be completed for too long. However, with support and a concrete proposal from your Chamber, there is a basis for taking this further step by 2022. However, an appropriate proposal to cover the Social Affairs and Employment budget is needed. I would like to point out, however, that raising incomes cannot be separated from reducing the necessary cost of living, as has been discussed repeatedly in the Cabinet and also in previous debates with your Chamber. As far as the cost of living is concerned, we have recently been faced with setbacks that affect all the people on the islands. I mention higher costs for energy, internet and water. This is still separate from the recent global increase in gas and electricity prices. Mrs Van den Berg asked whether the Caribbean Netherlands would also be included in the debate on possible compensation or mitigation measures. In principle, the Caribbean Netherlands has a similar approach to that of the European Netherlands. I would say that it is reasonable for the Caribbean Netherlands to be involved in the decision-making process on possible compensation. Let me put it very carefully, because that is a debate that is still taking place at the moment, also on the basis of studies being carried out. As you know, Internet costs are also high in the Caribbean. The Secretary of State for EZK is currently considering the possibility of extending the corona grant for fixed internet for a further six months. The extension of this subsidy is desirable because otherwise a huge increase in costs would occur at once on 1 January. We were just talking about occasional and structural. Of course, it's up to a new cabinet to see how you're going to do it in the longer term. But we must bear in mind that the revenue side and the expenditure side must remain in balance. Mr Ceder also expressed concern about energy prices in subsidies on energy. It's gonna expire. At present, the fixed connection rate for both electricity and water is already structurally subsidised by the Ministry of Electricity, and IenW, in terms of water, at the European-Dutch cost level. At present, the Ministry of IenW has no additional budget to take structural additional measures on the costs of drinking water. The State Secretary of EZK is investigating the possibility of investing in its policy participation Bonaire Fuel Terminals. This could allow the terminal to invest in a solar or wind energy project. I'm very much in favour of that. A number of your Members referred to this yesterday, when it comes to good investment, which leads to lower structural burdens. The goal is therefore to find an optimal mix of speed, cost reduction and sustainability, as the motion Chicken asked earlier. In all solutions, it is important that production is co-ordinated responsibly in order to ensure security of energy supply. Ultimately, it is up to the next cabinet to decide on possible structural measures to reduce the cost of energy and drinking water. This brings me to the end of the poverty block, Mr President.

That link is in the review of the energy tax, so that's also in all the thirteen chips we sent around Fit for 55 around mid-July or late July. The part about the energy tax review, that's what this is about. And I will see if we can add a comparison with other countries. So I think that that last part could perhaps be added, and that the other items may already be in Mr Dassen's possession. If he wants to take a look at this and then have supplementary questions, I can come back to that in a more specific way. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Mrs Van Esch tabled a motion, but first indicated that she wanted a judgment on another motion. Then there was a motion in part No. 349 of Mrs Van Esch's report on firewood, which we ask the municipalities to give serious follow-up to reports. I don't think that's a problem. Judgment Room. Shell's president-director has been asked because of her knowledge of the safety situation in the industry. Someone's already on the committee from the environmental point of view. I'm dissuading the motion. Mr Laçin mentioned Tata Steel, with the request to remain in good contact with the deputy. Absolutely, I'm very regular. Then the motion to part No. 351 on asbestos in cosmetic products. It's already forbidden. Enforcement is at NVWA. That's what I said in the AO. I will ask the colleague of VWS who is responsible for the NVWA for an opinion on this motion.

There is at least one point on which Mr Pijlman and I agree. That is the percentage he has just mentioned of what is being generated by so-called renewable energy at the moment. He mentioned 5.3, I mentioned 5.5. I was even a little higher, but I'm sure that's within the margin of error. But of course there are other countries, such as Sweden, that have a piece of cake. They just put a wheel under a waterfall and Kees is done. Electricity is virtually free: white coal, as it is called. We can never handle that, but we can handle nuclear power. Why doesn't D66 come up with that idea? If you talk about saving on CO emissions, there is really only one real alternative to electricity generation, and that is nuclear energy. Why don't you come up with that?

That's what I just said. We have, of course, made every effort in recent years to see what can be done to meet the Urgendavonnis. This is a big part of it. Coal-fired power stations are completely closed, which is simply not possible, because with the security of supply in the Netherlands we will have a great danger or problem. I don't think you'd like that either. As I have just said, we will have to look very carefully in the future at what additional efforts we can make, because I really do see that challenge. I would also say that it is ultimately about achieving our goals by 2030 and 2050. We all care about that. Those targets will be raised. This cabinet, if there is no new cabinet yet, or the new cabinet around the summer, will have to talk to a lot of people.

Yes, but the nuance was in the statement Mr. Heinen gave. I am not afraid to give an opinion at some point, but it was about the possible misunderstanding that I thought he was asking for a letter on a decision, a specific possible new ECB instrument. Well, the Dutch Bank is in the governing council. The Dutch Bank has an opinion on this and shares it publicly. That's how we settled the trial. What I would like to do, however, is to indicate, in a broader paper on the euro area, what the potential risks are, what the different bodies, including the ECB, can and what we expect from them. For example, Mr Heinen asked earlier whether we believe that the ECB's traditional role has been exceeded. I would also like to comment on stability: does the ECB not do too much; is there not too much intervention from the ECB? These are all things that we naturally have to debate with each other without, of course, knowing in this case that we are going to change a jota. If the ECB says tomorrow 'we are going to do A, B, C', it will do so in the independence of the role of the ECB, but the debate on this is important. I think those two can find each other. We haven't even had the debate yet, but I'm not going to send a letter tonight stating what I think of a possible decision by the ECB reported in the media. I'll take a look at the questions. Mr. Alkaya of the SP said that it seems that the cabinet is facing signals from society with distrust, as opposed to signals from business. Why don't households get five years of tax deferral if companies do? Yes, this is the same as the arrangement has been agreed with you, I believe. In the generic aid package, for example, employees were paid wages by the NOW scheme. That was part of the generic aid package. In some cases, restrictive measures have prevented companies from making sales. I understand the social sentiment that Mr Alkaya raises, but these are very specific arrangements. For the average citizen in need, there are other measures, through a different form of support that is already provided regularly, corona or no corona. Mr Van Dijck of the PVV asked for a reflection on the profits of large companies and on the risk of bankruptcy in small companies in corona time. I think that I and the Prime Minister have already explained what was intended with the generic support package: to provide certainty for entrepreneurs, to help them quickly and to mitigate the negative effects of corona as much as possible. But generic support also has its drawbacks. This also means that it does not end up very specific and completely in the right place. For example, it was also found in non-viable companies with low labour productivity and in companies in sectors not affected by corona. That is, of course, an element on which you say: can this be changed in the future and is that possible within our system at all? We're getting researched from preparedness, I'd almost say more targeted support, preferably sectoral, is an option if we're dealing with a corona crisis or another type of crisis. You will be informed about this after the summer. Mr Nijboer rightly asked about concerns about ICT. Well, in this case, we share it entirely, I'm afraid. It would be better if it weren't. The Tax Office already has the so-called multi-annual improvement initiatives. I believe that you had a technical briefing on this in January. A prerequisite for improving the ICT situation is the recruitment and retention of experienced personnel. Of course, we can all count and see that because of the current tight labour market this is extremely difficult. So that's a huge obstacle, but that's new, or relatively new. That does not explain, of course, how all the ICT problems in the Tax Administration have been able to accumulate. I know that the expectation has been expressed that the ICT system will have to be set up in 2025 in such a way that legislation is much more possible than in previous political stages. Anyway, that's three more years, and that's not exactly satisfactory. I also get the warning that the impact of new legislation and recovery policies, for example on box 3, must be constantly assessed and what this means for the maintenance and necessary modernisation of systems. Yeah, it's what I said: anything but satisfying. But there's a lot of work going on. Mr Grinwis asked: at the General Reviews a motion had been adopted to investigate and counter non-use; how is the investigation going, and how do we meet the motion? The evaluation of the Awir, the implementation and service of supplements, which will be completed in the summer, will include non-use. And, of course, figures on the extent of the non-use of the care allowance and the child-related budget are updated in accordance with the Grinwis motion. And literature research is also done on behavioural aspects and causes of non-use. Mr Nijboer asked: is the cabinet prepared to question the main issue of fiscal expenditure? "Fiscal arrangements" rather. Of course, we always have to take a critical look at tax regulations. This is also reflected in the policy and implementation agenda shared with your Chamber last week. It states that tax regimes can only be justified if they are effective and effective. Because, of course, a number of tax regimes have recently been assessed negatively. Before the summer 2023 you will be informed in a plan of approach. Mr Grinwis asked whether an update could be given on the implementation of the Grinwis motion. It does not say at which motion Mrs Grinwis, I must say, but I think it is about the complexity of tax regulations. During 2022, we strengthened supervision within the Ministry of Finance in the policy and implementation agenda. You've already had it. Well, I already named that. There's gonna be a plan of action. Mr Van Dijck has asked if the cabinet has a crisis approach in Groningen so that we can intervene more. Wait a minute: "Mr Van Dijck has asked whether the cabinet or a crisis approach in Groningen is needed so that the cabinet can take more action." I do not think that the phrase has been taken up entirely here in the haste. But the essence is: the Secretary of State for Mining discussed with your Chamber last week about Groningen, and about the progress of the damage recovery and the reinforcement operation. And you also exchanged with the Prime Minister. Mr Eppink asked whether the cabinet could make the real cost of migratory flows clear on the budget. The annual report of the Ministry of Justice and Security, Article 37, shows the expenditure incurred for admission, stay and departure from the Netherlands of foreign nationals, as well as obtaining Dutch citizenship. That's it.

Mr. Chairman. Mr Ceder is not only the last speaker, but also the last coalition party to speak. He was my last hope. That is why my question is whether arms supplies are really so sensible? There are also rules, such as the criteria for arms exports. They say no weapons to conflict zones, no weapons to countries where the region is unstable. With this cabinet sustainability becomes a celebration for the elite, because hundreds of millions of grants go to Tesla's for the rich. It's just gonna happen. To social tenants sitting through this cabinet with a towering energy bill, the Minister says very nicely: we will stop this arrangement. 80% of the money for sustainability goes to the most wealthy Dutch. That can't be true, can it? I would like to know from the Minister whether she is prepared to invest in the low-income and middle-income people right now by setting up a master plan for isolation.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I was visiting Victor and Hans yesterday. They both live in a rental house in Zoetermeer. Just over a year ago, they got six solar panels on their roof. They were at first a little hesitant and hesitant about it. But I was visiting them yesterday. I got a cup of coffee. Then I asked, "What do you think?" They said: well, actually this is very nice, because our energy bill is about €200 to €250 lower this year. If that housing association had also dealt with their house and made sure that it was well insulated, then of course the energy bill would have fallen even further and Victor and Hans would have suffered much less from these enormous energy price increases that are now there. The same goes for a cop, a teacher, a nurse who owns a store. Of course, he or she wants to isolate his or her house. But it will take just €20,000 or €25,000 to do that. And yes, they don't have that money on the shelf to do that. And then they won't be able to get those subsidies that are there for this, because you can only apply for them afterwards. I would like to make a number of proposals today to make and maintain this whole climate transition, which is, above all, a social transition as far as the Labour Party is concerned, feasible and affordable. I come now with proposals on the built environment, but I will come forward with all kinds of proposals in the coming months, including in the other areas. Firstly, the PvdA welcomes the national isolation programme which is also included in the coalition agreement. The problem is that, for example, the agent, teacher or nurse with his own house does not just have a lot of money on the shelf to make the house more sustainable. That is why the concrete proposal of the Labour Party to extend the Heat Fund, which already exists, is much further. An agent and a teacher should be able to borrow €25,000 at 0% interest so that they can participate in the insulation of the house and put those solar panels on the roof. For example, they can reduce their energy bill and contribute to climate change and to less dependence on gas. The Labour Party wants the housing corporations, like Victor and Hans, to be obliged to fill the roofs with solar panels as soon as possible to get that energy bill down and that all homes that are still very drafty and where the gas is being run through are well insulated by 2030. The Labour Party wants the third proposal that house milkers are also obliged to do so: solar panels on the roof, let the tenants participate and make sure that these rental homes are properly insulated. Now squeaks and cracks the power grid. We heard this last week in a debate. This scaling-up of solar energy is possible if the system operators are instructed to simply achieve much more storage capacity in the grid. We've heard that's possible. This brings together the energy transition, the rising gas prices, but also the necessary growth of renewable energy in the built environment. But in the very short term, of course, that will not help us at all. An agent, a nurse or teacher does not have just over €1,000 lying on the shelf to pay higher gas prices. The PvdA therefore wants the Minister and the Cabinet to fix this. The statement by Minister Kaag that no compensation will be made in the very short term is totally unacceptable as far as the Labour Party is concerned. This compensation must simply be provided, because people simply cannot do this. I'd like to get a response from the Minister. With these rising gas prices, you'd almost forget that we're here in the climate debate. That is a terribly important debate, because our beloved country is threatened by climate change. It is therefore a good thing that the goal of the coalition agreement has been raised. It is good that there is a separate minister and it is also very good that this person will play that role in the coming years; congratulations again. It is extremely important, as I have also shown in my example of Hans and Victor, that climate change is being tackled in a fair way. There is talk with the Labour Party about the 35 billion, about the fact that we need to invest it in our country, that we need to get rid of the gas and that the CO pollution goes down. But the life of that cop, that teacher, that nurse, needs to get better through climate policy. It's possible. You can isolate houses and take them off the gas, you can electric from A to B with cheaper and better ov and with electric subcars. We can generate a lot more green jobs, with a green industrial policy, than all those fossil jobs we have today. We will need a working guarantee fund, but I will make proposals on this later. It can be feasible and affordable, but the coalition must really change course. For the past four years, that has not been the policy. Then the subsidies ended up twice as much with the rich as with the people on less high incomes. Then the rich could buy an electric car, put solar panels on their roof and benefit from the subsidies, but people who didn't have access to that capital couldn't. Hence our proposal: make sure that these people can invest 0% interest in their homes and benefit from it. I am therefore looking forward to a response from this Minister. Climate policy must indeed be fair so that everyone can experience it in a feasible and affordable way. I also agree with the bright green words of my colleague from GroenLinks. It's nice that we complement each other so well. It is very important that climate policy is bright green and bright red. I think there will be more proposals for this. I would like to repeat two questions from her to the Minister, firstly the question of timing. I had the debate with the Minister of Industry yesterday. He's not gonna save May 1st. Then how are we going to know at some point whether it adds up to 60%? Secondly, there was the very important question of whether the Minister has the power to make these wonderful goals public. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Motion in part No. 76: It will not surprise you that I advise against it. I have already said that I do not think it is wise to withdraw from the Energy Charter, because then we will no longer participate in the discussion and place ourselves outside the ring.

Once again, we cannot just talk about palm oil and just look for a solution in this context, but I think that the Minister's portfolio of development cooperation and its responsibility for sustainable development objectives is really inadequate if she does not want to recognise that greater system changes are needed. If we eat less meat and dairy in the rich West, a lot of land will be released. We will then be able to grow oil crops in Europe. Indeed, they ask for a little more land than those high-efficiency plantations, but we can just have that. The Minister here shields with small farmers and says that they must be the carriers of a sustainable food system, which I acknowledge but not of such monocultures in which they have to work with their children in order to earn a decent living. I think the Minister should not ignore these effects. This debate is only about palm oil, but I will certainly come back to the Minister. I think she should acknowledge that the creation of this large-scale monocultures for consumption in the rich West does not fit in with the development goals she claims to pursue as minister for OS.

What's bothering me is this. With regard to the waste water injections, we have a Chamber statement saying: shut them down.
