Thank you, Mr. Chairman. What a crazy word market forces are. It suggests that something works without actually having to work. If the market certainly does not work, there are public interests in play that need to be protected, such as accessible care, proper postal delivery or a well-accessible country with an airport with sufficient destinations. Last week was therefore quite hopeful. We could all see that a number of parties who believed blindly in the functioning of the market for years now seemed more realistic. Ladies and gentlemen, public interests are not in safe hands with people who want to maximize profits. The fact that the market is being reduced in sectors of public interest is therefore simply sensible and I welcome it as a socialist. I therefore hope that buying a state interest in Air France-KLM is a trend break with the naive policy of previous years. If so, I'll ask the cabinet. And what does this mean, for example, for the planned privatisations? Think of De Volksbank, ABN AMRO or Eneco, the greenest energy company, which is also on sale. When I read the answers to our written questions about the secret operation of the cabinet, which only came in yesterday at 10:00 p.m., and when I put them next to the letters of the cabinet-Balkenende II, especially of the two VVD-persons of that time, Zalm and Schultz, I can only conclude that the Netherlands was naive when KLM was taken over by Air France. There has simply been gambling with the Dutch public interest. For years our interests were not in our own hands, but in the hands of the market and the French government. Only a few buttery agreements were the basis for this. Why was there no participation in the holding company at the time, in 2003, I ask the cabinet. The cabinet says in the written answers that this was simply not considered at the time. Is there nothing else known at the Ministry of Finance or at the former Ministry of Transport and Water State, today Infrastructure and Water State? Although things were bad with KLM at the time, I can't imagine that it wasn't considered at all at the time to take a share in the holding company. Therefore, I would like to ask you once again very sharply: in the run-up to the acquisition of KLM in 2003, there were no opinions or notes on whether or not to acquire shares in the holding company, and if so, what was the point of not doing it at the time? I would find it extremely strange and unlikely if this were not discussed at all in the ministries at the time. This is why I will shortly be proposing that a parliamentary inquiry be carried out into the situation surrounding the takeover of KLM in 2003. This must be prevented, at all costs, in the future. What is even more clear from the documents is that it was in fact the agreement to reduce the shareholder interest together with France. But if the French state is the only culprit, I ask the cabinet. Does the cabinet really think that the public interest of the Netherlands is safe with other shareholders, for example with state-owned companies such as China Eastern Airlines, which is already a major shareholder in the holding company? Or are other foreign shareholders or investors going to work hard for the Netherlands and the thousands of people working at Schiphol? Of course they won't. What difference does it make if the public interest of the Netherlands is threatened by a foreign government or by shareholders, by the market? Can we assume that this cabinet will always protect our public interests, regardless of who is threatening them, governments or market parties? Whether or not the government should intervene in the market is governed by the so-called Note Participation Policy. It dates back to 2013. In its written replies, the Cabinet states that it sees no reason to change this 2013 note following the purchase of Air France-KLM shares. A screening is only planned in 2020. That's way too late. I started by saying that thinking about the market, about what the market can and above all not, seems to be changing. Fortunately, the cabinet must learn from the mistakes that have been made in the past. A new and more realistic view of the skills and incompetence of the market must translate into new policies. For example, the 2013 Note Participation Policy states that making returns is a criterion for entering or not entering a business. But at Air France-KLM, that wasn't the trade-off, was it? It was all about the public interest and commitment in the company, wasn't it? That old policy isn't enough now, is it? I therefore believe that it is appropriate to review this policy as soon as possible and not to wait until 2020. Is the cabinet prepared to do so? Finally, the exceptional way in which this Chamber was informed of the nearly 750 million spent. Mr President, you know better than I do: budget law lies with the States General. We have the right to assess state expenditure and then, if necessary, approve or reject it. Did the Chamber have the opportunity to reject this purchase in advance? I'm really wondering. The De Wit Committee was clear: the Chamber should be able to control these types of acute purchases in advance and afterwards. It is possible to choose the route of confidential information. This is, of course, quite understandable in this case, and this is also apparent from the written answers. But what if a majority of Members of Parliament had not agreed to the purchase of shares at the time? Could we then debate it beforehand? I doubt it. Members of parliament even had to sign a confidentiality agreement to get the information at all. What if MPs hadn't signed the statement? Could they have done their constitutional task at all? I wonder, Mr. Chairman. The way in which this process has been conducted is more like informing the Chamber, while this is really about the budget right of the Chamber. And although I understand specifically this purchase of the cabinet, I do not know whether I can support this method of working, this way of informing the Chamber. In any case, this should not lead to a precedent for the future; we must discuss this further in the Committee on the Rules of Procedure and then draw our conclusions. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman. I'll start with the questions that have been asked. Then I'll come to the motions. I'll start with Mrs Teunissen. I note that it is not easy for me to satisfy Mrs Teunissen. In earlier deadlines, it was deeply concerned about deforestation and concerns about under-planting. In this contribution, she is concerned that forest planting is affecting biodiversity. It must remain as much forest for Mrs Teunissen, with military precision: it must not be less, but it must not be less. In its direction, I can only point out that this proposal concerns the phasing out of coal for electricity generation. I hope that at least I have her sympathy on that point. It's not about other things right now. I will give some thought to how this military standstill of forest areas in the world will then take shape. But we are going to talk about this in the halls. I have also listened to Mrs Faber and Mr Otten. Mr Pijlman asked me once again to go into this coordination. In all honesty, I cannot add much more to that than we are very seriously engaged in that pentalateral context. These TSOs really do their job and the Netherlands and Germany are closely aligned, in all areas, not only on the electricity networks, but also explicitly on hydrogen and also on the CCS infrastructure. It's all about these things. Could it be sooner? That is actually what Mr Vendrik also asked and Mr Pijlman is asking for it now. Yeah, it could be. If ETS is really going to do its job, then of course it will be over at some point. Then there is no such thing as a leak. So it would help enormously, in all kinds of ways. I have heard his call for vigilance on biomass very well. He also asks what we're gonna do with Urgenda. The section on Hemweg contained in this proposal for 2020 is, of course, explicitly aimed at this. There has been no other purpose in bringing it forward than Urgenda. There are many other things to do. I believe that Mr Vendrik asked for it even more precisely. I shall deal with this later. But Hemweg plays a role in relation to this bill. The fact that we would not be involved in thorium at all is not true, because there is state subsidy to NRG, also for nuclear research, indirectly via the lump sum of OCW for TU Delft, which works on the fourth generation nuclear. The Reactor Institute Delft is the coordinator of a European project in this field. So we do all kinds of things about that. A lot of countries do. Of course, we hope for a breakthrough there too. Mr Pijlman also pointed out that the SDE++ had not yet been designed on hydrogen. Now the question is whether hydrogen saves an sich as a medium CO. That is not the case in the immediate sense. It's an energy carrier. A power cable also does not save CO. But even if that had been the case, we still have to deal with a very uneven race, because the whole learning curve is still going on with hydrogen. It is therefore a very uneven competition to allow it to compete with developed techniques on the basis of cost-effectiveness. This is still relatively in its infancy, so that would not be a fair match. It is therefore important that we arrange for hydrogen in a different way. We do this through, among other things, the DEI, the demonstration scheme. That's 40 million a year and it grows to 60 million. That's gonna make half a billion in ten years anyway. There are also research programmes. But we are also working hard on all kinds of conditions, certification, standardisation, safety and a vision of market organisation, because how should we deal with this medium? In all these ways, we're dealing with hydrogen. We now have hundreds of companies in sight that are also planning to do something with hydrogen. In the north I have also spoken a few myself, but also in other parts of the country I will report soon. Something is happening in all kinds of areas. It is now important to select a few really concrete projects as well. On the working arrangements Hemweg I will come back at a later moment. Mr Vendrik asked the most comprehensive question about Urgenda, so I am now answering it most comprehensively. That's what I attribute to his question. We agreed on a package in June. That includes the Hemweg. According to the experts, there was an estimated 3 megaton effect on top of the Hemweg. We decided on a further gear package in November. Then there was another nitrogen package with a speed measure in it. This also soon adds up to CO savings. But we're not done yet. It's clear there's a verdict. I'm committed to that. I have to do everything I can to get it. The perspective is that further nitrogen measures are also needed. They go hand in hand with greenhouse gases to a great extent, because when we talk about ammonia on the nitrogen side, a lot of ammonia measures are synchronised with methane measures. That's a greenhouse gas. NO measures on the nitrogen side often run in parallel with CO reduction. So we have two issues in common, but one set of rules might work for both. So we're just gonna keep going. I never radiated that I felt the verdict served with the middle value. I never said that. I know what I have left to go. I don't suppose I'm gonna stop at midterm either. I know there's still work to be done. I know that a lot is still happening and that all kinds of things will have to roll out of the band step by step. I'm aware of that. I know I'm not ready. I have just said a few words about the North Sea Agreement. Whether Mr Vendrik calls it a growth agenda or a transition agenda, I leave it to him. I think his party wants it to be a transition agenda, but as an economist I can also appeal to sensible growth. I hear him say "wide prosperity." Let me put it this way: if broad prosperity is the best approach to happiness, then it counts, but also our earning ability. In the end, we will also have to be able to pay our pensions and the AOW. Care is getting more and more expensive. The ageing population is on the rise. We have to pay for all this. That should go hand in hand. That hydrogen or specifically the transition should be prominent in the investment fund, let me put it in the middle, because I do so together with my colleague in the finance department. So what we're thinking about will be announcements. I have already stated that it will be prominent in InvestNL's portfolio. I've already reported that in this Chamber. Are the corresponding CO rights withdrawn from the market? Yeah, but not by the Netherlands, because that's what the Market Stability Reserve is for. That mechanism consumes the excess rights itself. So we don't have to buy them anymore. This is a fantastic reform, which has been pushed by the Netherlands to a large extent. Sharon Dijksma deserves all praise for this masterful reform from 2016. More reforms are needed, but this was a very good move from her. I listened carefully to Mr Van Kesteren with his final legal questions. I have not been able to convince Mrs Gerkens in the field of biomass, I hear. But on one point, I do not think she does justice to my argument. I'd like to mention that. I'm aware that I didn't convince her. That is entirely up to me, because it was my intention to convince her as well. But I find the term "wave the doubts away" too thin. I've submitted a serious argument. I didn't rob anything away. She refers to twigs and leaves, but I never mentioned twigs and leaves. I mentioned the residual streams. Let me put it this way. My attempt was more serious than she suggests. I can tell I didn't convince her, but that's something else. How many petajoules do the coal plants give? Only three of them will be left by 2030. I have studied the hypothetical case that in one way or another all three would run with a reasonable number of hours of rotation, say 6,000 or 7,000. That would amount to 80 petajoules. That's it. It doesn't even matter so much on which fuel that is, because the capacity shouldn't be that different.

Mr Amhaouch speaks, so this is a perfect opportunity to interrupt my old friend again. You are talking about the need for international trust. We are of course a very small country, although with the sixteenth economy of the world. But I wonder: should we not, given what has been happening recently, also restore internal confidence a little bit? Shell and Unilever are all leaving. Foreign trade becomes a foreign walk. The location climate is under pressure. That is also part of foreign trade. The competitive position is incredibly affected. We are very busy with climate and all kinds of fun things. The charges are going up. We have also talked about China in the past. We have hardly been able to do anything about China falling over us. SMEs are deeply affected by this. Do you agree with me that we should also do something internally, instead of having a wonderful story here about all kinds of foreign things that we hardly have any influence on?

Don't bluff. Don't. I think that's very unwise. We have a history with that. You're bluffing about that the CPB would say you shouldn't take any extra action right now. That's bullshit. The CPB says that the consequences that exist today are not only due to rising energy prices, but also to structural wrong policies. It says that something needs to be done structuralally to help people with the lowest incomes and middle incomes. That is something other than that it would say that we should not intervene now. You simply repeat your answers, which you also give to colleagues all the time. They're just the same answers. I asked you a very specific question. I'm gonna stand here until I get an answer to that question. What proposals did the cabinet itself come up with? You have only responded to our proposals and said what cannot be done. What else did you come up with?

I would like to comment on it, because in the Provincial States you often see a lot of residents coming to us. They say: you will then be included in the framework of the energy transition and the climate agenda, and there you will also be very much concerned about taking part in the plans for windmills, but at the end of the story they will just be in your backyard. A new example of this cabinet is the heat pumps that will be placed in 2026. So it's only compulsion that hits the drum. So I do not really see what is democratic about it, and I do not understand why you have no confidence in the current functional management and that you want to throw it overboard.

We in the Netherlands have said that growth, as proposed in the Climate Agreement, must come from advanced biofuels and not from food crops. That's the deal we made. This is not going to attract additional palm oil, which Mr Madlener is talking about, because the growth comes from advanced biofuels, that is, from waste and waste streams. That's where we want to get the growth out of in the Netherlands.

I don't think it's ever nice when people start paying more taxes, but in the end, the question is what do you do about it as a government. One billion is now being released to build additional homes. It could have been chosen not to. It has been chosen to charge up to 1 billion less in landlord tax so that there is more space to build homes. Mr. Chairman. I was talking about various measures to share the scarcity fairly. Households with higher incomes are going to pay more. So the skewer doesn't have to be evicted from his home and can just stay there, but is asked to make a larger contribution so that the burden of others can remain lower again. Expensive houses in the neighborhood are no longer an obstacle to affordable rent. The WZ value still counts for a maximum of 33%. It is also important to give start-ups a fair chance against investors. That's why we got a letter from Secretary of State Menno Snel about the treatment in box 3. I will not go into too much detail because it is fiscally complicated. The investigation of lower borrowing capacity for buy-to-let homes and the investigation of lower transfer tax for start-ups will also contribute to that fair opportunity vis-à-vis investors. The Minister indicated that he would be able to inform us about this in October. Can the Minister state what progress has been made on the development of these measures? I think this is all very nice measures, and I welcome them, but I have also spent the last few months trying to create an emergency button to counter disproportionately high rents. Unfortunately, the scarcity of housing remains for a while, but meanwhile, bad landlords are struggling with usury rents and asshole behavior. I understand that this matter is complex, but I was wondering if the Minister could tell us what is going on with the development of this emergency button? And shouldn't we also look at the maximisation of rent increases, so that the effect isn't destroyed after a year? Another button we can turn on is the energy load. Less gas fired, less money tapped. A real no-regret measure is to isolate, but to tenants with only glass and without good insulation the website of the Empire says: turn the stove up a bit. Most subsidies are for property owners or landlords, while building wall insulation is already earned after three years and there are also opportunities for tenants locally, in Amsterdam and Leiden, for example. Why is there no national subsidy for tenants who do not want to wait for their landlord with sustainability measures? The Climate Agreement agreed that the taxation of gas should be increased and that it should be reduced on electricity. All new buildings become gasless and more gaps go off the gas. This is how we achieve the key climate targets by 2030. It was also agreed in the Climate Agreement that the right of initiative for tenants to get rid of the gas would be increased. However, tenants are still dependent on investments made by the landlord or corporation. How can tenants enforce sustainability of their property with their landlords and how can we ensure that sustainability for tenants will be cost-neutral or even advantageous? Because then we'll get everyone involved in making our homes more sustainable.

Mr. Chairman. When Mrs Mulder reported this morning that it was a thank-you day, I saw from the minister's body language that he had no idea what that was about. Thank you, yes. In the Netherlands there has been a habit of praying and thanking for a good harvest since the Middle Ages. Prayer day in spring, thank you in autumn. And as industrialization increased, the thank-you day for crop became a thank-you day for crop and labor. So let me just start today by thanking all those entrepreneurs who are fighting for the preservation of jobs and for the survival of their business. They form the backbone of the Dutch economy. But I also look with gratitude at a robust government that has built buffers and can now create a temporary safety net to take the worst hits. Mr. Chairman. For the Christian Union, the company is a community of values, where people work together for a common goal. We shape this community of values by how employer and employee interact and how they take responsibility for the impact of the company on the environment, the natural environment and society, here and far away. The company as a community of values is the foundation for an economy in which relationships between people are central and in which we behave as good stewards for creation. An economy that we want to pass on to our children and grandchildren, one that offers room for economic growth, but also peace and attention to what really matters. In that we take some nice steps. The cabinet has taken over my proposal for the social enterprise, the bvm. As far as the Christian Union is concerned, the bvm is the banner for that economy of the future. The company with a social mission will increasingly become the standard and ever less the exception. In addition, we see the choices for imvo and for Rhineland-Palatinate conditions in case of state aid to individual companies that this cabinet formulated at the beginning of May. We see the adopted motion on the national company guarantee that can further shape these ideas and we see plenty of attention for family businesses, including from the political point of view. Family businesses are the example of the company as a community of values with by definition a long-term focus. That is the Netherlands, that is enterprise and we want to cherish these companies. At the start of the corona crisis, we saw a number of companies changing quickly, but it was unheard of that we had to get the most vital products with an air bridge from Asia, with weeks of delay and only after political pressure. We need a manoeuvrable, innovative manufacturing industry that makes and exports smart products. The economic basis is also our manufacturing industry in the 21st century. The Netherlands must learn technologically and in terms of production to stop its own pants together with its neighbors. I would like to hear from the cabinet about the implementation of the Heerma/Segers motion on strategic dependencies of vital sectors. But you can never predict exactly what you need in the future, so don't suddenly build a mouth cap factory. We need a versatile and agile manufacturing industry, with smart, practically trained technicians. Technicians are literally vital. That's why I'm going to focus on the three m's, people, means and measures. People first. Even with today's unemployment, there are major shortages in the manufacturing industry. We lack tens of thousands of practically trained professionals, while at the same time many recently graduates do not know how to get a job. Vocational education in science and technology must be made more accessible, including in study costs. We need to invest heavily in technical VMBO, MBO and HBO training. Until universities, we must make these studies attractive where employers are raving at the gates when there is a graduation ceremony. Does the cabinet feel this urgency with me and does the cabinet share my view that we should dare again to steer the influx into education? There should be a brake on training which has a lean labour market perspective, especially in times of crisis when many people need to be retrained. How is the cabinet going to steer this so that we can train the professionals of the future? That is an EZ question for me and not just an OCW question. The second m stands for means. Investing in innovation pays off. That is why it is a good thing that the Growth Fund is going to be there. What does everything I have said in this regard about long-term focus, agile manufacturing industry and training professionals for the Growth Fund mean that we have to take this green and circular future into our hands? How are we going to ensure that the whole country benefits from the Growth Fund, knowing that this innovative manufacturing industry is also located in Twente, in the Achterhoek, around Brainport, near Chemelot, in Southeast Drenthe? How does the Growth Fund strengthen our earning capacity across the country? And how's it gonna relieve the Randstad? Mr. Chairman. The cabinet supports R&D with the Wbso scheme. Very well, but isn't it also time to look at an extended first disc or a new second disc, to stimulate companies to do more about innovation and not just make it cheaper? Very well that the Secretary of State supports sustainable shipbuilding on a multiannual basis, but is the maritime industry also covered by the European recovery fund? After all, we now see that other countries are also supporting their maritime industry. Does the cabinet guard the European level playing field in this very international sector with severe competition? When is the government going to buy something really innovative? The number of SBR projects is still very low. It seems that purchasing departments of governments never think about buying innovation-oriented products, while it allows you to support the Dutch manufacturing industry and SMEs in a very targeted way. Can the Secretary of State ensure that the number of SBR projects increases across the whole range of government, right now, in crisis time? Mr. Chairman. The third m stands for measuring. The calibration of measuring instruments is of great importance for the Dutch manufacturing industry. For years I have been concerned about the availability of measurement standards and the continued existence of high-quality calibration facilities in the Netherlands. The staff turnover at our national measurement institute VSL is high and the corona crisis has made the financial situation more serious than ever before. I still believe that it was a wrong choice by the previous cabinet to reject this institution and put it completely on the market. The need to make a financial contribution now shows that. The basic infrastructure of metrology is vital infrastructure which should be in public hands. But now that it is as it is, the government must at least have control over the services offered by the institute and the unique measurement standards associated with it. I note that the Secretary of State is aware of this, and with her letter to this effect she is taking a number of important steps. However, the various tasks, roles and responsibilities of the Ministry, the Institute and the Board of Experts are still simply too unclear. As the government's concerned controller, I just want to make sure that all the services that are crucial for the Dutch high-tech manufacturing industry are continued, crisis time or no crisis time. I'd like a response. Mr. Chairman. Then there's the climate. We see that the Netherlands is becoming greener and cleaner, but we need to take additional steps in our care for creation. The Christian Union believes it is important that we build a climate-neutral economy and society together with citizens, cooperatives and entrepreneurs. The KEV shows that it needs a strong tooth in the coming years, with the major challenges of heat production and doubling energy savings. A national isolation program as advocated in the Segers/Klaver motion that helps people to make their homes more sustainable is more urgent than ever. It is therefore a good thing that all sectors of the economy take their responsibility quickly and that there will be a strong CO levy for too many greenhouse gases emitted by industry. But the Council of State is critical. I know the Minister of EZK as a rasoptimist, but more measures are really needed here. In November there will be proposals from a study group. Do I find the Minister at my side when I ask him to look with me at these proposals with an open mind to see what we can quickly pick up so that we do not move on to another cabinet period? Mr. Chairman. There is also a regional and local energy transition, but what I miss is a clear message from the Empire. When the Minister of EZK once again prices a nuclear power station or when the Minister of BZK thinks that all wind on land is going to fall into the sea, municipalities find it a bit more difficult to create support for the local transition. Because why a windmill in my garden, if Mr. Wiebes is going to build a nuclear power plant anyway? Is the Ministry willing to support the municipalities in the local transition in word and deed? And is the Minister prepared to adapt the national rules on local property and citizen participation in such a way that bumps are removed so that this can really get going? Mr. Chairman. The Christian Union and the CDA advocate that most of the Just Transition Fund be used to boost the hydrogen economy in Northern Netherlands. What is the situation with regard to the implementation of the motion for a resolution on this matter? What means and instruments does the Minister provide to enable the scaling-up of the hydrogen economy and thus achieve the objectives set out in the Climate Agreement? I'm closing up. I started with the explanation about thank-you day for crop and labor. And yes, there's a lot to be thankful for, even in crisis time. But gratitude is never complacency. Ora et labora, pray and work. We need to get our hands on a delta plan manufacturing industry, for training professionals, for building a fully circular economy, for innovating and creating the necessary transitions so that we build the 21st century economy, the economy of our children. And maybe we should adjust that age-old habit of a thank-you day for crop and labor to this time of year. A thank-you day for crop, labor and innovation and then the Minister and Secretary of State, knowing them, will probably join us. Thank you.

Can I try to be very sharp? There are two aspects in my head that I completely separate. If that does not work for Mr Wassenberg, he must say so in his response. On one side of the wall is the gas extraction. We need to get it back as soon as possible, not to 12, but to zero. There are no financial considerations not to go back to zero faster than can be. The only consideration is that you have to avoid that by doing it too fast, well, I'm not going to repeat what I just said in cold winters a problem with security of supply comes. I seem to have just turned Groningen and Limburg against each other; Mr Kops just pointed that out to me. I didn't mean to, but I tried to use that example to point out that there would be nationwide risk. Okay, that's one piece. There is no other consideration. There's no ulterior motive not to go back to zero. There's no financial motive; I'm underlining it here again, with capital letters. Do we agree?

Mr. Chairman. During the debate on the Autumn note, I was also here and I was interrupted by my highly valued colleagues from the PvdA and GroenLinks, in particular about the energy bill. I have to say, that was right. At that time, I could not say much more than that in the framework of the Climate Agreement our commitment was to reverse the unfortunate reduction of the discount and preferably more than that. I am really pleased today that we can now have the debate on the Spring Note with and definitely more discount on the energy bill and a shift in the storage of renewable energy towards companies and a heat fund from which home owners can also invest without savings in making their home more sustainable. I hope that my esteemed colleagues will now appreciate these wonderful developments together with me. It is good to reflect together on "June month of agreements" and to look forward to what is needed. Mr. Chairman. There's a lot of beauty in the spring note. Large amounts, but big things are also done with small amounts. Take the approach of anti-Semitism in our country, the approach of jihadism, of drug dumping, the extra money for getting out of prostitution, 41 million extra for science and technology education, and of course the 40 million for the lock at Kornwerderzand. Mr. Chairman. After years of scarcity, the coalition agreement finally offered a new perspective for municipalities. They would greatly improve so that they could properly carry out their extensive tasks. The previous cabinet had intervened hard and now it would be different. The practice, however, has proved to be unwieldy. Mr Nijboer pointed that out. Since 2015 with the Wmo and youth care a number of open-ended schemes have been thrown over the fence and they are almost without exception lacking. It is a good thing that this cabinet came up with large sums of money in the Spring paper. At the same time, we know that for many municipalities these amounts solve barely half of the problem, while for other municipalities this is different. This step-on-step afsystematiek, which in the coalition agreement seemed so good for the municipalities, is in practice a turnoff for them at the moment. Mr Nijboer also pointed out this. What is the Minister's view of this problem? What can he offer congregations and the Chamber? In the run-up to the August decision-making process, is the cabinet prepared to take a round along the municipalities in order to get up to speed on their budget preparation? Mr. Chairman. Two weeks ago, the Commission's regulation of work came up with its first pen fruit title in what kind of country do we want to live in? This question is one of the most pressing questions of our time, because the labour market is making it more flexible. It is not the case that we stand by and look at it purely. I am thinking of the Labour Market Act in balance, compulsory disability insurance and minimum rates forzzp'ers. But it's gonna take more, and fast. For one in five workers work in temporary employment and one in eight workers work inzzp'er. It takes about ten more years, and only half of the workers have a fixed contract. And that is not a natural phenomenon, but the result of too large differences between these groups. It is a gap, creating an unprecedented flexibilisation almost unnoticed. Young people are the main victims of this. It is precisely the Minister of Finance who should be concerned about this. Why? Well, this minister "threatens" to become the prime minister with purely budgetary surpluses due to years of economic growth and prudent fiscal policies. And while the cabinet is investing again in crucial public tasks that have been over-involved in the years to come, we find daily that it is not easy to bring the service back to an acceptable level. Whether it's the Tax Administration, the Food and War Authority, the UWV: the financial attacks have taken their toll and you don't just make up for that in one cabinet period. This alone is a reason why, in the next recession, automatic stabilisers should do their job so that public interests, good service and so on are not compromised. But one of the questions that comes out behind the Borstlap committee is whether the automatic stabilisers will be stable enough in future in times of recession. Will they still be stable enough? And has not continued flexibilisation in the labour market triggered a process whereby, in the next recession, massively flexible workers will be dumped, or forced to work at lower wages, andzzp'ers will be allowed to bite? Does this minister have sufficient control over the impact of this flexibilisation trend on public finances? Because the figures for economy and society have been wonderful on the outside for a number of years since we crawled out of the deep valley after the crisis, but let's not forget that we skated on thin ice all this time. Let us therefore work after the pension agreement and the Climate Agreement to close one of the biggest gaps of our time, a real social issue, with a labour market agreement. For although work is not everything, work is valuable and contributes to meaning and dignity for many. Thank you.

As the political elite is gaining more and more power, more and more power is being taken away from the people. The huge tax burden and regulatory burden are increasing the pressure on SMEs. Our farmers and fishermen are also gradually being devastated by increasingly suffocating rules. As a citizen, you'll only have a job with the government or a multinational that will set up your life together: what you eat, how much energy you use, how many miles you can drive, or you can still fly and what you can think. And those tricky populists you take to court, demonize and shut you out. Their supporters are blackmailing you financially by threatening to take their jobs. How much longer are we gonna take this? Why are we being led to this European slaughter? Why are we being robbed of our freedom? It is high time we got out of that madly runaway European train before it derails even further, and we escaped through the emergency exit. There is no other way out of taking back our sovereignty and setting up our own lives. We shouldn't be afraid. Fear is a bad counselor. We must take back our country and our freedom. The only exit is a nexit. That's it, Mr. Chairman.

I think we need to find another time to talk about Saint Anthony. Then as a Catholic from South Limburg you should explain what role he plays in your life. We're gonna talk at another time. Madam President. If we are thinking about parts of the Netherlands that have been abandoned, then there is one province that I would like to mention in particular. That's Groningen. Yesterday afternoon I had a digital meeting with members of our party and representatives, mainly from Groningen and partly from Friesland and Drenthe. What has remained with me are not so much the very concrete complaints, but above all the despair and the deep disappointment that there was: do they see us? It took a torch ride to make it clear again: "Look at us. Listen to us." I find that painful. I find it painful to see that in my own party, to see that people doubt whether we see them. But I also find it painful to see where that extra gas extraction came from. Was there really no alternative? It is so contrary to the decision of the previous cabinet. I also find it complicated what the Prime Minister said, namely that there could also be a risk with security. Is that right? That's impossible, isn't it? If we have a balance between gas extraction and safety, doesn't safety always have to have the primacy? Can he explain that again? It is good that the cabinet has raised the budget for the subsidy scheme for the Groningen houses, but it was painful and embarrassing to see how people had to line up. They've experienced it as humiliating. It was painful that there had to be a fuss before that arrangement was completed. The bottleneck was inadequate. Think also of the timing of decisions. Just before Christmas, there was the decision to move the child's heart centre. And then there was Minister Blok, who announced on the last day of his term that this gas extraction is going up. Make a fresh start here, too. I am pleased that there is a special ruler for Groningen and for what is called "Mining." Secretary of State Vijlbrief went to Groningen and had good talks there. I'm happy about that. But how can the recovery and strengthening operation be accelerated and improved? That's the question. Wouldn't it be a good thing if the executive also physically kept office for part of the week, or parts of the year? For example, I know that the town hall in Slochteren is empty, so that could be a beautiful place. Madam President. It is significant that confidence is the smallest and distrust is the greatest at the edges of our country. That is why I am pleased that, for example, there is a perspective on the Lely line, that there is a physical link between regions. That is why I am pleased that regional deals remain possible, that they will be closed again. It is crucial that the government invests in that region and, together with local authorities, is shoulder to shoulder with that perspective. But make it clear that this cabinet is there for the whole of the Netherlands, not only for the Randstad, not only for the cities, but for everyone. That's my passionate appeal to the cabinet. It is not just a cabinet of and for satisfied people, but for every human being. A cabinet where every person counts. In the study of Cuperus and De Voogd it becomes clear that in addition to the places of mistrust there is also a strip of confidence. Colleague Heerma pointed out the same thing. From Zeeland via parts of Zuid-Holland, Utrecht, the Veluwe, to other parts of Gelderland and Overijssel. Indeed, there is another word for it, namely: the Biblet. That's not a strip where people are just rich. It is not a region with only believers. But it is a strip where many people have not forgotten to see each other, where people trust each other, where there is noaberdom. That is why it is so crucial that that government can be trusted and that that government also trusts its citizens. It is crucial that there are once again counters with serving officials, officials who listen, who take someone by hand and seek until the problem is resolved, and that there are servants. That is why it is so important that what has often been made subordinate and often not interesting is now a priority of the cabinet, namely: implementation. The point is that the basis is restored and there is room for human measure in legislation, that an exception can be made if it is simply not just, if it is not true. There must be a basis on which trust can flourish. That is why a good income is needed. You need to be able to live and work. The point is, there's more certainty. There must be room for that society. I told you before: freedom of education is not the toy of confessional parties, but is what the Netherlands is, namely space for difference, space for parents to start their own school. A society without religious stress. A government that is a partner of society. That is why I am pleased that we are continuing social service, the place where young people learn to do something for another and where they are encouraged to see each other. That is why it is a good thing that large law firms also take their share when it comes to social law, that that is not just a hobby of a number of passionate lawyers, but a responsibility of everyone. That is why we in the Christian Union Group also take the pandemic, the virus, as seriously as the social and mental damage in our society in the corona crisis. That is why we as a group are critical of 2G, because it drives people apart and we see much more in measures that require something from all of us, such as testing more often and in more places. Today, an investigation came out that also underlines this. At least what is at odds with working on trust is driving polarization. Those are politicians who talk about the democratically elected government as a totalitarian regime, who talk about the institutions of our rule of law, a fake parliament and fake judges, who talk about the free press baths. Polarisation leads to hatred, to threats, to extra security, to politicians who go from misery to something else, to an unliving society. That is why I would like to ask the cabinet and also propose to do more research into this polarization in the Netherlands, about its costs, but above all about what can be done against it. For example, social media platforms have a responsibility but they do not take it sufficiently. I am very concerned about that. In that strip of confidence also resonates a story Jesus once told. He has a kind of visual story in which there is a king who has before him righteous and unjust. He then speaks to the righteous and says, "You are righteous." When I was thirsty, you gave me a drink. When I was naked, you gave me clothes. When I was in prison, you visited me when I was sick, you visited me, and when I was a stranger, you took me in. But the righteous ask: when then? They had no idea they had done that for the king. Then the king says: you have done so for the slightest of brothers and sisters and therefore for me. This resonates in a bench of Major Bosshardt where a picture of her stands in front of her old house in Amsterdam, in which her image is written in large letters: serving God is serving people, serving people is serving God. I started with St. Anthony. I have now arrived at the Salvation Army via the Biblebelt. I've had the entire ecclesiastical map of the Netherlands by now. But that is not only reserved for Christians. Of course not. This is the beating heart of the Netherlands. Take care of each other, look after each other. If we do that, we can have faith in the future. Thank you.

Dear Mrs. Bruins Slot, dear Hanke, When you were a kid, you had two dreams. Your father was mayor and at the kitchen table it was often about politics, but you had other plans. You wanted to go to law school, and you wanted to be an officer in the army. Both dreams have come true. You became a lawyer and later commander of the Houwitsers. You were sent to Uruzgan in Afghanistan. That made a lot of impression on you, and it was also indirectly the reason to run for Parliament in 2010. During your broadcast, you saw what could go wrong in a country where a government is absent and lacks trust in society. Once again, it made you aware of the importance of a good and reliable government. As a fresh MP, you went back to Afghanistan in 2010. The dusty roads to Chora were replaced by asphalt; in Tarin Kowt light burned everywhere. You saw economic growth, opportunities for a better future for the Afghans. You just mentioned a few lessons from your military career that you were able to apply here in the Lower House. An important resemblance: it's both human work. You have to keep asking questions to the people around you and in the country. Eventually, the best ideas come from below. And you don't do it for yourself, you do it for others. On top of your very first girl dreams, other dreams came true. In 2005 you became Dutch champion hall hockey. You said about this during one morning fishing with General Dagblad journalist Jan Hoedeman: "The main task as goalkeeper is to make sure that the ball doesn't come to you." Johan Cruijff couldn't have said it better. But just like with him you later think: there is still a core of truth in it. As a member of parliament, you gave others room to play the game. You didn't come to the fore. But when it came down to it, you were there. One of the pillars of the CDA, you've been mentioned in a newspaper article in the last few days. One of your greatest qualities is that you can ask difficult questions. It seems very common for MPs, but it is not always. We saw it when you were a member of the temporary committee on ICT projects in the government, but also when you spoke about defence, sports or medical-ethical issues. You managed to maneuver your opponents in hypothermia in difficult situations, with calmness and patience. You didn't grow up, but you didn't let them put you away either. Like that one infamous time in the debate with Mr Thierry Baudet. He said, "I quote, "that he thought it was cute that you were so naive in life. I'm not going along with that reasoning. Noord-Nederland, Groningen, is not considered targetted area for nothing. Choosing half plus one means that 49.99% goes to other parts of the country. Is that fair if you look at what has happened in the past with gas benefits and the Economic Structure Fund? 1% of the natural gas benefits from the FES have ended up in the north of the Netherlands, 88% have ended up in the Randstad and the remaining funds have ended up in the other regions. Surely it is only fair that this money should be concentrated in the North of the Netherlands?

Yeah, we have a date. Who could have guessed? That kind of unexpected thing just happens with the OCW budget. Mr. Chairman. I had just mentioned KLM, which invades schools with running competitions to fill them with advertising. Shell, which was forced by the judge to reduce CO emissions this year, is trying with technical festivals and children's councils to glue the youth, while it is busy trying to kill the earth. My party is asking the Minister to better protect children from that. A greater role for the education inspection, for example, would be obvious. We are also curious whether the government is ready to work on stricter measures in advance of the next evaluation of the sponsor agreement, so that they can be implemented immediately if influence does not stop. What possibilities does the Minister see for converting this sponsor agreement, which does not work, into legislation that does work? I'd like a response. Mr. Chairman. Finally, I have some questions about the BPRC. I think the minister was expecting it. In 2016, the Chamber unanimously voted in favour of the final phase-out of trials on non-human primates. The plan drawn up by the BPRC itself is about 40% reduction, to 150 tests per year in 2025. The zero that the Chamber asked for is far from in sight, but that is really what the motion asked for. Can the Minister reflect on that? I'd like a response. The BPRC itself reports that it reports annually progress in monkey trials to the Ministry of OCW. Is that what's happening? And if so, how many tests on monkeys were carried out in 2020? Finally. Of the 13.5 million euros in the entire national budget going towards animal-free innovation, 2.3 million is earmarked for the BPRC. That goes to transition, but also to animal welfare. But, of course, those are other posts. Money for developing animal-free research should also be spent on animal-free research. Animal welfare must be an independent cost. Is the Minister prepared to assess the contribution to non-animal innovation to the BPRC and to increase it annually at the expense of the contribution to animal testing? Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr President, thank you. I will start with a few points that were partly still there after my answer in the first period. I also have one question from the second term. Then I'll get to the motions. I come first to the questions, starting with the question about the nursing home care places. I had a conversation with Geert Wilders from the PVV. And yes, it is, of course, true that waiting lists are increasing and that the labour market is tight. We're working really hard on that. There is a difference between active and inactive people waiting on the waiting lists for nursing home care. Clients who are actively waiting are actively mediated by the healthcare office. This also usually works within the standards. It's gonna happen as soon as possible. The inactive have been given an indication and often an offer, but do not take advantage of it for them. They get care at home and they're on the waiting list for an interview. They have therefore indicated a particular place of preference and are awaiting it. That's one. Then two. A motion was adopted by Mrs Agema of the PVV calling for a review of that distinction between those two categories. The Minister of Health, Welfare and Sport has promised to come up with a response to this question. He's hoping to send it next week. This is without prejudice to the duty of care offices to provide sufficient places in nursing homes. Every year we make sufficient budget available on the basis of the advice of the Dutch Healthcare Authority. Waiting lists are also taken into account. The VWS Minister will send a letter next week on the development of demand and capacity. He will also address the question of how these two relate to each other. In December, a letter will follow on the issue of existing capacity, including in relation to real estate in relation to demographic developments. So there will be documents and then the debate will take place further. The second theme is dementia. Indeed, the number of people with dementia indicators is expected to double towards 2040. The RIVM expects a doubling of 172.000 people to 337.000 people. This is also taken into account in the annual growth of the available budget, but it calls for more than just resources. That is why there is also considerable investment in the quality of nursing home care. That's what happens with the program Home in the Nursing Home. With the Work in Care programme, we are committed to providing sufficient care staff. The Langer Home programme is working on the quality of care. For the Work in Care programme, 50 million extra has been released from the VWS budget. This is specifically used to maintain staff and train people for care, making a total of 420 million available for this subject. Nevertheless, more needs to be done in the future, because demand for care will increase significantly over the next 20 years. The number of employees in the care sector and caregivers is not likely to grow to the same extent over the next twenty years. This means that a number of fundamental discussions need to take place on how to organise care. That is precisely why VWS leaders announced that they would come forward with proposals in the first half of next year, before the summer, to better organise care and make it future-proof. In the same context, there was another question from Mr van der Staaij about measures to get enough hands on the bed and, if necessary, unorthodox measures. The cabinet wants to try to do something about this, but the question is exactly what measures work. Unorthodox, yes. But they must also be effective. It is not easy to solve this problem. That is why we are already looking at how innovations in care can help to do the same with fewer people, of course, while maintaining quality. The cabinet also shows what needs to be cared for in the region. Then we can also look into whether and, if so, what unorthodox measures can work. The outline note will therefore be given and sent in the spring. It will also examine the type of measures needed. That does not alter the fact that a great deal is already happening. I would just like to refer to my previous answer on the Working in Care programme, which also looks at a sector-wide approach. Then it is intended that it is measurable and there is a noticeable result. This is done through three lines of action. First of all, it is intended that more people should opt for training and a job in health care. By doing so, we are trying to increase the influx and the number of re-enterers and side-intromers; in this sense, there is again analogy with the education issue. The second has to do with learning: learning better in care. This means that there is sufficient availability of sufficient and good traineeships, including in order to increase the efficiency of training. The third is working differently. It is important that employees in the care find it more pleasant in the care, so that they can work well there. This means that the workload needs to be addressed. It is also about the question of what we can do that is necessary in the field of training, of being able to develop and of getting a good team mix. All these factors need to be right when it comes to the question of choice, the issue of training and learning, but also to ensure that people have a good time. Additional funding is available: for training, for advice to job seekers, for career interviews and for a recruitment campaign. We keep a finger on the wrist, even several fingers on the wrist, through the Committee Working in the care. The Spring Report is due to the Chamber this autumn. Then there was the question about the azc in Gilze. For this purpose, in general terms, the shelter is sober within the azc's and consists of accommodation, living expenses and access to basic facilities such as medical care. This is also the case in the scheme for asylum seekers and other categories of foreigners. Specifically in Gilze it is a maintenance and improvement programme, so that this reception site can be used for a longer period of time. It's a monumental building in Gilze owned by the COA. The COA has a duty of care to maintain that monument. There is the specific circumstance that this is not just an asylum-seekers' centre, but an azc in a monument. Then there is Mrs Marijnissen's question which I would like to return to. I was informed about the content of the documents during the week before Grapperhaus sent his letter to the Chamber, so that is prior to 10 September last. The Animal Party: the CETA Convention. It's about a claim in relation to Groningen. Here's what I'm gonna do. NU.nl reported on a pamphlet by Milieudefensie, FNV en Handel Anders!, in which they argue that the EU Trade Treaty with Canada, CETA, may impede the phasing out of gas extraction in Groningen. The link these NGOs make between CETA and Groningen fits within their criticism of investment protection in general, but frankly, in this particular case, they really miss the point. It is precisely in view of the criticism of investment protection that CETA's Treaty text has been modernised and the right of governments to regulate and the public interest has been confirmed. CETA thus grants foreign investors the right to compensation only in the case of expropriation which is not in the public interest or where no adequate compensation has been paid. During the phase-out of the Groningen gas extraction issue, the Groningenveld, a public interest is sought and agreements have been made, also in the financial sense, with Shell and ExxonMobil in the main agreement. Part of the agreements contained in that agreement is that the NAM, Shell and Exxon renounce any claims on the State in connection with gas reserves in the Groningen field that will not be won. Then there is Mr Segers' first-term question about a one-stop shop for sustainability. The way in which Mr Segers describes it cannot and must not be the intention. The ambition of the cabinet is to support and facilitate people in the sustainability of the built environment. A system has been chosen in which everything around the house, the street and the heat plans is located at the municipality. I do not want to rule over the head of the municipalities, but I think we should take this kind of example seriously, so I take it seriously. At regionalenergiestof.nl you can see whether a municipality has an energy window. Such a point of contact can, of course, help to request and assess a quote or other questions. The climate agreement has agreed to broaden the points of contact with energy. VNG and Rijk are now discussing proposals for minimum criteria, standardisation and standardisation. That will therefore also help the neighbourhood approach. I think it is important that citizens are properly supported and informed in this way. That must of course be free in the base. Municipalities can choose to offer detailed personal advice through these points of contact and could cost, but the basic opinion should be free of charge. My colleagues in the cabinet, Mr Ollongren of the Interior and Mr Wiebes of Economic Affairs and Climate, will, in their consultation with the municipalities, draw attention to the need for the basic information provision to be available free of charge as far as we are concerned. In addition, efforts are being made to develop widely available care-free offerings for citizens and businesses. You will be informed about this by the Minister for the Interior, Mrs Ollongren, this autumn. Finally, a question from Mr Kuzu's second term. It was about my presence at remembrances. I'm very regularly present at a lot of remembrances. I take these suggestions very much to heart, of course. For example, in 2012 I attended the commemoration of slavery. It is attended annually by a member of the cabinet, each year by another member of the board, usually from the corner of Education, Social Affairs, Home Affairs or Justice. The commemoration of Srebrenica is attended in The Hague by the Minister of Defence. The Netherlands is represented in Bosnia at diplomatic level. I am not going to complete my agenda here, but I am, of course, taking note of Mr Kuzu's suggestions. Once again, I am present at many commemorations and it is also very conceivable that I will be present at such a memorial, but I am not going to record it now.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The proposed legislative amendment implements a European directive agreed by the European Parliament and the Council. It also partially implements our Climate Agreement. Transport becomes a step greener. 14% of the energy must come from renewable sources, but there is no obligation to add it. Mr. Chairman. We support the proposal, but we also see it as a transition proposal. We believe that, in the end, the sectors concerned will not be able to achieve the objectives by using biofuels even though this proposal is not just about achieving them, but that, for example, green hydrogen is the solution for them. Biofuels are theoretically a good solution for greening transport, but they also have practically major disadvantages. Biofuels are often imported from Europe, but also from the USA and China. Bulk transport from these parts of the world on fossil-powered ships whose greening is still in its infancy will undo much of the environmental gain. I said it last week, I say it now and I say it this afternoon in the debate on reducing the use of coal in electricity generation again: cabinet, work on the hydrogen agenda. Hydrogen can mean the greening of chemicals, for example, hydrogen can mean the greening of heavy land transport and hydrogen can mean the greening of shipping. The Netherlands must make much more haste with the hydrogen agenda, says D66. If we compare our country with, for example, France or Germany, then we must do very much to ensure that we do not lose the battle, and that we have great opportunities through the extensive international gas network to transport hydrogen gas and to play a central role in Europe, which can mean a lot for maintaining jobs and for international trade. For this reason, too, it is important that the parties do not exclude each other in this formation, but quickly come to a new government. I would like a reaction from the Secretary of State, not so much on the formation of the Council of Ministers, but on the hydrogen agenda. Mr. Chairman. We very much appreciate how the Secretary of State is also committed in Europe to preventing biofuel from being extracted from soya and palm oil. This is no longer happening in the Netherlands, but it is not yet international. We also appreciate how the Secretary of State is committed to implementing the Schonis motion to prevent indirect land use in biofuel production and to consider soya and palm oil as a high ILUC risk. That brings me to the enforcement and implementation of this proposal. Implementation of this proposal is bureaucratic and enforcement problematic, as it is difficult to oversee the entire chain internationally. In fact, in order to do it right, a new instrument, the BKE, is needed to measure greenhouse gas emissions. But the NEA is very critical about it and has serious doubts about enforcement. Therefore, it is stipulated that the BKE will not start for the time being. But that does raise the question of what enforcement is going to be like. I'd like a response. Mr. Chairman. That is also why we need to move towards a more sustainable system that certainly applies to aviation and shipping which cannot do without hydrogen. We therefore consider this proposal to be the most feasible, but certainly not the ideal means of greening transport. In addition, we will have to answer a great many questions in the proposal for a decision on energy transport, but this framework will, of course, be very helpful. Mr. Chairman. Our group is looking forward to the answer of the Secretary of State. Thank you.

We have also made proposals, for example on the closure of additional coal plants, for the next two years. I also hope that Mr Jetten is prepared to look into this. But I see his answer in this way: it is indeed an obligation on this cabinet to produce results. And just saying that it's "the goal to achieve the goals" is like a little too noncommittal.

I would like to hear from Mr De Roon, after which I will respond to his proposal, whether his party, or his group, or his foreman is prepared to support these sanctions. Whether his party is prepared to restore unity in this parliament. Whether his party is willing to make it clear to Russia that this is not possible. I would also like to say to you, Mr President, that the majority of this Chamber is saying that we want the cabinet to look at how the increase in the energy bill can be taken as well as possible. These are motions that have already been tabled here from the left to the right, which have been shared and which the cabinet is looking at. That's not new. That wish exists, Mr. De Roon. So you can add another proposal to that, but the wish from the Chamber is already there in a majority. The question before us now, Mr. De Roon, is much more urgent. Confess color. Where is your party? Are you here for the Dutch interests, or are you representing others' interests?

No, I don't have one here. But knowing her, that's never gonna take long. Mr. Chairman. Then there's the motions. The motion in part No. 911 is a speech-out. So I don't have to give them any advice. The motion in part No. 113, with reference to the debate, I should like to advise against. We have discussed this in detail. The motion in part No. 114 is about the increase in the energy bill. Significant measures have been taken: the energy tax, the energy allowance for minima, a budget for minima and a budget for insulation materials. We're holding the finger on the wrist. In view of all these activities, I would like the motion in part No. 114 dissuade. Then the motion to part No. 115. The coalition agreement includes an investment for pandemic preparedness, including for flexible scaling-up of intensive care. I want the motion in part no. 115 dissuaded. The motion in part No. 116 has no cover. Moreover, the coalition agreement provides for a structural allocation of 200 million for this type of business. I'm deceiving the motion in part No. 116. The motion in part No. Mr Wilders' 117 concerns the 60 billion for the climate and nitrogen fund. All that has to go to purchasing power. With reference to the debate, I would like to discourage that motion. The motion in part No. 118 is about taking away the right to vote and stand as a candidate. On this point, I would like to say that the removal of the right to vote requires a judicial decision. So that's not up to the cabinet. The Constitution and the law provide a basis for crimes that seriously affect the state system, but I do not believe that there is any reason to change the legal framework. I want the motion in part no. 118 so advise against it. The motion in part No. 119 is a pronunciation. The motion in part No. 120, I'd like to leave judgment room. We naturally support the importance of tackling cybercrime. That's what the coalition agreement says. Entrepreneurs also already have the attention in the cybercrime approach. The motion aims to strengthen it. The motion in part No. 121 is about the gas extraction. Gas extraction is completed as soon as possible and is justified. That is also laid down by law. That's what the Cabinet is doing. I reject this motion because the cabinet cannot now give guarantees about the gas extraction that is needed this year. The Secretary of State shall inform the Chamber before a decision is taken on all relevant estimates, security frameworks and considerations. The motion in part No. 121 is therefore not recommended. The motion in part No. 122 is about power inequality. I should like to say the following. That ibo comes in April and we come in for the summer with a reaction. Let us have the debate on this. Perhaps I could ask Mrs Marijnissen the motion in part No. 122 in that context.

Thank you, Mr President. Also on the situation in Ukraine a question to the Minister. The Minister discussed this with his colleagues. I'd like to hear more about it anyway. As far as D66 is concerned, there are two effects. The first is, of course, the effect of the import of Russian gas, which is, as is well known, used for the production of fertilizer. The largest industrial gas consumer in the Netherlands is a fertilizer manufacturing company. The second effect is, of course, the export of animal feed by Ukraine. Cattle feed is actually a bit the fossil fuel of current agriculture. So we need to reduce animal feed. That is exactly the transition that the cabinet has put into circular agriculture, because that only gives proteins to animals that people cannot or do not want to eat. Could the Minister respond to the view that, as Europe, as the Netherlands, we can reduce our dependence on the rest of the world if we switch to circular agriculture? Thank you.
