I don't regret anything. And I'm not sorry I didn't listen to you before. The situation has changed. It is always the VVD Group that I have always argued from the outset about reducing CO emissions, without any taboo. This means that we are in favour of nuclear energy. This means that we are in favour of Carbon Capture Utilisation and Storage. Now, in these circumstances, the question is: can we make better use of these elements to keep our energy supply balanced and as cheap as possible and to broaden our base? Because we have to meet these climate objectives.

Mr. Chairman. Of course, I would like to thank the Minister for his reply. I am not going to say his "extensive answer," because there are some questions that remain here and there, including mine. Anyway, it happens sometimes. I repeat a single one in the second term. The Minister said that the annual supply of biomass is monitored by the PBL. He also mentioned the point made by Mr Van Kesteren, who said: should we not take the place in 2015 and see if we are still on the right track with this road towards the closure of coal plants? What does the Minister do with this monitoring? What does that mean? If there is scarcity, price rises or whatever, what instruments does the Minister have to use? That's what I meant when I said that reports actually don't give you anything, because your economy eventually runs on electricity. I would like an answer from the Minister. The Minister said, I think, on Mr Van Ballekom's question, whether we could postpone the discussion of the law for a number of months: I do not understand that. This law is about 2020, he said, and biomass doesn't play until 2030, when the coal plants are closed. But that's a little weird, isn't it? Because if we now know that the coal plants are going to close, we are now looking at biomass and now it is important that there is a framework for biomass sustainability. Then you can't say: that biomass doesn't come until 2030. This is the time we are talking about: how do we get good biomass, how do we get sustainable biomass, and all those questions that have been raised in this debate. Did the Minister mean it when he said that biomass will not be dealt with until 2030? Then I asked how much gas we could generate, thinking that maybe we could keep the use of biomass as low as possible. I asked whether the Minister would see a combination with CCS in the future. Then, like Mr Crone, I said that we need to do more in Europe. The minister said, preferably to bet on ETS. But you can do one thing and you can't leave the other. I would think that you and your commitment to ETS, as well as trying to cooperate with neighbouring countries as much as possible. I'd like to hear from the Minister how he looks at that. Now it seemed a bit like: I choose ETS, so I leave everything else. That's not supposed to happen, is it? We talked about biomass. Many groups have expressed their concerns. I have, let me be honest, just heard the Minister say too often: biomass is in the mix, that is part of the mix. As if, because the fact that we need that biomass, we no longer have to think about it that it is very acidic that it does increase CO emissions, that it becomes more polluting. Then we can stop all sorts of stories and say all kinds of things, but at least in the time of one generation it is. While we're all doing it because we want to bring CO emissions down. I understand that the Minister says that we need it and that it is in the mix, but I would really like to hear more from the Minister about the concerns that are there. With that...

Eric Wiebes, of course, was the one who said at some point: we're gonna close it. That was the goal. We're on our way to that target. That is what Mr Nijboer and I share. It is now about the pace at which we achieve that goal. As far as the VVD is concerned, that pace cannot be high enough. That is why I have just said: go before 1 April to see what possibilities there are to refrain from this extra gas extraction. I really challenge the Secretary of State in that. I really think we have that commitment to Groningen. But I just don't want to make false promises here either. I can do all kinds of tough language around here, but I don't like it.

That's not very clear. To say that safety weighs heavily is another thing than to say that safety is one thing. We already have an emergency plan that is already in place to ensure that safety can actually stand on one. Then I have a second question. The spokesperson of the Christian Union says: if the extraction goes up, then there will be extra money for Groningen. It was added in the media that that money is for damage recovery and reinforcement. If the gas extraction doesn't go up, doesn't Groningen get that extra money?

Sure. I'm doing the same thing. This is very often the case on Friday at the press conference and in the conversation I have then, but I now understand that Mr Segers does not see it every week. Shame. It's always in the top ten best-visited programs. I was also thinking partly because Mr Segers was looking at it. But without madness, the answer to that is yes. But let's get these two aspects out of there right away. There are two major concerns. I wanted to deal with the first major concern in the performances mentioned by Mr Segers, but also at other times, for example in May at the VVD Congress, when I spoke about this in a party context. That is about the great concern in the world about climate change, about the fact that it's two to twelve and that if we don't take action, we're taking big risks with the whole system we live in. That's one side. That care lives with a lot of people. This can be translated into air quality in the short term. If you don't believe in the CO problem and global warming, then the fact that we are living here on one of the most polluted parts of the world may be enough motivation for me to believe after a few regions in China and Hong Kong. For the climate skeptics, I would like to say that you can also have the dependence of the Middle East and Russia on your energy supply as a reason. There are so many reasons to do this, but for me the direct, personal motivation lies in the great concern for the system in which we live and the thought that this generation needs to clean up this mess and can't move through it. In that sense, it's kind of like the state debt. You don't move it to the next generation, and you don't move this shit to the next generation, if only because it might make it impossible for that generation to fix it. That's one concern. The other concern is: but how? There I see a bright spot in this debate. Call me an optimist there you have it again; sorry, I can't let it go either, but if I listen to this debate and see what it's about, about whether we do the industry via the Asscher route or via the cabinet route, I think: you know, you might get out of it. If that's the big debate in the Netherlands, you might get out of it. So you could work on that after a lot of battle, because it's going to be a lot of battle in the campaign and so on and you could eventually agree on a path with perhaps more than 100 or perhaps more than 125 seats in Parliament. A path where you meet the goal, where you take everyone in the country and no one suddenly has to cancel their holiday, sell their car or buy their heat pump tomorrow and take a huge loan. A path where you can take away all those worries. Ladies and gentlemen, the viewers at home, we have 11 years. After that, if you take it until 2050, we have 31 years. It doesn't have to be tomorrow and we're gonna do it in a proper way. We're not gonna make life impossible for people in their personal lives. In addition, there is the third leg of the triangle as I always have it in my head and I even drew it here: the companies. That is the point of the discussion I just had with Mr Asscher and others on how to ensure that companies participate properly and that competitiveness is maintained. But that is also a concern, namely that we do not get that right, that we only go for the 49 and do not take the other things into account or that we say: oh, what a disaster; purchasing power is falling all the way through the floor, so leave the 49 alone. So you have to settle it in a balance, with broad support, after which you can say to the Netherlands: this is now the plan with broad political support. So it's probably about cabinets. That's why I'm so supportive. In addition, you are not dependent on the elections of 2021, but roughly set out a path for the coming years until 2030 and 2050, with the rest that goes with it: boys, we can do this together in a decent way. And, you know, that was what I believe Mr Asscher said, so it can be fun, because then we can also make a lot of money from it.

At first I heard a bit of a brake on sun and wind, because you are actually going to look more at the demand side, actually at the loss of energy needs. JA21 is, as we know, critical of solar and wind energy, very critical. We are looking at the impact that this has on the climate we see, on the landscape. We also look at the costs and problems that people are experiencing, also in terms of health, by placing these huge ugly wind turbines. So I was hoping that you, as a Party for the Animals, could embrace that a little, because it is soiling. I think that's an important aspect of placing all those turbines. I can see the Minister nodding: it is indeed soiling.

Good morning, allies. Welcome to two minutes of debates entitled Mining/Groningen. One is the follow-up to a committee debate which took place before the recess on 1 July. The second took place on 15 September. I would like to welcome both directors, Mrs Ollongren, Minister for the Interior, and Mr Blok, Minister for Economic Affairs and Climate Policy, as well as my fellow chamber members. For the first two-minute debate, seven speakers spoke. Mrs Beckerman has requested the debate, so I give her the opportunity to use her for two minutes to table motions.

Mr. Van Hattem and I see it quite differently. I think that the municipalities also see it differently from Mr Van Hattem's description here. It's just a joint task. The municipalities and the co-governments have taken them on because they also feel that they have a responsibility in this regard. They consider that they themselves should have an influence on how the declaration is completed. That is the whole concept of the Regional Energy Strategy. This gives them a lot of space to fill in. Once again, they regard this as their task and their responsibility. So I really do see that quite differently from what Mr Van Hattem is describing.

First of all, the point of substance: the rise in energy prices. Of course, the measures announced by the cabinet through the energy tax also provide relief for SMEs. Once again, as we pointed out at the presentation, I do not want to give the impression that we can eliminate all the cost increases. However, energy-intensive SMEs will benefit significantly from this. Moreover, I do not want to hide the fact that energy prices are then partly reflected in a higher price of products, including bread. I do not see Mr Azarkan right now, but that is one of the driving forces behind inflation. Then there's the point about the contacts. The trade association and its chairman are, of course, very welcome. I don't want to hide the fact that I usually start my weekend at the local bakery in Enkhuizen on Saturday morning at 06:30. The dogs have to get out anyway, so I can hear on the spot about the sweetness and suffering in Enkhuizen and specifically with the bakers. But it's not about personal anecdotes. Entrepreneurs are welcome. Then I get to the point...

I would like to make a number of specific points, starting with information. The Secretary of State says she wants to improve current information. In her letter yesterday, she mainly points to the way of burning and the time of burning, while in our opinion information should focus on air pollution and its impact on environment and health. As far as we are concerned, wood-burning must therefore be discouraged. Does the Secretary of State agree with the SP? And if we want to discourage firewood, it goes without saying that we are going to end the subsidy on pallet heaters as soon as possible. On the one hand, discouragement and, on the other hand, the granting of subsidies is totally unbelievable. As far as we are concerned, research into the desirability of subsidies for small installations is therefore superfluous. I'd like to advise the Secretary of State as soon as possible. Information should focus not only on current wood producers, but above all on the general public. Because we know that when the energy bill goes up, there is a refuge on wood stoves. And what account goes up because of government policy? Indeed: the energy bill. The high-energy bill hotline that the SP launched on Monday is red-hot, I can report to you. Is the Secretary of State prepared to focus information also on the general public and not just on the stokers of today? Mr. Chairman. Germany and Belgium already have stricter requirements for wood stoves. In order to prevent wood stoves that will not be used in our neighbouring countries from coming to the Netherlands, the Secretary of State will also introduce the Ecodesign Directive in the Netherlands by 1 January 2020 at the latest, she writes. But the question is, of course, Mr Van der Lee also asked this question: what happens to the heaters that are already being used, those older, more polluting heaters that can still be purchased this year? What do we do about it? The Ecodesign Directive has not yet solved this problem. Does the Secretary of State agree with us? Finally, Mr President, I come to enforcement. There are rules regarding nuisance in the neighborhood. But how are they maintained? What rights does someone who experiences nuisance, went to the neighbors and got zero on the record? A report to the municipality and, with luck, someone who comes to check in, is not enough. Maintaining a national problem must also be regulated nationally. We need to outline frameworks so that there are no differences between the municipalities. Is the Secretary of State prepared to look into this? As far as we are concerned, direction by the Secretary of State and setting up frameworks are necessary, including with the Clean Air Agreement, which is now being drawn up. Is the Secretary of State prepared to include wood stumps in them and set enforceable targets in them? Thank you.

Thank you, Mr President. Let me begin by asking this outgoing Minister of Finance what it was like yesterday at Ecofin, whether he was still addressed on his construction in the British Virgin Islands. As we have seen from here, the newspapers in Italy were full of them. So I would like to know how people reacted to that news. That brings me to the credibility of this minister. The question is of course: can he still act as a warrior against tax havens and tax avoidance, now that he himself has used such a construction on the British Virgin Islands? Compare it with a Minister of Justice and Security who wants to tackle drug policy, but rather ran a coffee shop himself. How credible is that? The minister plays here in this house the alleged innocence and wants to end it with "2009 was a different time," but he doesn't get away with it. Normal people just pay taxes in this country and they don't retire in Guernsey and they don't help a boyfriend with a start-up in Africa with €26,000, which you still have. That's not normal, Minister. The minister wants us to believe he didn't know he was investing in a letterbox company on a Caribbean island. But nobody's gonna believe that either. 'Cause if you transfer $26,000, you know what to do, don't you? Then you know what you invest in, especially when you're 34 years old. That's a car. Or does this minister have too much money? It could be. Nor does he supposedly know who those other investors were. That also sounds unbelievable, because it was a friend club, that's how we were able to read. They were all friends of the Leiden student corps Minerva, of McKinsey, of ABN AMRO, the old boys network. Mr. Chairman. If you analyze it, that whole construction was built to avoid tax: pure tax planning. You earn your money in Kenya, where the Vpb is 30%, then you channel it to a holding company in Mauritius.. a commonly used construction to avoid tax in Africa, where the Vpb is 0%.................................................................................................. This has been considered. Thought of the Zuidas whizzkids. This place stinks. It reminds me of Sywert van Lienden, also one of those CDA benefactors, who spotted 9 million with his mouth cap deal. So to speak, he wanted to do the right thing. Just like this African minister, Sywert wanted to do good for public health in the Netherlands. This minister knew very well what he was doing and if he had called Sywert, he would now be able to cash, because by now that start-up of the minister is making 5 million sales and 900 people are on the payroll. That's not a small start-up anymore, that's just a big company. If the minister had cashed his shares now, he'd have made a hell of a lot of money. The question is therefore: how credible is this minister? And how credible is this minister in Europe? I told you in the beginning, the Italian newspaper headlined: from prosecutor to defendant. This Minister with his lifted finger and his strong attitude towards southern Europe is no longer credible. Mr. Chairman. Speaking of credibility. The cabinet headed by Mr Rutte has plunged the Netherlands into a major crisis in recent years. We are in the midst of a housing crisis, an energy crisis, a migration crisis, a care crisis, an education crisis, a security crisis and so on; one crisis after another. How credible is it, then, that this coalition, which has caused all this misery, now wants to make a start? They want to clean up the mess they've caused and they promise to get better. But nobody's gonna fall for that, right? That's like a pyromaniac says, "I promise to put out my own fire." It doesn't work. It is therefore not surprising that more than 70% of the Dutch population have no confidence in this. Mr. Chairman. Let me run by some crises. First of all, the purchasing power crisis, which is well known to us here in this house. People's purchasing power has stopped since the turn of the century. People crave a little air in the wallet. Despite the fact that the economy is growing by 3.5%, next year we will get nothing in purchasing power. The Netherlands is impoverished. More and more people don't make ends meet. Meanwhile, the Netherlands has about 250,000 working poor, we were able to see in a source of the ESC last week. 1.5 million people in the Netherlands suffer from problematic debt and poverty. That's the Netherlands in 2021. Meanwhile, everything becomes more expensive. We have seen it: the care, the own risk, the energy bill, the messages. Everything has become a lot more expensive in recent years. Take the gas. Nowadays you pay more than €2 for a liter of gasoline. Why do we pay €0.50 more in the Netherlands than in Belgium and in Germany, so I ask the Minister, or actually the Secretary of State. Half of the Netherlands is now filling up in neighbouring countries. It's been going on for years. More than half of every gallon of gas goes to the state treasury. The PVV says: lower excise duties below the level of our neighbouring countries so that they can make our state treasury here instead of the other way around. Mr. Chairman. Then there is the energy crisis, which the newspapers are full of. Gas prices are going through the roof. Meanwhile, we pay more than €100 per megawatt hour. That was the beginning of the year €17. 550,000 households now live in energy poverty. If this goes on like this, we're gonna be in the cold in winter. This year the energy bill increased by €500 and next year it will probably rise by €550 again. We're heading for a direct energy disaster. But what does this minister do, what does this cabinet do? Nothing! Other countries have now taken action. Italy, Greece, Spain, France, they all reduced the energy costs for families. And this minister leaves the whole of the Netherlands in the cold. Then there's the pension crisis. That's something like that. The pots are bulging out. Meanwhile, in ten years' time, the pension assets in the Netherlands have doubled from 830 billion to almost 1,700 billion. However, pension funds must be poor and pensioners have not been indexed for ten years. Pensioners pay the bill and now lose 11% of purchasing power. A math example. A retired person with a small supplementary pension of €700 is now missing after ten years €200 per month, because there is no index. That's inexplicable. The immigration crisis. Under the guidance of Mr Rutte, 900,000 non-Western migrants came to the Netherlands. That's a city the size of Amsterdam. That has cost us 200 billion so far, in care, benefits, housing, you name it. Why isn't anybody talking about that? When we ask a question about the Millions note, they say: we are not going to calculate that. We must not know what the open borders cost. The policy of open borders now costs the taxpayer EUR 20 billion a year. Mr. Chairman. Under Rutte, our society has visibly changed. In the big cities, more than half of the newborns are non-western. So count out your future. It goes on and on. The COAs are filling up again. We were able to see it in today's papers and yesterday's papers. Last month alone 3,000 asylum seekers came into the Netherlands. The PVV therefore wants to close the borders for all asylum seekers and migrants from Islamic countries. It can't go on like this. We're gonna be strangers in our own country. So cut it off and close the borders. That brings me right to the housing crisis, which is also such a huge crisis right now. Partly because of the migration there is no house to get in the Netherlands. The housing shortage has now risen to 30,000 homes, and if anything is released, 27,000 waiting status holders are ahead. So the starter in the Netherlands is screwed and the waiting lists are getting longer and longer. Apart from a shortage, the houses are now priceless, as we know. In a year's time, prices rose by almost 20%. A terraced house now costs four tons. In 2013, that was two tons. In seven or eight years the prices of the houses have doubled. Living is priceless and also the rents have increased exorbitantly, in the last ten years under Rutte by 30%, so that 800,000 tenants can hardly pay their bills anymore. We also see that there are no rentals. The stock of 2.3 million has been the same for ten years, because corporations don't build. Of course, it's the landlord's tax. Therefore, the PVV is also in favour of abolishing the landlord's tax and the suffocating rules. Mr. Chairman. Then there is the supplemental affair, such a crisis, a crisis that stopped this cabinet and sent it home.

They buy in that power and the compensation is about the power they buy. So these companies can't change that themselves.

Mr. Chairman. Isolation of homes and buildings is a good thing. Well insulated buildings cost less energy. Non-use of energy is still the best step for the climate. But isolation can also bring disadvantages. Fire safety is one of them. The fire in the London Grenfell Tower temporarily woke us up. But now we're a few years away and few seem to be concerned about what happened then. Recently, the municipality of Nijmegen presented the results of an inventory of buildings with façade plating, the fire safety of which may be at stake. That's 62. It didn't cause any fuss. According to experts, risks have not disappeared. If there are 62 properties in Nijmegen alone for further research, this will be a lot more for the whole of the Netherlands. I'd like a response from the Minister. Mr. Chairman. The Minister instructed the municipalities to make an inventory of possible risk exposures in their municipalities. That overview appears to be there by now. Is that right? Can that be made public? Is the Minister aware of what action is being taken? More and more municipalities want high-rise buildings, but the fire department's ladders reach a height of 30 meters. Up there, the fire department can only fight a fire inside. The fire department wants more fire safety to be considered in high-rise plans. The use of better building materials is advocated. According to the fire department, about 10% of construction costs should be reserved for fire-proof construction. It is at odds with the affordability of new buildings. How do we ensure that we build safely, but also affordable? I would also like to receive a response from the Minister. How does he think that balance can be guarded? Mr. Chairman. I would also like to raise the issue of solar panels in relation to fire. My colleague Agnes Mulder has asked questions about this before. The fire department's worried about this. Those solar panels are sometimes poorly installed, as it turned out last weekend during the storm, and they make it difficult to put out fires. In the meantime, there are over 700,000 solar panels on Dutch homes, but is there sufficient attention to fire safety aspects? When the panels are connected over multiple premises and when they catch fire, the fire spreads from one house to another, from number 7 to 9 to 11. The fire walks right over the rooftops to the other houses. Thus, with the new phenomenon of solar panels, we are also faced with new problems, including new challenges. Can we do something about this? Is there a need for regulation? Are agreements with the sector needed? Is this on the table with the minister? Can the Minister respond to that? Mr. Chairman. We have received an extensive letter from Brandweer Nederland and the Association of Insurers. I assume the Minister himself knows that letter. There are several aspects to which our group would like to hear a response from the Minister. For example, it is claimed that it is wrong to install façade coverings and carry out maintenance work on them. Is that right? Is that right? What would be a good reaction from the government? It is also written that in the Netherlands it is even allowed to work on flammable insulation with open fire, which means that there are unnecessary fires. This is prohibited in other countries. What does the Minister think of the idea of doing something about this? Mr. Chairman. Finally, I would like to raise the issue of vulnerable groups who are not able to flee quickly enough in the event of uncertainty, when there is a fire, for example. We have discussed this extensively with the Minister before. The Minister responded in his letter of 31 January with the state of play on the implementation of various commitments and motions on fire safety for older people. We have made several proposals for this. Much has already been done, and I congratulate the Minister and the Cabinet. We are curious about the results of various studies that have been started. However, I would like to comment on chimney fires. That's 2,000 a year in the Netherlands. How can we in the Netherlands together ensure that something as simple as a chimney fire, which often has to do with maintenance, can be prevented more often and better? What can we do about that? I would also like to hear a response from the Minister. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Thank you for the opportunity to be here today in your Chamber and to talk about the BZK budget. I would almost say that this is in several respects the trap, this year's trap and the trap of this cabinet. Maybe I can start by saying that I'm doing this a little bit with mixed feelings. As I usually start my letters to the Chamber positively, I would also like to start this debate positively. In fact, I would like to share with your Chamber that the budget as it stands is, in its entirety, a budget that I am proud of. This budget is actually about a lot. Among other things, she's dealing with the reinforcement operation for Groningen. That is an incredibly important file that BZK has included in it halfway through this cabinet period and on which we have concluded an administrative agreement. We got extra money for the National Coordinator and extra money for stuck files in Groningen. There's 342 million in this budget. This budget is also about improving services for people, as a direct result of the report on the childcare allowance. Precisely because the municipalities are so close to their citizens, 130 million are reserved for better services by municipalities. This budget is also about tackling energy poverty. She's about making social real estate more sustainable. She deals with a concession for small landlords because of the freezing of rents and the construction of flex houses. And I could go on like this for a while. That's what I wanted to say first, Mr. Chairman. Then there's today's topic. As Mrs De Boer also said, the reason why the Upper House has taken this opportunity today is that there are still questions and wishes about the part to live. I would also like to make a positive start here. It is not for nothing that I stress every time how important it is that people in the Netherlands can live well, fittingly, nicely and pleasantly. That goes for everyone in our country. At the same time, of course, I can see that there is a large deficit. Mr Kox pointed that out. There are people who have to wait and who cannot find a suitable home with them in the place where they want to live. This naturally leads to discomfort and also to a feeling of impatience: how do we solve this? I feel the same impatience. At the same time, I think I can also see that during this cabinet period the change was made, the shift from cutting back and reforming to building and investing in the housing market. Much has been achieved there and we will see these results in the years to come. This could only be achieved through cooperation. This concerns cooperation between the Empire and the other governments, provinces and municipalities. But also the corporations are of course a very important partner in this. This also applies to the developers and the builders, who have hired people again and made sure that during the pandemic there was also simply built in the Netherlands. That's really special. That's something to be proud of. At the same time, I fully agree with everyone who says that more is needed. I will come to a number of other areas in a moment. Now I happen to have mentioned the building, but it is also about the whole rental policy. It's also about affordability. It's also about sustainability. These are all kinds of elements that are important in the policy that has been pursued and that can hopefully be extended by the new cabinet. First of all, I would like to answer a number of specific questions. First of all, I come to the Tax Plan. When we spoke about this last week, Mrs De Boer, with others, said quite strikingly that we were still awaiting the coalition agreement. In the meantime, we know the content of this. So what many of us were hoping for was also materialised in that coalition agreement. This will therefore be a task for the new cabinet. This is about abolishing the landlord's tax. I have often said to the Chamber that it is actually inevitable to abolish that landlord's tax, because in the long term the investment capacity of the housing corporations is simply being eroded. So I was also happy to see, with many in this Chamber, that the new coalition has decided to abolish the landlord's tax. That happens as of 2023, that's how I read it. I think there can be no doubt about that. In the series in the coalition agreement, the proceeds will be charged to zero from 2023. It has therefore been abolished de facto. I know that parties in this Chamber, including GroenLinks and PvdA, have argued that they should be abolished a year earlier, namely the next financial year. I have spoken about this before in the House of Representatives, and also here too. I think that for the whole sector, for the housing corporations, the fact that the new cabinet will abolish this landlord's tax by 2023 will have a huge effect. We are already seeing the impact of the 500 million; we discussed this in detail last week. Following is the abolition of 2023. That means a huge increase in their investment capacity. This means that much more can be built in the long term, that more can be preserved and that more maintenance can be done. This is extremely important for the housing market. He hasn't been abolished by next year. I did not find any budgetary room for that. Luckily, while the cabinet was outgoing, I was able to do a number of things for the housing market. But I couldn't do more for that landlord tax than what we discussed last year. Full abolition next year would cost another 900 million; I have no budgetary room for that. But once again, for the whole social sector, it is abolishing as such what it was about and that is what is going to happen. Then there were the questions that were more about the Housing Fund. As far as the Housing Fund is concerned, I would almost say that we have set it up together. It was the result of a political consultation in the Lower House between coalition groups and a number of groups in the Upper House. It was very enthusiastic, by the way, so it was very good that the Housing Fund could get there, with 450 million. In the meantime, it has found its destination, so the best projects have been awarded. That is not the only thing that is going to happen for the coming period, because we have also made 1 billion in the budget available for housing. There is also 250 million for a fourth tranche of the Housing Impulse. It will be part of the 2022 budget. That is simply part of the budget that this cabinet has submitted. Why are we doing all that? Because we do regard this housing as a priority, and we consider it extremely important. The same applies to the Housing Fund. That's not just housing, I'll say, that's restructuring. It is about improving the quality and living environment in the most vulnerable areas in the Netherlands. However, almost 22,000 homes in the immediate vicinity of the homes are handled. That is why there is a lot of enthusiasm among municipalities. There were 15 mayors who sparked this up. They have once again drawn attention to this and called for it to be continued. I was also very pleased that I saw in the coalition agreement that a follow-up is being given to the Housing Fund, and that it therefore responds to the call made by these municipalities. Mrs De Boer and Mr Crone said that there were more plans and proposals than money. That was true for what I can now call the first tranche of the Housing Fund. That's right. That was because it was limited to 450 million. There were more plans, and there were also more plans that crossed the line qualitatively. So they basically had a sufficient score as a final score, but there was no State contribution for it, because the money was run out. That's how it works for these kinds of constructions, of course. If there is limited money, it may be that there are proposals that make it to the finish line, but do not get any money at this stage. Those projects don't run away. I will also be very happy to show at the time of the transfer that there are already projects that a new ruler could try to prioritize. I'm not in charge of that. I want whoever gets to do this beautiful file, to give up the stick, and at the same time I don't want to rule over my own grave. There are a number of points which fall more into the category of 'other' or 'other' items. Mr Van Hattem has made a number of points which he often makes. I'm gonna try to just answer the actual questions. Should Dutch house seekers longer look for a bigger house, and what is that because of? There's just a big cut on the housing market. This means that it is difficult for many people to find a suitable home for different reasons. Therefore, this cabinet has always been working to increase the supply of housing in all segments of the social sector, but also in the other segments, so that there is indeed a flow on the housing market, so that people can move and leave behind another home that is suitable for other people. But it's not easy to find a place to live, is it? I think it will take at least eight, nine, ten years to rebuild and improve that housing market. I had a few more questions from Mr Kox. He asked what he called the crooked growth, the difference between the buyers and the tenants. Of course, we've run a rental policy. That is what we have had heated debates on here. Luckily, we've found each other again, when it comes to rental policy. I do think it should always be a combination: how can you ensure affordability for the tenants, while at the same time improving the starting points for start-ups in the housing market? We have adapted the rental policy in this respect by, among other things, the one-off rent reduction for low-income tenants and high rents and by maximising the rent increase in the free sector. These are all measures that I am very pleased with. More affordable construction for start-ups has been stimulated mainly through the housing impulse. We introduce the possibility for municipalities of social purchase with priority for starters of interest to the municipality, for example people who already live in the municipality and otherwise have to leave or people who work in a sector that is important to the municipality. Those are all policies that really make a difference, which the municipalities like to make use of.

Whether they do so legally in the same way is another question. But it is well known that our eastern neighbours are in the process of phasing out coal. That is a whole programme, which ends in 2038, or in 2032, to finally close a huge amount of coal-fired power stations................................................................................................................................................................................................................................................. Unfortunately, coal does not fit in with the Paris solution.

Thank you, Mr President. Thanks also to the members of the cabinet, who want to have three women and one man with us at this late hour this important debate on purchasing power development. My group very much appreciates that. Mr. Chairman. What is at issue in the First Chamber is legislation, in this case a budget law. The key question to ask is: does this budget law provide an answer and direction to what is currently going on in the country? That is the key question I will raise in my speech. What's going on in the country? I say nothing new: the security of existence of large groups of people is under severe pressure. We are not talking about purchasing power plates with +0.5 or -0.5 and whole point clouds where you can get anything. We are not just talking about people who have been on or below the poverty line for a long time. Of course, we are also concerned with those people, but there are much larger groups of people, and that is actually quite unique in society as we know them over the past few decades, who have a great deal of trouble getting out each month, or are lacking in regular monthly money to pay for the energy bill and the groceries. So the question is whether the supplementary budget for SZW, which we have with us today, will answer this question. Let us be clear: it is not really about the SZW budget alone. It is about the whole of the national expenditure framework. That is why we welcome the fact that the directors of finance are behind the government table as well. Is the government doing enough? No. Does the government do anything? Oh, yeah. We're not gonna faint; the government is definitely doing something. The €800 for people with a social minimum is a gesture that is complicated in implementation, but is at least a gesture that actually means something to people who are at the level of assistance. With a lot of political push and pull, €500 was added last week. That brings me to the question of why that has been so incredibly difficult. We all see that this is not a question of the left or the right; it is a politically broad question of the fact that these people have really fallen into trouble. The least there could have been is that this €800 had been extended more heartily and earlier by the cabinet to an amount of about twice as high or to the €1,300 it is now. Anyway, anyway, it finally came about and we appreciate that. But we all know it's too little. It's not enough for those people. I also experience them daily in my work: people who can't pay the rent, who are at the bottom, who walk by the food bank, who nibble on their food, et cetera. For this group, €1,300 is too little, but it is far too little for the group that earns just a little more, the low middle incomes that are just not at the level of the social minimum or at 120% of them. They just don't come out and they don't get a penny. We should be ashamed of ourselves! I am not saying that we could have seen or seen this crisis coming. It's four verbs in a row, but I think it's true. I am not saying that we could have predicted this inflation either. Economists are capable of much, I must say, of the economists in this Chamber, but an economist who gives an adequate prediction of the future, I still have to come across. However, I say that we should have developed the social foundation and the social resilience of our society in good times in such a way that a major crisis such as this would have been able to cope with without the consequences of it bringing millions of people into great financial worries. We should have done this by taking structural measures, such as raising the minimum wage and related benefits. Yes, it's finally being worked on, but after a long time of whining, slow and at a much too slow pace. By setting up financial buffers and instruments that can be deployed in times of crisis, so that we do not have to be panicked by policy. It's called fixing the roof when the sun shines. The power inequality in the Netherlands is enormous and there is really easy power to transfer or to roam, without us having to be afraid that we would end up in too egalitarian a system. I say that especially for those people who have great concerns about it. Mr. Chairman. None of this has happened and now we are taking emergency measures, because special times call for special solutions. If we then look at the supplementary budget for Social Affairs and Employment, we find that really insufficient. Yeah, we're looking at the broader picture. This extra €500 has been included in the supplementary budget, which we in the committee have said in broad terms today: hammer it out as quickly as possible. So it has become €1,300. Something has happened to the fuel tax, which, by the way, often does not produce anything for the people who really are at the minimum, because they are no longer able to drive cars. The reduction in the energy tax also offers some relief. I'm not here to bitch. I am not here to say that it is all bad, but I say sincerely from the bottom of my heart and also from our point of view that it is really too little, especially for the people with an income just above the minimum. This budget is therefore inadequate and has been discussed in detail in the House of Representatives last week. All kinds of concrete proposals have also been made. In the end, nothing has come out that can count on a majority that will help people with low middle income in the coming months. We've been thinking about doing that again. In the end, we chose not to do so from our group. There is no lack of good intentions for the future, but they do not yield anything. Then we are talking about specific measures, specifically to give this group of people extra money. I do not mean all the fine things that can be included in the budget for 2023 or 2024, because with the budget for 2023 you will not get through the autumn. When the heating season starts again, about from October, I see the people whose energy contracts have now gone to flexible €100, pay €150 more. They're already panicking and panicking at my desk, like, we're not gonna figure it out, what are we gonna do? Mr President, this is a very important speech. It is also our role in this Chamber to look with commitment, but also with distance, at legislation that is being presented to us. Unfortunately, the Group of the Greens/European Free Alliance has no choice but to conclude that the legislation that has been submitted to us is inadequate on this point. Legislation does not provide a good answer to the fundamental questions raised by society and to the legitimate demand of the population for public protection. I'd have liked to have come to another conclusion, but I can't. I am, of course, curious about the contribution of colleagues and about the answers and reactions, reflections, of the members of the government in the first term. Thank you.

Thank you for keeping the Minister in touch at least. What strikes me is... That's why I specifically mentioned the fairgrounds. They provide affordable entertainment for everyone, including for Jan with the hat, as opposed to those expensive amusement parks, which not everyone can afford. We sometimes forget that these bakeries... That word is not meant to be derogatory, but it is always about "the bakery on the corner" from childhood. That's what it's called. They provide a primary need for life. I'm really worried. I have been a Member of Parliament for 15 years so far, and I hope to be able to do so for a while. I suddenly got a message from the baker's foreman. He said, "I want to talk to you." Then I think something is wrong, because I haven't heard those people for 15 years. I am very concerned, even though this is more on the plate of my colleague Kops, who is already committed to this. How can those bakers, who have a very high energy bill through their ovens, pay it in a minute? The bread and everything they make is a primary need for life. That's nutritious and healthy. That's a primary need for life. That is why I would like to draw particular attention to it, even now and also on behalf of my colleague Kops.

Mr Baudet spoke of "a warm invitation to come back." It is about the dictator who used poison gas against his own people. I hope that we are critical of people who attack their own people. I'd like a response to that. And then I still have the question of exactly how Mr Baudet sees it, because if you are going to deport people, you must have intensive cooperation with that country. People have been tortured by this regime who fled from it. What indication does Mr Baudet have that all this would be safe again? Because the Secretary of State has also indicated that people really need to fear for their lives. I am therefore curious to see exactly how Mr Baudet sees this.

If delivery via Nord Stream is not restarted on 21 July, this will not lead to acute problems, but will entail major risks for reaching the filling levels throughout the European Union. What I myself foresee is that the market will react very restlessly to this, so that the price, which is currently at a very high level, can rise even further.

I have a question for Mr Raven. I hear him making a warm plea for solar and wind energy. I can also hear him being a warm opponent of coal energy. I can understand that very well, also from his background, with everything that has gone wrong in the past, of course. I also hear he's against gas. My question to Mr Raven is: how does he plan to catch the intermittent current, if there is no sun and no wind?

But that part of that raise from three to seven because of that nitrogen plant is about this gas year. But it is now about saying quite effortlessly that 2022 is not going to work either and that it is going to be 2023. That's about the next gas year. Then that factory is there. Then that factory works. Then why can't the cabinet make it clear to the Groningers today that it just stops in the gas year 2022-2023?

No, that's the second point I wanted to make. There are many households in the Netherlands, but also small SMEs, who have been having huge problems paying their energy bills for months. The war in Ukraine has greatly strengthened this, but it was already going on because the energy market has been very strong since the revival of the economy after the corona pandemic. Those people are only doing one thing: they would like to conclude a normal energy contract, not a monthly contract, but preferably a long-term contract with certainty, at a much lower price. I myself do not think it is of any interest to those people that we are discussing the guarantees of origin here with each other. They would like to see a quiet energy market in which they can purchase an affordable contract. So I think we should keep two things apart. There is a price for guarantees of origin, in the sense of the administrative burden that companies pay and also pass on to the customer. That's very clear. This concerns the €3 I referred to earlier. And there is a market in which guarantees of origin may be traded. That's where the market value comes in all directions. It's a lot higher sometimes. But that is a business-to-business trade that the consumer does not in principle suffer from. This is purely about the administrative burden, to which Mr Atsma also asked. In my opinion, these are acceptable, because they also speed up the energy transition and give transparency in where the energy comes from.

That's exactly what I'm asking you. We had a wake-up call. When Russia turned off the gas tap towards Ukraine, we took action at once. Then there was to be a European Energy Union, built on five pillars. The first pillar is precisely that security of supply. There is also a bit of sustainability and a bit of innovation. It is precisely in this first pillar that I expect something from the European Union. With 27 Member States, you can be complementary. Which buttons can we turn on? Is that storage or risk spreading? We're still dependent on gas in the next few years. But let us not only depend on the Russians, but also make it somewhere else as long as we don't have that transition yet. Those are all buttons we can turn. I would also like to ask the Prime Minister's reflection on this. I have also been briefed when the European Energy Union has reported for the last time. That's 2019. Then we thought: okay, the rest will be fine, that will blow over. So no! We had a wake-up call with Ukraine in 2014. I think this is a second wake-up call. I think that is enough to revive this and to find solutions. I agree with Mr Van der Lee that we need to look for solutions, a toolbox or what we are going to call it, as Europe. Our discussion on raw materials and energy prices is one, but let's do a little rebalancing. This applies to a number of areas, and I shall come back to this in a moment, but on energy we are out of balance.

Unfortunately, I am not going to give a super-concrete answer to that now, because we are really working on it. We have agreed in the Norg Agreement on how this storage is filled with low-caloric gas for the use for households and hospitals, not only in the Netherlands, but also in Germany and Belgium, which also partly use it. In part, we have what was agreed in the coalition agreement, so fortunately already in practice. There are also other gas deposits in the Netherlands to which you want to impose the mandatory filling more. We haven't finished that legislative change before the summer, so we need to think about other ways to stimulate the market to fill the gas deposits. That's what we're thinking about right now. I'd rather give you a complete answer in that letter of inquiry soon than give you a half answer now.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. A budget debate without the VVD; I have not seen that before. But I think they're still meeting. If I listen to the first messages, Mrs Kaag has delivered a whole pile of melons that they are now devouring there. I look forward to tomorrow, and I hope it is, because there is a lot of work to be done on the VVD's election programme if that is to be a little bearable. Mr. Chairman. I am speaking today on behalf of GroenLinks, because my colleague, Mr Van der Lee, had to be a Member of Parliament with another obligation. I'll start with purchasing power. It's gonna suck for next year. The cabinet has taken some measures, for example for the energy bill. There has also been serious money made available for this. But that does not alter the fact that people are all going backwards next year when you start on the zero line for everyone in the autumn; in the Social Affairs budget that zero line is announced. There is huge inflation and there are energy price increases and higher petrol prices, as the PVV said. There are also higher costs for groceries and the rents go up. Everything's getting more expensive. Then you can say "I'm a missionary and there's going to be a new cabinet" but the next cabinet has exactly the same composition. The economy is likely to grow next year, and we need to see that with corona, but we're going to take it from there, and people are going backwards. The PvdA is of course mainly concerned about the tenants, the elderly and the low and middle incomes. My question to the Minister is why he did not prevent this with the cabinet. That's just a political choice. It could've been with Najarsnota. In fact, I argued for this last week with Mr Maatoug. Mr. Chairman. My second main point concerns under-utilisation. That is a financial term, which means that the cabinet had all plans that did not deliver. This is reflected in the broad budget, and it now appears in the Navy's note. About the infrastructure you could say: well, there were very few trains in the corona year and very few cars went by road and that, although it is a miserable reason, is just an opportunity to do extra repair and maintenance. But nothing could be further from the truth. There are all under-utilisations in infrastructure: by rail, by water, across the board. I'm also calling it "Defense." It is well known that the Minister is very much in favour of making extra money available for defence, but it is not being spent, not on the military, not on material, not on investment, actually on nothing. On the whole, what was budgeted last year is not being realised. That's what worries me. Or take the subsidies for renewable energy. The climate is not a problem for some parties, but it is a problem for this cabinet. There's 365 million left on the shelf. A large part of the opposition has been warning us all year: be more clear about what you want to stimulate. And now it's just on the shelf. What I found very amazing was the social lawyer, the legal aid. There are huge deficits there. I read an interview this weekend with Anker and Anker, the famous Friesland penalists. They also said: you're actually doing it just because of your social involvement, but for the hours you put in it, of course, you can't do it. And then I don't understand why tens of millions of people are left lying around for social lawyers and haven't been spent on them, when there are such shortages. Or nitrogen. There is a huge problem with housing and the housing shortage; I do not have to convince anyone of that. And there was 133 million available to buy out farmers, I say by heart. That was not so much to buy out those farmers as to make housing possible there. That's what we figured out last year: that's what we're gonna do. But it's not true. And, as is well known in the Finance Committee and, unfortunately, also in the supplement parents, the compensatory allowance is not going as planned either. There was money for that too, to pay out to parents before 1 December. So that doesn't end up in that place. I ask the Minister to go into all seven areas. How is it that the cabinet has such plans, but they are always not being implemented? Mr. Chairman. My third and final point concerns both Groningen and Limburg. Groningen first. It's known that the NAM doesn't want to pay the bills. How does the Minister ensure that NAM continues to fulfil its obligations for years? You see the bill going up. The cabinet's still guessing it'll get the money next year, but you'll just have to see if they'll finally pay. I also have a somewhat more technical question about this. The Navy note says, I believe in the last sentence, that new earthquakes have not yet been taken into account. Well, I can give the Minister one thing on a note: there will be new earthquakes in Groningen. They're still out there every week. If that's not already in the estimates, how does he get the NAM to pay for it? And shouldn't the estimates be adjusted? Mr. Chairman. My final point is Limburg. The cabinet said, because of the floods this summer, that it is going to compensate. We really have the question whether this is enough with the budgets that are now available. I also ask the Minister to respond. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Thank you, Mr President. On Twitter, we saw an announcement from the European Commission, and they are quite excited about the fact that they are going to present a new EU Green Deal tomorrow. Maybe you think that's good news, but they're already pointing out that it's a new growth strategy for our economy, our people and our planet. I say to the Prime Minister: that does not go together; there is a very costly mistake in thinking, which, frankly, we cannot afford anymore. A planet that will not grow any further cannot cope with eternal economic growth. When it comes to money, we in Europe have agreed that budget deficits should not exceed 3% per year, but does the Prime Minister happen to know what the annual ecological deficit in the European Union is? This is about the resources that the Earth can provide each year and regenerate on its own. How quickly do we get through this every year in the European Union? Mr. Chairman. As far as the Animal Party is concerned, this great mistake of thinking that the economy must continue to grow must be the first off the table. Economic growth is not the solution but the problem. I would remind the Prime Minister of his words at the national climate summit after the Paris Convention was concluded. He said: there was urgency in the air in Paris; there was a broad shared feeling that the time of waiting has passed and that the time has come to act. I would like the Prime Minister, with that thought in his head, to judge the European Commission's climate plans that are being presented. Because if we do not say goodbye to the idea that we should always grow, and if we do not say goodbye to agricultural subsidies for the next 365 billion a year; and they go to dairy farming to a large extent, while dairy farming is one of the biggest sources of dangerous greenhouse gas emissions in agriculture, so you are subsidising your own climate change for the next seven years. And if you want to achieve a goal in 2030, you have only two years left on 1 January 2029. Mr. Chairman. The European Union will also have to make a real change in its policy on renewable energy. So as long as you continue to call biomass sustainable, you encourage biomass to be used as a sustainable energy source in all Member States, you encourage a country like the Netherlands to grant it 11.4 billion and stimulate forest cover around the world. There are whole forests in biomass plants. Can the Prime Minister promise that he will work to ensure that biomass falls out of the sustainability framework? Mr. Chairman. Then there's the trade deals. If you want to pursue a climate policy as a European Union, you cannot make deals with countries that impose less climate rules on their businesses, ask less of their agriculture than the European Union does, and b directly cause deforestation and threats to human rights. I am referring, for example, to the trade deal with Mercosur, including Brazil. We have already asked the Foreign Trade Minister a few times where she is drawing the line when it comes to human rights. We know that Bolsonaro has said that he considers the indigenous people to be parasites. And we know that violence against these people is increasing. These people have begged the House of Representatives to say no to the Mercosur Treaty. The Foreign Trade Minister has so far not been shrinking while people have been murdered again in the last week. Where does the Prime Minister draw the line when it comes to concluding trade deals with Heads of Government who simply do not care about human rights, climate and the need to protect our forests? And if the Prime Minister has forgotten, I would remind him of his appeal to the European Commission this summer to speed up the Mercosur agreement. That was a letter from Angela Merkel that he signed. Yeah, I get that Angela Merkel wants that, because that's good for the German car industry. But the Prime Minister must stand for the Dutch farmers, mustn't he? And how did his note to the European Commission actually fall to the farmers, whom he has often spoken over the last few days? Farmers are not waiting for unfair competition from cheap products from Brazil. Mr. Chairman. Finally. Today, the First Chamber approved the ban on the use of coal. That in itself is a joyous fact. Now there's one thing in the way. That is the Energy Charter Treaty, which provides investment protection to foreign companies that have invested in Dutch coal plants and are now threatening billions of claims. Is the Prime Minister prepared to call tomorrow in Europe for the withdrawal of that treaty with regard to the Netherlands? The Party for Animals has already asked Parliament questions. I can imagine that the Prime Minister cannot answer all of them at the moment, but that we should get out of that treaty, that seems clear to us. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Yes. Now I'm getting boring, because I'm also asking for the motion in part No. 1017 to be retained. It's about sun on the roof. I have already announced to you that Mr. Rob Jetten is coming with a solar letter. We come with a solar letter, but he's the first signatory. This will undoubtedly include collective initiatives for rooftop solar panels, but in order to give priority to households in energy poverty, there may well be a very complicated planning issue, which I do not know whether I can live up to. I would also like to say this: would you please take this motion? Then we're gonna go jigsaw puzzles. Now I know what you want and I'll show you what we can do in the solar board.

This really needs to be done with the rulers of finance. I don't have the details of this myself. One more thing before I get to the motions. That's about taking over those private debts. I would like to echo what has been said about this by the Secretary of State for Finance. I am very glad that the Dutch Railways have done this now. I also very much support her appeal, on behalf of the entire cabinet, to do the same. This, of course, affects energy companies, housing companies, banks and health insurance companies. That would really help. I'll make that call through the camera of the House of Representatives to the energy companies, the housing corporations, the banks and the health insurance companies. Then there's the motions. The motion in part No. Mr Dijkhoff did not ask for comments from the cabinet. The motion in part No. 8 by Mr Wilders, I advise. I therefore advise against the motion in part No. 9. I also advise against the motion in part No. 10 by Mr Wilders. Recently, in December, the rules of conduct between officials and members of parliament have been relaxed. The cabinet is now much more relaxed in the relations between the Chamber and officials and will give a favourable assessment of any request for contact with officials, but it is important that ministers continue to carry out the ministerial responsibility for the administration. This also follows from our constitutional system of ministerial responsibility. The motion in part No. 10 is therefore dissuaded. The motion in part No. 11 by Mr Omtzigt c.s. It's not up to the cabinet, is it? No. Then I shouldn't say anything about that. I'm not gonna judge that. The motion by Mr Omtzitt/Van Dam in part No. 12 is about the State Commission functioning rule of law. I request that they be retained. The cabinet will come before 17 March with a response to the ROB opinion and the annual report of the Council of State, and in the spring with a response to the documents of the WODC. So I would like to ask for the motion in part No. 12 to be retained. Otherwise, I'm gonna have to dissuade her. Motion in part No. 12, hold on. The motion for a resolution (Doc. 15 gets, as far as I'm concerned, judgment Chamber. The cabinet response has already stated that the principle of proportionality must be guiding. I would therefore like to interpret the motion in such a way that we look at how the general principles can be more firmly anchored in the Awb and that the way and scope are involved. So motion to part No. 15, Judgment Room. The motion-Klaver c.s. in piece No. 16 about the algorithms also gets judgment Room. The Cabinet recognises the need to ensure that algorithms do not discriminate and that the government should be as transparent as possible. I welcome the fact that nationality, ethnicity and place of birth will in principle not be used as an indicator in risk models for combating fraud, unless there is an objective justification for such data processing. By that remark, it receives a ruling from the Court of Justice. That is going to be quite a situation, because it is a lot of information. So we will also have to look at how we can set up a register that describes which complex algorithms the government uses and which have a substantial impact on individuals or society. The motion-Klaver c.s. in piece No. I'd like to advise against 17. Minister Dekker informed the Chamber of the additional budget released for legal aid, in particular in the field of personal and family law, and the adjustments to the system which enabled him to free up funds in a forward-looking manner. The Minister also promised the House of Representatives earlier that this would be his response to the Van der Meer Committee, which asked for 170 million euros. This subject will also be discussed tomorrow in the general consultation on subsidised legal aid. So the motion in part No. 17, dissuade. The motion in part No. 19 on the parliamentary survey does not require an opinion from the cabinet. The motion Segers c.s. in piece No. 25 also does not ask for a reaction from the cabinet. The motion-Van der Staaij c.s. in piece No. 28 is also a motion that does not ask for a reaction from the cabinet. The motion Azarkan/Van Kooten-Ariës in part No. 30, judge Room. As part of the legislative test, this is already done by the Ministry of Justice. The Azarkan motion in part No. 32 I'd like to ask you to hold. I understand his desire to do diversity for the government in this way too, but I would argue that this motion should be held until after the national coordinator's investigation against discrimination, so that we can take it one step at a time. So the motion in part No. 32 I ask you to hold. The motion in part No. 33 is about broad screening discrimination. If I may interpret it in such a way as to involve this in the already announced state committee, I would like to leave the opinion on this motion to the House. The motion Azarkan/Van Kooten-Ariës in part No. 34 I must advise against. If there is an objective justification for the use of nationality or ethnicity, this is permissible, for example when it comes to electoral fraud by individuals from certain countries. However, unjustified use of nationality or ethnicity must be rejected. Of course, we agree on that. The Azarkan motion in part No. 35 I'm judging Chamber. We support the need to look at this. We need to consider what legislation could possibly regulate this. I want to keep the possibility open that we are not laying this down in formal legislation, but first in guidelines, because the issue is so evolving that we need to be able to adapt the standards quickly. The motion Azarkan/Van Kooten-Ariës in part No. 36 doesn't ask for a ruling from the cabinet, I guess. No. The Van Brenk motion in part No. 38 I must advise against. It calls for an independent investigation into the removal of the administrative justice chapter from the Council of State. I have already explained in my first term that we see no reason in the report to review the organisation now. I have also mentioned that the Council of State itself is already in the process of reflecting on this. So motion to part No. 38, not recommended. The motion in part No. 39. Dissuade. The motion in part No. 40, also dissuaded. As a cabinet, we are not going to interfere in the design of the investigation announced by the Council of State. The Krol motion in part No. 41 does not ask for a response from the cabinet. Finally, I would like to make the motion in part No. 42 as this could pose a problem for some members of the cabinet. So motion to part No. 42. Dissuade.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. At the end of the debate, I say it at home: I do not really trust that this approach to the problems in Groningen will work out. I hope I'm wrong, but I'm scared, and I expect we'll be here in a year and no flute yet in Groningen. This is because a model is being used, a technocratic approach is being adopted, damage and recovery are not being combined, and the strengthening and vision of the future of the villages are not being properly regulated either. That's what I'm worried about. Unfortunately, we will talk about it more often here. I have one main motion, supported by the full opposition. Not all parties are present. I hope to receive support from the coalition next Tuesday. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Before I begin my speech, I wish those who make their maiden speech today every success. We're talking about two esteemed colleagues in a few minutes. Mr. Chairman. Our house is on fire. We need to move. We have made global agreements to reduce our CO emissions. With the law proposed by the Minister, we can take an important step and take action. But the final goal is not yet in sight: to combat climate change. As far as D66 is concerned, it is really painful that a court ruling was necessary to keep the cabinet to its own goals. D66 is very clear: we would have preferred that the judge did not have to use it at all. We must achieve the goals and the Dutch must be able to trust that this will happen. We must take into account the concerns of climate strikers and of the Grandparents for the Climate. What kind of signal are we sending to the next generation, the young people, for which we are doing it? I spoke to the climate strikers last week. Their concerns about the consequences of climate change for their future are great. They're asking politics to take action. That's what we do in this room. Mr. Chairman. This cabinet is a missionary, but climate change is not a missionary. D66 has put this cabinet in the green, but it is not enough. The whole world is now going for climate action. Joe Biden, on the other side of the ocean, rolls out one ambitious billion-dollar program after another. Germany got a right-wing hit and turned this into action as quickly as possible: 65% in 2030 and climate-neutral in 2045. That's what they decided in a week. Ambitious climate policy is the future. We now need to focus on green recovery. Mr. Chairman. Yesterday, for the first time in history, the CO price was higher than €50 per tonne. I have been able to work on this European system in Brussels for many years. The success was not always visible. There were even voices to stop, but we went through with it. Because for solving complex problems there are no quick fixes. With a sharp rise in CO prices, the urgent need for compensation for energy companies is becoming less and less acute. That's the profit of this system. What CO2 price has the Minister taken into account when drafting this bill, and is that still a real starting point? Because the price has risen very rapidly over the last few weeks. Two. How does the Minister intend to avoid overcompensation? Does the Minister choose to work with forward prizes and, if so, why? Does the Minister agree that the general interest is better served in working with ex post compensation on the basis of real prices? For let me be clear: D66 does not want to pay too much in compensation, not at all as the CO2 price rises. A third question to the Minister is: are the corresponding ETS rights withdrawn from the market in the context of the limitation of coal burning due to the integrity of our European system? Mr. Chairman. The growth of sun and wind is fast. The price of CO is rising; I just said it. There is therefore no point in continuing to subsidise these black coal plants. The already promised subsidy on biomass is a financial infusion for coal-fired power stations, which we have to get rid of in the long term. There are more and more reliable clean alternatives to energy generation. That is what we must do. Can the Minister confirm that biomass is finite and, if so, by when? Mr. Chairman. The intention is now to close all coal plants by 2030. As far as we're concerned, we need to speed this up. With the rapid growth of solar and wind energy in the Netherlands and the rising CO price, we can say goodbye to the coal power plants faster, but to achieve that we need political leadership and a much faster roll-out of wind farms at sea. The report prepared under the direction of Laura van Geest talks about 10 gigawatts when we start the preparations in 2021. Last Sunday, 9 May, it was Europe Day. Then we will look at what Europe has brought us, such as a European prize for pollution. When that CO2 price rises, the business price for fossil energy, such as coal power plants, is getting worse. That brings me to the following three points. Firstly, I would like to ask the Minister how he intends to speed up the closure of coal-fired power stations, so that they close not only in the Netherlands but throughout Europe. Secondly, negotiations are under way for the closure of the Rotterdam coal power station Riverstone. For D66 it is clear: once closed, remains closed. How does the Minister prevent Riverstone from getting back into the hands of some venture capitalist? Thirdly, we need to take care of Riverstone's employees. We must help them to find a new, future-proof job, with the help of a social plan and in consultation with the workers. Is the Minister already discussing a social plan for Riverstone workers with the workers and the workers' organisation? Our group is keen to be clear about this. Mr. Chairman. With the closure of the coal plants we are not yet there. This cabinet and this minister are missionary, but climate change is not missionary. What else is the Minister gonna do? Because we have an expensive duty to the next generations to really work on ambitious climate policies, to work on the further roll-out of sun and wind, to work on the development of sustainable and innovative techniques and to provide jobs for young people with a real, future-proof green job. We have a chance to work right now. With billions of domestic and foreign recovery funds, we can build that green economy of the future. This morning CSR Holland was standing here on our doorstep. They told us that entrepreneurs who are already doing sustainable work are more likely to face the blows of the corona crisis. We'll give it to every entrepreneur. That is why I ask the Minister how he is using national, international and European resources to get greener and thus stronger out of this crisis. We are moving away from coal and need new energy sources. How will the Minister speed up clean energy production? Just now take the chances of accelerating wind energy at sea, my advice to the Minister. There is a chance of 10 gigawatts, for example in the north of the Netherlands. Finally, I ask the Minister to remain in talks with the Urgenda Foundation. I also call on the outgoing Prime Minister to talk to them quickly. I would have liked to have a plenary debate with the Prime Minister, but my appeal to the Prime Minister stands. Mr President, in conclusion.

I understand that, but the Prime Minister is talking about 'wide support' and 'provoking the hand', so I was just looking forward to that. Let me just ask you a very specific question. As I have indicated and maintained, also in the wake of interruptions, I believe that the costs are enormous, and far greater, wider and more comprehensive than what is sometimes mentioned in one or two reports. We have also discussed the cost of isolation, the cost of a heat pump, in the interrupting debates, but we have not yet discussed the cost of purchasing expensive electric cars. Whatever is mandatory, whatever has to be done, because once again, in 2050 the whole of the Netherlands has to get rid of fossil. That is the harsh demand set out in the Climate Law. So cars need to be replaced. All cars must be replaced. Trucks, tractors, ships, you name it all! Everything's gonna be more expensive, across the board. Food, food, the cost of electricity, driving, flying, renting or buying a house, renting or buying a business property, concrete, steel, medicine, a beer, because that too is brewed with gas. Everything really gets a lot more expensive. We believe that these costs amount to a total of 1,000 billion. The afteraccount can be found on our website. So people's purchasing power will collapse. Purchasing power will collapse. We have no option of investing in education, in care, in infrastructure, in security, in housing. And what's in it for us? If all doomsday scenarios come true, even if you believe what Jetten and Klaver believe, then the Dutch efforts might possibly heat up the earth by 0.00007 ̊C less. So this huge operation is also completely pointless once again. Wherever you put these costs, it is a question of whether we do it to the citizen or to companies that are going to pass it on to the citizen. So the people in the Netherlands pay, via taxes, through more expensive products, through a higher energy bill. Those costs will end up with us. My appeal today is addressed to the coalition, but also to the voters in the Netherlands. Choose the Netherlands. Let the mind speak. Drop the climate bill. Invest the money that is now being thrown away, spent on completely pointless measures, in building a thorium reactor, in research into real innovation, in reducing charges to stimulate activity...

The Minister thinks so. CE Delft says to us: that security of supply is greatly overrated. The House has said that we will at least stop subsidies on biomass. That's not controversial.
