I've had the whole block of dismissal, so I'd like to skip the subject. Mr Van Haga, Mr Van Weyenberg and Mr Aartsen had questions about the NOW and the coincidence with other subsidies. We have, of course, rigged the whole package with wide support schemes. In calculating the turnover reduction for the NOW, subsidies are counted as turnover. Of course, this was done mainly at the beginning, because some sectors simply receive subsidies. In education, art and culture and care there is a subsidy to finance buildings or staff. If you didn't count that, you'd, as it were, double-subsidise. The difficult point is that if we now make new aid measures, such as the fixed-cost allowance, or in the previous round the TOGS, which, of course, are also included as revenue by accountants. You cannot distinguish in an audit what the money is meant for. It's just revenue and therefore revenue. If you make separate categories for this, it is also uncontrollable for accountants. We'll have the risk of fraud. So it's in here. It's all about this. The NOW grant itself does not count in the turnover, because then you get a kind of circular reasoning. So it's not. We have of course read that this week, but that is not the case. There is a lot of uncertainty in the estimates. We have chosen an advance and a reference month and made an estimate of the decrease in sales. In retrospect, it has to prove exactly how much it has been. The risk of set-off, paybacks or defaults is rather high when a company has to estimate in advance how much turnover loss is being made. It's complicated at this time. We have therefore opted for a margin of 80%. So that is not the 100% subsidy, but 80% subsidy, which reduces the risk of post-taxation. We have a different dilemma with that. You can create liquidity problems for entrepreneurs. We therefore have other arrangements from the Minister of EZK, namely the guarantee scheme and that kind of thing. Mr Van Haga and Mr Stoffer had a question about seasonal companies. Of course, in package 1.3, in last week's letter, we found a solution for seasonal companies by moving the reference month from January to March. The question also concerned an alternative calculation of turnover. That's not possible, because then it becomes uncontrollable again. We compare the sales for the months of March, April, May now it will be June, July, August and September with seven months turnover of 2019. Why those 7 months 2019? An audit has been carried out and annual accounts have been established. The following will soon be determined by auditors at the large subsidy amounts, so that you can compare it well with each other. If you have to calculate which part of the turnover is made in which month, it is actually impossible by the large number of companies. We have made it simple, but we have listened carefully to the criticism of the seasonal companies that they had relatively few people on the payroll in January. That is why we added the possibility for March last week. As a result, the most recent wage data "March" can now be used for the NOW 1.0 and instantly for the NOW 2.0. Mr. Chairman. I am going to try to get through the questions about employment and labour market policy quickly. Many questions about education have been asked by the Christian Union, the CDA, the Labour Party, 50PLUS, Van Kooten-Arissen and DENK. Of course, we have our regular "lifelong development" and education policies. We have the SLIM budget and the STEP budget. Those are all things we have by default. In addition, we also released 50 million for the Netherlands in the support package 2.0 last week. That is not a very large amount, but it is an amount that applies for the second half of this year and that can be deployed quickly. It is actually intended as a kind of lubricating oil to detach the R&D funds in the sectors. It is intended to enable online training. Why? There are a lot of people sitting at home right now and not working. There's an offer, except it's behind a pay wall. Well, make it available to sectors so people can track it. But the intention is, and that was also stated yesterday in the agreements we made with the social partners, that additional agreements will be made in the coming period on the detachment of these R & D funds, something Mr Klaver talked about. We are doing this in order to involve the social partners in this training and retraining policy and to help them move from one job to another. Mr Heerma, for example, referred to part-time work. Mr Terpstra, all kinds of industrial sectors, as well as Willem van der Leegte van VDL, have asked for a part-time WW, so that it can be combined with job retention and room for training. In the agreements we made yesterday, it says that in the coming period, we are going to create a working agenda with the social partners to set up such instruments and to think about how to use them. We would like to join the existing instruments. Another example is cross-sectoral R&D funds. How can you use the money built up in one sector for education and training to retrain you to a job in another sector? All these creative ideas need to be detached in the coming period, together with the trade unions and employers, in order to shape that agenda. I have already promised the Chamber that I will explore the possibility of this part-time WW. That's what we're doing. The truth is that the old part-time WW before the Work and Security Act can no longer be said. I say it to Mr Asscher, but I do not know why! So we're going to have to get to a new design. When you talk about 1.8 million employees, it is complicated to shape that, because you have to keep track of individual WW rights of 1.8 million workers. So it's really a complicated puzzle we're thinking about right now. Mrs Van Brenk asked if the AOW age could be reduced. As she knows, I do not think that is a sensible idea, because of what economists call the "lump of labor failure." That is the idea that less offer leads to the filling of vacancies by young people. In the 1980s, this did not work. For example, none of the VRS has had that effect. That is why I am not in favour of this. What I am prepared to do, as I agreed in the pension agreement with the trade union movement and the employers, are agreements on sustainable employability and the possibility of part-time and early retirement. Mr Asscher asked for this and I included it yesterday in the letter with the trade union movement and the employers. Sustainable employability and part-time and early retirement can also play a role in discussions at sectoral level on what is sensible policies for this crisis. As you have read in the newspapers, we are now working on the implementation of the pension agreement, the allocation of this EUR 800 million pot and the legislation for the RVU proposal. That's, I'll say, the fine on early retirement. That will bring us to the Chamber, hopefully soon, as soon as we have the pension agreement. But we are also taking it into account in the work agenda that I agreed with the social partners last night. Mr Asscher stands still!

I'm always happy with the conclusion that insight comes with the years, especially since we're all getting older. I'll leave it to you. Mr. Chairman. Abandoning the law would also save the Secretary of State the difficult determination of the disadvantage compensation. We look forward to the answer of the Secretary of State.

Mr. Chairman. It's restless on the climate front. Our companies and residents are looking for clues, security and direction. For the CDA, the direction is clear, namely that we are going to get Paris. That is why I went with a number of colleagues to the Madrid climate summit. With our own eyes we could see team Holland working there. Compliments for them. Mr. Chairman. Recent IPCC investigations outline black scenarios. On 9 December an article was published in the Volkskrant about a study of climate models. The conclusion of this study was that the climate models have been right for 50 years. Knowing this, I am pleased that Europe has indicated its willingness to increase ambition. If the European Commission's Green Deal is feasible, affordable and contributes to our employment, the CDA will look at it with a positive basis. Our question to the Minister is when we can get an impact analysis of this Green Deal. Mr. Chairman. It is worrying, however, that the rest of the world does not yet show that sense of reality. Countries such as China, Brazil and India still seem to be stuck in the groove at the moment, which will have to supply the developed countries first and they will have to go to work afterwards. This picture also emerged at the meeting of the Interparliamentary Union in Serbia in October this year. The IPU has been in existence for 130 years and more than 160 countries are members. What the United Nations are for governments is the IPU for us as parliaments. At this meeting, I spoke with India on behalf of our geopolitical group of Western countries, because India had submitted an energy item on the climate. My Indian colleague told me that he has the impression that Western countries want to share knowledge, but that they hardly do so in practice. He also indicated that the agreed funds would not be provided. After a tough negotiation, the conclusion was that we should deliver what we agreed in Paris and that, if we want to get below 2°C, the developing countries would have to make their contribution even now. In all conversations, we are a party to the fact that we cannot and will not do without the inhabitants. The same goes for the Indian colleague. He's been facing increasing flooding in his district for seven years. That also makes him and his constituents restless. This is a shared responsibility. Mr. Chairman. This brings me to climate and energy exploration in our own country. There is a Dutch Climate Agreement and a Climate Act. The Planning Office for the Environment has passed on the agreement and there is a reflection by the Council of State. The Council of State states that the first draft climate plan is evidence of a robust climate policy, which is also expected to lead to a significant reduction of greenhouse gases. However, the Council lacks a legislative programme in relation to the future of our society in 2050. I therefore entirely agree with Mr Van der Lee; let us therefore stick together. Does the Minister pick up this glove and, if so, when can we receive it? Mr. Chairman. The Council of State concludes that climate policy remains a paper reality if it is not feasible for citizens, businesses and other public and private organisations for a variety of reasons. That brings me to the question of governance. How does the Minister handle this with society and with the participants at the tables and other parties, such as co-governments? What is the response to the letter from Aedes, which states that the PBL charges too low a cost? Mr. Chairman. In the letter of 1 November we read that the Minister wants more sunshine and that school boards have received a letter on this matter. That is a good thing. They can borrow money for roof insulation and solar panels. How's the mood? And are there any obstacles to these developments? What can the Minister do about it? For example, we read that there are problems with the insurability of solar panels. Mr Ronnes and I have already asked questions about fire and solar panels. Is working with a quality mark, as they do in Belgium, a solution? You get that label when the installation is checked and the panels are properly installed. I would like an answer from the Minister on this point. What they do in Belgium is to recycle the panels. They ask for a recycling contribution in advance. We actually do the same for electronic equipment. So we would like to hear from this minister whether he is prepared to look at this for the solar panels as well. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. We are talking today about decentralisation. Anyone who looks at our debate will suspect that we are facing the following questions: is decentralisation good, should it be more, should it be less? I just heard Mr Rombouts say: if we are also going to have a piece of self-reflection as the First Chamber and I think he also means the Second Chamber, then you have to think about whether you really want that decentralisation. As a lawyer, I'm always inclined to look at the rules of Thorbecke's house. I have to say that I came to a surprising conclusion, perhaps even surprising to the minister present here, because the questions'more or less decentralisation' or'must we get rid of it', we can hardly answer when we look at the rules that apply to us. Article 117 of the Municipal Act surprises me: our minister promotes decentralisation for the benefit of municipalities. There is therefore a legal obligation for the Minister to decentralise more and not less. I do not know whether Mr Rombouts is aware of that. The principle that as much as possible should be regulated at a decentralised level also sounds sympathetic. It is also in line with Article 108 of the Constitution, another fundamental rule of our house of Thorbecke. In the first paragraph it is very solemn: the power to regulate and govern the administration of the municipality is left to the municipal administration. Mr. Chairman. The fact that municipalities like to stick to the adagium "decentrally what can, centrally what needs" is understandable. In the Interadministrative Relations Code, with the agreement between Rijk, provinces, municipalities and water boards, the adage is also laid down in Article 2. By participating in that Code, the Empire has agreed to that adage. The same applies to the principle set out in Article 1 of that Code that the greatest possible freedom of policy for local authorities should be achieved. When we look at the VNG position paper, they go one step further: strengthening the autonomy of municipalities. Mr. Chairman. Article 117 entered the law 30 years ago by means of an amendment. This led to the Minister's obligation to promote decentralisation. In the desire expressed in the position paper, that principle actually echoes. But, and then I come to the point that I would like to present to myself, to all of us here and to the Minister: is that still from this time? We live in a special time. The corona crisis requires far-reaching measures. The global warming and the loss of nature and biodiversity threaten our survival. The chance of new zoonoses hitting us is real. Growing inequality defies our solidarity. The young people have checked: no homes, a threatening future for themselves or for their children, a society with a lack of culture and a lack of meaning. What can municipalities, using their own freedom of policy, do to solve such problems? Are the challenges facing the public authorities not such as to raise the question of whether the adage of primarily decentralised and autonomous municipalities is still correct? Is it not becoming increasingly clear that more central regulation and control is needed? The Council of State also points out this in its April briefing: "This call for more central control stems from the large and sometimes conflicting claims to the limited public space available due to the need for much more housing, the spatial effects of the energy transition and the nature conservation challenge as a result of the nitrogen problem." Doesn't the Council of State say here that thinking about the relationship between central-central and the primacy of decentralised policy freedom and autonomy is somewhat behind the facts? The climate crisis and the prevention of a new pandemic require a substantial reduction in our livestock. As far as our group is concerned, it has to be 75%, other groups have said 50%, and some groups that are very keen to grow up have a percentage off it. But no matter how you turn it, the livestock and agricultural areas will disappear. That requires national direction. It's not municipal, it's rural. The land released can be used for nature and housing, but that also requires national direction. In order to achieve climate requirements, more stringent environmental legislation is needed and the Empire will have to take the lead on monitoring and enforcement. That too is central interference. We have to go to green towns and villages, new buildings must be nature-inclusive, with green roofs and facades, and municipalities will have to meet minimum standards for quality greenery per inhabitant. We need to move towards gas-free houses, insulation, sustainability, in short: towards rural building requirements. Mr. Chairman. Those who use their common sense see that there is no escape. To solve today's and future's needs, many regulations and policies are primarily required at central level. A central control and direction will be inevitable.

Madam President, thank you very much. When I look at the pieces, I find a bit of a green blur in the eyes of the European Commission. I also have the impression, however, that this blur has caused the vision of subsidiarity to disappear rather firmly. Of course, on these issues too, European cooperation is urgently needed. Let there be no misunderstanding about that. This is the case for issues such as cross-border energy infrastructure, circular production policy, aviation emissions, car emissions and an effective emissions trading system. That's all true. But the Commission is going a lot further in the Green Deal. I'll mention a few things. A comprehensive review of national energy and agricultural plans; by Brussels. Policies against congestion and air quality problems in cities; checked by Brussels. Survey of national budgets to see if they are green enough; through Brussels. A European competence framework for greener education and education! ........................................................................................................................................................................... Money for the sustainability of school buildings; Brussels involvement. Removing national regulatory barriers to renovation; its implementation controlled by Brussels. A climate pact to convince the public and to encourage citizens' initiatives; Brussels is monitoring it. Addressing energy poverty; Brussels directs. And perhaps as a kind of blow to the head: the task of EU institutions to engage in direct dialogue with our citizens. Isn't that exactly the position from which it's thought? That is contrary to any kind of subsidiarity, isn't it? Mr. Chairman. Maybe this is a lot of useful things here. I don't want to talk about that right now. But does Brussels really think that he knows better on these points and can the Hague or Vienna or Lisbon? Not to mention the European climate law, with which Brussels wishes to claim the power to set individual intermediate targets for CO reductions and to make the far-reaching targets for 2030 and 2050 binding on individual Member States by regulation. Such objectives have a huge impact on our society. They should not be regulated by a European climate law. They are the responsibility of national governments and national parliaments. That is why we find it unimaginable that the cabinet in the BNC sheet is actually criticising subsidiarity in the one paragraph. I am convinced that this does not do justice to the motion adopted about six months ago, the first of which was my name, which calls for an explicit review of the principle of subsidiarity. The cabinet itself has promised a thorough assessment. I guess we still owe it to him. I have a specific question for the Minister: how and when will the cabinet implement it? Does the Brussels cabinet choose a firm, own position, a position against this claimable behavior, rather than moving along with a scratch here and there in the margins? A sustainable course is necessary, but let us not give up the helm. The cabinet is very committed to 55% CO reduction in 2030. Does the Minister know what this means? I will give the answer: no, because there has not even been an impact assessment. It's the reverse world. Then you might also ask yourself whether the Minister really thinks that there will be support for the climate agreement on this point again. What are the good words about feasibility, affordability and acceptance if this unfeasible 55% target in 2030... I say again: an unfeasible objective, as it turns out......................................................................................................................................................................................................... To make a long story short: it's either one or the other. The question is, what does the cabinet choose? Does the SGP opt for green cooperation? Yes. For a green superstate? No. Thank you, Mr President, for your patience as well.

Mr. Chairman. The VVD promised us less immigration, but breaks asylum record after asylum record. At the VVD, the mortgage interest deduction stood as a house, but it is now carefully broken down. And that's how it's gonna be with the billing. A week ago the website of the VVD said: "We were, are and continue to be charged." But the way things are going with the VVD there's some kind of investigation now and, pay attention, eventually the road will just come, thanks to the liars of the VVD. Therefore, in conclusion, the PVV says to this cabinet: stop that, stop that climate madness, stop that nonsense and finally deal with the real problems in this country instead of the climate boom. The Netherlands has no climate problem, the Netherlands has no CO2 problem. Among other things, the Netherlands has a problem with Moroccans who make our pools and our streets unsafe. That's a problem! The Netherlands does not need heat pumps, solar panels and electric cars at all. We need closed borders, we need fewer immigration, fewer criminal asylum seekers. In addition, we do not want to take out loans from some vague heat pump fund. The Dutch want their money back. Dutch people crave relief, a little more purchasing power. Get that over with. So I don't believe in that. I don't believe you should reward such companies with a one-off buy-back. I thought the agreement was horrible in general terms; you know that. The distribution of costs and benefits that Shell and Exxon have benefited so much from went more to the government. Let us make laws that are better, namely damage and reinforcement in one hand. So let the Institute not only compensate for the damage caused by private law, but let it deal with it from a village and district renewal perspective as Shaeffer did at the time, and as Eberhard van der Laan did. No, Mr. Chairman. I have a question about the first motion. I think Mr Koerhuis is asking for an interim evaluation, an interim examination, in his motion, but that is already there, isn't it? If you don't mind, I'm going to start by welcoming the other motions and then answer the questions. The motion in part No. Mrs Kröger's 1025 calls for a CSR risk analysis on hydrogen imports. I really thought that was one of the most interesting parts of the committee debate. I have been persuaded by Mrs Kröger that it is very useful to do so, so this motion gets judgment Chamber. The motion in part No. 1026 by Mrs Kröger and others on the hydrogen ladder and also on the motion in part No. 1027 by Mr Dassen and Mr Grinwis on the explicit weighting of hydrogen use I am going to advise against both. I see it as the task of the government to ensure the scaling up of wind at sea and the electrolysis capacity and the construction of hydrogen infrastructure in the coming years. Furthermore, I think it is really up to the market to determine where the hydrogen can best be used. The motion in part No. 1028 from Thijssen and Van Raan asks for the target for electrolysis capacity to double to 1 gigawatt by 2025. I would also like to scale up as quickly as possible, but because the large wind farms in the North Sea really come into operation after that year, I think this will be a very expensive goal to set ourselves. I'd rather go up faster in the years after. The challenge of the Chamber is to go towards 8 gigawatts than raise the target for electrolysis to 1 gigawatts by 2025. So I'm afraid I'm going to have to dissuade this motion.

Judgment Room it will be. The motion in part No. 273 instructs me to pass the climate agreement through the shredder. There is no climate agreement yet, so I could request that the motion be held, but since that does not work, I will advise against the motion, because that immediately gives the clarity that this Chamber is asking for. Then the motion to part No. 274. It calls on the government to reduce the energy bill and so on. No, we do purchasing power management annually and overall. We don't specifically do that about the energy bill. Should it be the case that other forms of CO taxation are introduced with such a refund lock, we will see it later. I need the motion in part no. 274, so it's not advisable. The motion in part No. 275 calls for an EU-wide improvement of ETS, including a minimum price for the energy sector, a system that we currently have in the Netherlands. I propose that this motion be left to the discretion of the House. The motion in part No. 276 is not addressed to the government. The motion in part No. 277 calls for the recommendations to be added to the inventory of measures. There is very clear language about this in the coalition agreement. We are now in the process of getting a pass-through and then we will see again. The motion in part No. Thus, 277 is something I must dissuade. The motion in part No.

I am not apologizing; I want to explain it all. If those words were not well chosen, I should have reworded them. I didn't want to say anything but this. Everyone prefers to turn off the gas valve today, at zero. Not 12 billion, but zero, today, quit, done, over. But I can't. Because if you do that now and you know that an important part of the gas supply in the Netherlands is still dependent on the Groningen gas, then you take risks. That is what I have tried to express with that apparently not very good example. Limburg versus Groningen: it could also be a nursing home in Groningen; that is of course not relevant at all. It's about that, if you do it too fast and there would be a cold winter and you come below a certain level of security of supply, then you run a risk. That's what Wiebes is about, because we're extremely committed to getting that 12 billion next year. Or we can, we really need to look at it together. We cannot say this with each other now: that is a guarantee. It's an effort obligation. It can't be a guarantee, because you have to map how much gas is needed, also taking into account cold weather and so on, and you have to consider how fast you can switch off. That is being worked hard and I would point out that, when the cabinet started, we were on a phasing-out plan, where we were from.. what was it? 23 to 21.3 went. I believe that at the end of the cabinet period we had reached 20 or so. We have made a dramatic decision to do so much faster. As far as I'm concerned tomorrow is zero, but that simply cannot be done. I don't want to go into the technical question of how fast to 12. That's what Wiebes is gonna say. But this is what we want.

I will also consider how we can bring less ideology and more facts into the whole climate debate, because that is the only way we are going to do this with each other in a sensible way. I'll be at sea by wind. I'm almost done, Mr. Chairman. I have some things to say about agriculture, but I can be quite brief on this, because that is, of course, from my colleague, the Minister for Agriculture. Mr Boucke says that the energy we use must be clean, preferably generated close to home; how can we tackle the opportunities for better European cooperation in the construction of wind farms at sea? I share the wish that the energy we use may be generated clean and close by. That is why cooperation with neighbouring countries is taking place at three levels: in the European Union with the EU offshore wind strategy. In cooperation with nine countries called North Sea energy cooperation, and in bilateral contacts with neighbouring countries, both EU Member States and the United Kingdom and Norway. With Denmark, for example, we have a cooperation agreement to explore how energy markets can better work together via wind energy at sea and whether an energy island can play a role in this. So this is an important appeal from Mr Boucke, who we are trying to shape and shape in different ways, because this is also shared in all the other countries I have just mentioned. Then Mr Van der Lee had another question about the current cap of 35 terawattures on land. That's not consistent with Fit for 55. It's also a debate we have on a regular basis, Mr. Van der Lee. The current Climate Agreement states that, in the event of an increase in the target, small-scale sunshine and wind at sea will be considered first. It is up to a next cabinet, in consultation with co-governments, to ask you the same question, to determine whether the current target of 35 terawatts on land should be adjusted. Mr. Chairman. On agriculture there were a number of questions, which I will try to answer, but I must say that Mr Agriculture Minister, of course, can do much better. The Animal Party had a question about the common agricultural policy. How are we going to reduce animals, reduce methane emissions, and ensure that there is a real transition in agriculture? As the Netherlands, we are firmly committed to sustainable agriculture, circular agriculture and less greenhouse gas emissions. That is why the cabinet has taken various measures. With part of the money made available by this cabinet, farmers who wish to do so can voluntarily stop or make the switch to less intensive livestock farming. There is, of course, also work at EU level on the transition to climate in agriculture. This is done, among other things, with the new common agricultural policy, the EU-methane strategy and the "farm-to-table" strategy. Then there was another question about how protein transition is stimulated. Let me give you some examples of how the cabinet stimulates protein transition. LNV and VWS subsidise campaigns of the Food Centre that encourage consumers to eat according to the Disk of Five. This creates a more sustainable, healthier and plant-based diet, one with a balance in the consumption of animal and plant proteins. The "Everyone does what" campaign stimulates the consumption of nuts and pulses. The National Protein Strategy promotes the cultivation, processing and consumption of protein crops. We also support the European Commission in promoting sustainable food consumption from the same Van-Boer-to-Bord strategy in Dutch, they are no better, Mrs Leijten, whom I have just mentioned. Then I had questions from BBB about the reports that the emissions of cows have been overestimated three to four times. I thought Mrs. Van der Plas referred to the IPCC report. The warming effect of methane is powerful. Regardless of the method of calculation and regardless of the source, reduction of methane is an effective way to limit warming. Reducing methane emissions is therefore important in order to achieve global climate change. You will also receive a reply to the written questions you have put to the Minister for Agriculture next week. He'll go into that further. Then Mrs van der Plas said: food is a first need for life, but people must have enough money to buy their food. She asked: what does climate action really mean for the quality of life? Of course, I share Mrs van der Plas' view that food must remain affordable. As far as I'm concerned, we can do the same. I hope I have been able to explain all evening that I stand for climate policy that improves the quality of life, how we live and how we deal with each other. I also really believe that climate policy offers all these opportunities. It's up to us to shape that in a smart way.

Mr. Chairman. I'm a little confused, because I thought I'd get questions about the CBS investigation. Last week the CBS came up with a survey on income developments in the last ten years, from 2007 to 2017. In that we have seen that incomes have indeed fallen behind during that period. This, of course, was largely due to the financial and economic crisis that has taken place, which has led to a sharp rise in unemployment and a fall in wages. As a result, on balance, there was limited income progress over the whole period. The cabinet said at the start of this cabinet period that it wants to support incomes. That is why, for example, we have included in the coalition agreement measures to reduce the burden of EUR 5.2 billion. That's on balance; that's all pluses and minuses. They are included in the coalition agreement. What is also positive is that this morning the CBS figures for the year 2018 showed that household income has increased significantly again in 2018, as more and more people have found a job. People have either come to work from a benefit or have seen their income rise. Mr De Jong is now asking for a reversal of a number of policy intentions in the government agreement that were discussed on Prinsjesdag, such as the VAT increase and the energy tax. You will understand that I cannot go into all the details during Question Time. In part, it is also the responsibility of other directors. I would like to say, however, that in general this cabinet reduces the burden on balance. Yes, there are measures to increase the bill, such as the VAT increase, but on balance there is a greater reduction in the burden on labour. As a result, according to the most recent insights of the Central Planning Bureau 96% of the Netherlands improves in this year. These are positive developments. Finally, Mr President. We see that in the first two or three months of this year collective wage increases are increasing. I'd almost say: finally! Of course, that took a very long time. The shortage in the labour market also leads to higher collective wage increases, which fortunately increases the disposable income of workers.

Thank you, Mr President. We talk about historical and special times. And that's not ironic. The euro is in decline, the cabinet is tripping from crisis to crisis, inflation is getting out of hand, the ECB keeps pushing money, the energy transition does not really want to succeed and immigration figures break all the records. To the extent of disaster, Putin invaded Ukraine for the second time on 24 February. Experts would've warned me about it. Few believed Putin would really be that crazy. Looks like the dictator made a mistake. Especially when you talk about the first weeks of the raid, you can talk about bath planning, but also about bad execution. It seems that he thought he could quickly take a number of cities, drop the government and install a vassal, such as the Belarusian Lukashenko. Ukraine, however, offered very courageous resistance. In the meantime, the West showed a rare consensus: sanctions, military support in the form of weapons and ammunition, but above all the terrifying force of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation. All were and are factors that have prevented the full Russian annexation of Ukraine to date. But let there be no misunderstanding: it is NATO that guarantees our security. It is therefore logical that NATO should join Finland and Sweden. As far as JA21 is concerned, these countries are of course welcome. I am happy to say this, also to both ambassadors present here. These countries meet the criteria laid down, as Mr Koole has just indicated. As far as we are concerned, the accelerated procedure can certainly be applied. Membership not only offers them the much-needed nuclear umbrella, but it also demonstrates why we should not use a European army. Finland and Sweden choose the strongest partner to ensure their safety. They do not come here to ask to participate in some semi-imaginary European army. My group is therefore in favour of the proposed extension of NATO Quick Reaction Force proposed by Secretary General Rasmussen. The security of the European Union and its countries and the security of the Netherlands and its allies depend on the strength of NATO. That's why Putin has been so miscalculating. As a result of his invasion, he got an upcoming NATO member state on his Russian borders. This was precisely when he wanted to prevent Ukraine from tying itself more closely to the West and thus giving Russia a western threat at its borders. Putin knows that NATO is the great power of the West in the military sense. Sweden knows that, Finland knows that, and my group knows that. That is why we will always argue for the minimum 2% of GDP, not only in promises as made in Wales, but in real doing and delivering now. I would like a reply from the Minister as to whether he agrees with our group. Finally, Mr President, my group is also in favour of rewarding the good and punishing the bad. We are very curious to see what arguments and instruments are being used to ultimately convince Turkey to agree to these two applications for accession. We would also like to hear that from the Minister. We look forward to the answers. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. We're in the middle of a second corona wave. This has a major impact on our economy. Entrepreneurs indicate that they can carry it harder and harder. They're threatening to fall. And the semi-intelligent lockdown proclaimed by the cabinet will, of course, again be the proverbial neck blow for many entrepreneurs. That actually means that the bad predictions about our economy and our society are coming true. It's getting harder. The second wave scenario of the CPB assumes 1% additional economic contraction and an economic contraction of 3.5% next year instead of the earlier expected economic growth. Unemployment is likely to increase by many percentage points and public debt is 10% higher. It's going to be about 72%. Mr. Chairman. If you were to make a graph of the sovereign debt that is huge and on the other hand make a graph of who is the most popular minister, then Mr.Wopke Hoekstra is on the right as the most popular minister, while he has also spent an enormous amount of money. Unbelievable. I think he spent more money than the entire Den Uyl cabinet sometime in the 1970s. It's unbelievable. Moreover, I do not think there is any coherence there, as Mr Baudet often suggests. At least, there is a connection, but no causality I'm gonna let you get out of there quickly. In any case, a lot of money has been spent. The question is how that's gonna work out. My question is: does the government already have a scenario for how to deal with the budget in the second wave? When will the Chamber be informed? Written questions have been asked. It has been stated that these financial estimates are simply not there. I can't imagine. Otherwise, I'm gonna ask why there aren't. Why haven't the scenarios been calculated? To what extent are the principles and policies presented on Princess Day still realistic after that second wave? We talked about it last week, and we already referred to it then, but when will the corona aid package be reviewed in the light of these changing circumstances? Does the government share the view that, given the second wave, the austerity of the aid package is not at issue and that additional measures may be needed? Today, the last General Financial Reviews, at least that is my expectation, of Minister Hoekstra, are assisted by two State Secretarys. We used to have one, but now we have two. We can take stock of the situation a little bit. If we take that balance, then we can only look at the housekeeping booklet, not only from the Netherlands, but especially from the Dutch. DENK stands for a government that actively wants to ensure that we share the wealth in our country fairly. On this subject, we must note that the cabinet has contributed to greater income inequality. If you want to say it a little scientifically, you actually come to: if you make little money, you get less, and if you make a lot of money, you get more. That's the conclusion. People with a lower income got less from this cabinet at every Princess's Day. Last year and the year before, we had the luxury of talking to each other about 0.5% income growth. Now that's over, too, but I've been doing some math for a while. Someone who earns €75,000 has received almost €1,500 from this cabinet in four years. Someone with an income of €20,000 to €25,000 has had to do it with a small €300. Of course, that has everything to do with the increase in the burden: the increase in the care premium, the absurd increase in the rents, if you can already find a home, the towering own risk and the anti-social increase in the tax on fruit and vegetables. If we include local burdens, such as waste taxes and waste-water taxes, then the low-income people are simply in the dark. The conclusion is therefore that this cabinet has increased income inequality. My first question to the cabinet, or actually the second one by now, is: how do they look back on that? Is the Minister of Finance satisfied with the distribution of income? The greatest form of income inequality is actually in wealth. 1% of the Dutch own 25% of the assets. 10% of the Dutch own 70% of the assets. That's actually absurd. It's actually just unfair. Only in ultra-capitalist countries such as the United States is this inequality even greater. I would therefore like to ask the cabinet what it thinks of this hugely unequal distribution. Despite the fact that the gini coefficient in power has fallen slightly in recent years, it simply cannot be justified and we must also look at what this cabinet has done. It can't be that 10% of the Dutch own 70% of the assets. Then something about the growth fund. What are we supposed to do with that? The Netherlands has had a similar fund. It wasn't exactly a success: the Fund's economic structural strengthening. It existed from 1995 to 2010. There was about 40% of the natural gas benefits in it. The new growth fund is filled with cheap credits. The reason is that the government can borrow so cheaply. Of course there's the following underneath. It sounds so beautiful: we want to increase our earning capacity. But, yeah, how are we gonna do that? Do we not have the same problems as with the FES, namely that the money is looking for projects instead of the other way around? Of course, I'd like to give Wopke and Wiebes their place in history. In that sense, Minister Hoekstra has already earned him. He's seen the biggest sovereign debt ever, including in percentage. I think it was in 1922 that we had 10% deficit, but that was due to sewers and military setbacks. That was 200 million, by the way. This is going a little higher. When it comes to the growth fund, it seems as if the starting point was: the interest rate is low - even negative for the government - we have money and then we are going to do something with it. We have to do something with that. Why is this 20 billion not being invested, for example by Invest-NL or regional development companies? These banks have a little more experience. They're also investment vehicles. They have experience with corporate accounting. Mr. Chairman. Then there is the advisory committee that is going to decide on those projects of 30 million and above. Who see names like Jeroen, Laura, Robbert, Feike? I would say: isn't it time at this time for a little more diversity in that club? I am therefore considering a motion on this point. Mr. Chairman. What is also not going to work to get the Netherlands critical is a blank cheque for the big companies. I already talked about this with the colleague of the VVD. Well, then, of course, I'm talking about the Job-oriented Investment Discount. Two times two billion. That's 4 billion for the years to come. There is no form of elaboration and the cabinet has already decided that the tax rebate for large companies will be introduced. The cheque has already been signed, while it still has to be made clear how the government is going to do it, what the terms will be and whether it is going to do anything at all. I never know why the Minister is prepared to go into his deepest fibers, at least that was the Prime Minister in the dividend tax, who happened to be 2 billion to issue that blank cheque of 4 billion for business. In any case, I hope to be able to get an answer to that before 5 October.

Mr. Chairman. The apologies are too late, far too late, because for years now it has been known how extensive and hopeless the situation in Groningen is for many people. Let's not forget that in 2013, just after the quake at Huizinge, the gas crane was even opened further. Then the SodM already advised: boys, do not; reduce that gas extraction to the safe level of 12 billion cubic metres. And then the Minister says very nicely: we still have to find out if that is possible, if all this is possible. That's really incomprehensible. I have two motions. The Minister says that it is a core task of our diplomats to facilitate action and serve the interests of our companies abroad. But of course it's about what you facilitate and what kind of business you facilitate. If a company like Shell or other fossil industry companies in developing countries say "it is in our interest to pump as much oil as possible out of the ground here, regardless of its consequences for the environment of the people or whatever it means for human rights and so on," it should be that an embassy says: we are not cooperating. If there's a whistleblower who's gonna pay attention to that, shouldn't that find the way up? Does the Minister agree and has this always happened in the past?

At the autonomous pace of the clean-up, of course, this kind of thing is included. You're assuming that people in the economy make certain trade-offs. But what you see is that the people who are actually hacking into that investment and wondering if they can afford it out of their small savings are not going to get it. Those people will be left with a problem that they cannot solve themselves. The step I would very much like to take with this Chamber is whether we can help those people from the disadvantage they are in to a plus situation, in which you get them off the asbestos roof and in which we make a link with sustainability, which also reduces the energy bill of those people. We do not leave people with a house with a roof that means substantial depreciation, because they cannot get a loan because they cannot be eligible for it from the banks. We are talking about these people, and we could help them with the system that we could actually put together, coupled with this legal basis. I shall deal with this later. It is also good to have a picture of the costs we are talking about. Sometimes the amounts go all the way. It's good to know what we're talking about. Reconditioning costs approximately between €9 and €30 m, depending on the size of a roof. The removal of an asbestos roof is about 25% more expensive than removing a normal roof. Because at some point, you normally have to replace a roof, just as well as you might have to change your window frames. Everyone knows: if you have a merchant house, you have to take into account maintenance at your home at some point in time. Of course, the roof is always a major cost, which we all postpone as long as possible. We could show that kind of behavior at that kind of big expense. But if you look at the extra cost of removing an asbestos roof versus a normal roof, you can see that that saves about 25%. Of course, when you set such a deadline, we ask people to remove something earlier than usual. But then it is important to know that all these roofs are already at least 30 years old and we are 50 years after the peak in delivery. So that means that for a lot of those roofs that moment when something has to happen is getting very close, or actually has already passed. Of course, prices per metre depend on size and circumstances. Some of you have referred to the slate roofs. That is indeed a specific category, a small group, for which it is indeed more expensive. So there are indeed situations where you can say: here is a specific problem. We must pay particular attention to this, so that those people do not feel that they are simply caught in a trap. So we have to do this through customization and support and with a programme-based approach, through coordination, through the programme agency, through a national fund. These are points I would like to mention.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Then I have another motion. It is about a specific issue that the NVDE, but also parties from the entire solar panels sector are running into.
