It seems to me that their submission is sufficiently supported.]] [[She's getting No. kst-30196-662]]

Mr. Chairman. It's an honor and a responsibility to stand here, to be elected, to represent, to fix things. But it also feels weird standing here, uncomfortable. Because with this heart of our democracy something is not right. Although this parliament represents the entire Dutch people, it is not obvious that I too stand here today. "You're a wolf in sheep's clothing," I was told. "A threat to the rule of law," was written about me. I'm told time and time again, you don't belong here. That doesn't just happen to me. Structural and institutional is the problem, in this Chamber, in the Chamber and in society. This exclusion has been going on for generations. I grew up with it and my little brother doesn't know any better. The day before the election, he saw me watching a debate. He took a look at the screen and saw Rutte and Wilders talking. Do you know what my little brother asked me then? He asked me if the men tell us to leave again. My brother's 11. It has been said, repeated and repeated to him, to me and to many Dutch people for a long time, that we must fight, adapt and be grateful. We should stop whining, work harder, talk nicely, leave history for what it is and especially not question traditions. It's all supposed to be fun. Be normal. You're lucky you were born here, because that's where it's worse. Shut up. Walking on your toes, but not in those sneakers and not in those pants. Get your hands out of your pocket, but don't put a fist in the air. Just don't be one. What am I gonna tell my little brother? What the hell are we doing? With this country, with each other. How can I change and contribute if I'm not supposed to be there? What am I getting into? I don't have all the answers. It's falling and getting up. But what I can say is that this place is from and for everyone. It should be, but too many Dutch people wonder every day: who can be, who can do and who can talk and decide? But also: who doesn't? At school, in the street and in the office, in the media, at board tables and within institutions: who determines the words that make up reality? And who doesn't? The climate crisis would not be so bad, and we should not complain and complain. It doesn't have to be that fast, does it? That's bullshit. Young people are rising up all over the world. 'Cause why go to school when the world's on fire? Too many people pretend they don't. Too often problems have been reduced in this Chamber and outside, and responsibility should have been taken. I'm part of a generation that grew up in crisis, a generation that doesn't have the luxury to look away from problems, but has to deal with them. We have learned that all forms of injustice are connected and that we should not let ourselves be played against each other. So we get up together. Against exclusion. Against the climate crisis. Against inequality. For an honest society, in which we leave nothing unspoken and hold each other, give and receive space, in which we are there for each other, even when it asks a lot of us and in which we are honest, even when it's complicated. Whether it's about biofuel, like today, about the climate crisis, which affects us all, or about the future we share on this fragile earth, it's all connected. I often think of the British Ella. She was only 9 years old. Ella lived on a busy street where for years the limit on air pollution was constantly exceeded. After a judicial investigation, this was partly recognised as her cause of death. It took far too long for this to happen, because her mother had to fight hard for it between grieving. Three guesses who lives relatively often in this kind of neighborhood, because the homes there are cheaper. Who you are, what you look like and how thick your wallet is, that matters, even in the Netherlands. Since the asthma patient Noëlle moved, she ended up in intensive care three times. Her pulmonary doctor sees a connection to her living environment. Noëlle is 6. She lives in a village near the port of Rotterdam. I have become increasingly aware of how the climate crisis increases existing inequality, how important climate justice is, how important justice is, even when it comes to biofuels. Surely it is not possible for families with less money to be deprived of their right to food because we are going to throw food in the tank here? If we allow palm oil, soya or maize to be grown for biofuels, it will drive up food prices. Forests and forests are also being destroyed for agricultural land. And too often that's land that's been robbed. Fortunately, we are starting to find each other more and more for real change and there is a broad movement emerging with the realization and experience that profit against one form of injustice and exclusion is profit for all of us. Because we may be the generation of the crisis, but we are also the generation of movement and connection. Worldwide, we rise in the footsteps of all who have gone before us, of all who dared to dream, do and be. That can only be done if we do not ignore problems and shift them to the other, to the future. This can only be done if we dare to face up to problems and take responsibility: here and now. That's what this is supposed to be about. So we can fight an intersectional battle, be there for each other, even if it asks a lot of us. So we can be honest, even when it's complicated. Maybe mostly. It should be about how everyone is of value and should be free. Free from worries about the future. Free especially not to be normal. Free to let each other be, even if it's hard, even if it's searching. Falling and getting up together. For the planet and all that lives. Done. For ourselves. For my little brother. For yours. For Ella. For Noelle. For our future. For hope above hatred, from the Chamber to the street. Thank you.

In my opinion, there are also people who think that we should keep an eye on the viability of other parts of the Netherlands. I am also responsible for spatial planning through the National Environment Vision. In its development, we are actually doing much more on planning and spatial planning than we have done in the Netherlands for years. This is indeed about living, but also about accessibility, the energy transition and also about the point that Mr Raven is making about the viability of the whole country, and about what you should or should not do for it. It's all over the place. I get the point, but I don't think you can simplify it by saying that not building in the Randstad, and that somewhere else, by definition, is in favour of livingability. I believe that this has to do with many more factors, such as accessibility and the wishes of people themselves. Because where do people want to live? We do not know whether this corona crisis, the working at home and all the ways we have now to be productive without having to go to work if you have that type of work offer opportunities for what Mr Raven says. So I think it is wise to take this into account, but I do not think it can only be done on the drawing board.

Absolutely. Of course, you're not gonna map it out and then do nothing with it. I myself simply do not know the answer to the question of who could provide additional capacity there and what exactly the consequences are. I have heard the figures on the size of cereal exports, but also on sunflower oil, for example, and on the quantity apparently produced. What that means in terms of disruption of the world market and shortages is apparently enormous. By the way, you should probably add the part of the production that Russia is responsible for. You have to ask yourself whether Russia is going to make that available to the West happy. The tragedy is: who gets in trouble first? Those are, of course, people in those countries who are already having a hard time. The Netherlands is not the first country I am concerned about, in any case not given our own agricultural sector, but also not given our common purchasing power and our common ability to sustain this. That's really different in some parts of Africa.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I had ten motions, but since the chairman was so strict, I don't have any motions right now. So I'm gonna cut you some slack again! Sometimes, when you look at these kinds of climate debates, it's all trouble and torment. And yes, 20% of electricity is now from renewable electricity sources. This will be over 70% by 2030. So let's be a little optimistic about that. The cabinet that has been there for the past four years has not done anything for nothing. We should be a little proud of that, too. I think the key question of this debate is: how do we link this bill to the policy we are going to have for green hydrogen? The Minister has indicated that Europe is still coming up with a whole story on this issue. We are going to talk about this in the Chamber ourselves for a long time. If I have to make the key question concrete: we will soon be able to hang green guarantees of origin on hydrogen, if it is produced with electricity that also has green guarantees of origin on it. We call it green hydrogen in the Netherlands, but what does it mean that we can call it green hydrogen? Or are we actually saying that we're going to hang these COOs on that hydrogen, but we're not calling it green, and we're not going to do anything with it in policy either? I would like to have a little more clarity about that. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

It is tempting to look only at the energy account within purchasing power and only at the ODE within the energy account, but that is totally inadequate. The ODE is 10% or less of the average energy bill. Again, the total account for a household with average consumption is not higher but lower compared to 15 years ago. It's gonna stay that way. It is still important to look at this as a whole. The Netherlands is not a country that should be ashamed of income differences.

We're threatening to repeat ourselves. I have a bit to say about this; perhaps this reassures Mrs Kröger and that we can get a little closer together. Again, we also want 100% sustainable palm oil. We're not there yet based on the RSPO. If there are any further questions, she may ask the question again at once, because I think I will come back to it. It's not like we don't want anything. I need to see where I left off. Indonesia and Malaysia, in particular, are large palm oil producing countries. I focus on Indonesia, where 16 million people make their living. There are major problems with land rights. That has just been discussed in the debate. It is primarily a responsibility of the Indonesian government. But what can we do? Can the Minister comment on this? The Indonesian government has established a three-year halt to the expansion of palm oil plantations. That's some kind of freezing time. This raises a problem for the income of workers and their families. It is sustainable for the climate but socio-economically certainly not sustainable. How can we help bridge years when production is shut down in certain regions in order to catch nature's breath? Can the Minister indicate what other policies Indonesia is taking? Is there a road map, for example? What can we do to support that? Then there is the delegated regulation of the European Commission which identifies palm oil as a threat to sustainability. Indonesia and Malaysia have serious problems with this. I understand that, too. I understand that Indonesia has threatened to stop the negotiations on a trade agreement and even threatens to terminate the Paris climate agreement. The wrongs in the sector can be dealt with precisely by setting conditions for trade together with Indonesia. I would like a response from the Minister as to whether this is the desired effect of these delegated measures. Malaysia would have sent a letter to the Netherlands. What did the Netherlands say to that? Mr. Chairman. Finally, I come to Mr von Martels' motion. The Dutch system remains based on the share of renewable energy and not on CO performance. We would like to move on to a system based on the contribution of biofuels to CO reduction.

Mrs Ouwehand is concerned with two subjects, and one of them has just been the subject of a debate with Mr Jetten. That might give me a chance to put down something of a difference of vision. Then I'm going to answer the second part. Mrs Ouwehand just said to Mr Jetten that her criticism of the climate tables was that the government could not throw it over society. Those were about her words. My criticism, when I think about these climate tables, is that society may not have been sufficiently involved and that there was not enough ownership in that society. A city like Amsterdam, a city the CDA likes to criticize, has recently set up a climate council, really for citizens to participate actively. I'm sure Mrs Ouwehand didn't mean to throw society over the fence. No, I think that society itself should be more involved, because a lot of people will benefit if they experience more perspective of action. That's one. Two. When it comes to climate, I must confess that I personally have less sense of this than several people here in this Chamber. I am pleased that Mr Klaver has chosen Mr Jetten for very long discussions on this, but it is a fact that we young CDAs have a lot of knowledge and a lot of energy in it. That was also congratulated by Mr Jetten; thank you, I will pass it on. It has also been seen in our party. Both Derk Boswijk and Henri Bontenbal have deliberately stepped forward on behalf of the group in order to move forward in the field of nitrogen and climate. They show that these are not subjects, of which we are only stuck in 'if there is only support', but that we are also prepared to take a step forward and still say: but it is important that there is support for them.

Mr President, I would like to respond to that. That is possible, but we have seen that it is really a question of whether you should want those technological solutions to reduce nitrogen emissions from a barn. Those air scrubbers cost a lot of power. So the real question is whether you should want it if we need to save energy. And its yield was assessed more positively than it turned out to be in reality. So the farmers invested, the subsidies went and the Rabobank said: yes, but then you have to take more animals. It seems in the letter that now lies that at least part of the cabinet wants to continue with that policy. And that seems so unwise to me, so I hope that Mrs Dik-Faber and the Christian Union will withdraw from that.

Depending further on Russia? Then the VVD, Mr Erkens, is probably not really aware, because at the moment about 19% of the gas we consume in the Netherlands comes from Russia, so cut it out. But indeed, gas is a very good import. We do that from countries like Norway, Canada, Great Britain, it can come from anywhere. We can actually pump it up from the North Sea, that's all fine. So we can get it from anywhere. Where we don't have to get it from, it's Groningen. There we must immediately stop the gas extraction, as the PVV has said so many times. But a party like the VVD has trained that for years. It is because of the VVD that has been at the helm here in this country for years that people are in deep trouble.

I have said from the outset that our policy shows how we feel about our responsibility, how we carry it out and how we try to include others in it. Whether I should take the leap of responsibility immediately afterwards and do as much as possible to legislation or compliance in Indonesia or in Malaysia? That is not feasible, not even for the Dutch Government. You're gonna need international agreements for that. At the moment, we are still committed on a voluntary basis and to the best possible quality. It is also about farmers, about incomes, about very vulnerable families and people. We want to do this thing together, which is the vision of development cooperation, because the voluntary basis is likely to produce much better results in the end. A number of countries have focused on overall sustainability. There's a deal about that. The reason why countries such as Indonesia and Malaysia respond to some of the statements that are being taken, for example from the Dutch public debate, is that they feel that there is inappropriate, unnecessary and unproductive pressure being placed and that they are being made for obligations that they simply cannot fulfil. That can also mean an escape route, which means that you can get more so-called illegal palm oil, so to speak................................................................................................................................................................................................................................................... We want to do this together from a shared responsibility, not from a solo responsibility of the Netherlands alone.

That concludes this two-minute debate. I'll suspend for a few moments and then we'll continue with the same Minister on Hydrogen. We also continue with about the same speakers, so as far as I am concerned we can also proceed immediately. As far as you're concerned, is that okay? Then that's what we're gonna do. Then I'll reopen the meeting right away. Go on, let the bell ring.

Mr Nijboer challenged me, Madam President. I was in fiscal policy. Speaking of the middle class, the dogma of the 1980s was "lower burdens, smaller government." In practice, we are seeing a trendal decline in top rates for the highest incomes, a trendal decline in VPB rates and low taxes on capital, but still high workload and a mad marginal pressure on the middle groups. Why does this cabinet stand up for the middle groups? Why a lower top rate, when the real marginal burden is with the middle class? Why at the same time a higher rate for the first disc? We are putting the tariff structure together, with the effect that we are only increasing the problems of marginal burden pressure for the middle class. This fundamental problem remains and is being transferred to another cabinet. If we really want to get rid of the surcharge disaster and the phasing-out routes in tax rebates and still want a fairer tax system, then a flat tax after the introduction of the surcharge system is the worst ideologically motivated idea from the VVD and the CDA. I'd like a response from the State Secretary, please, along the lines of Section 3.1 of the Compatibility Act. And why should lower macro estimated care premiums be compensated with an increase in the rate in the first disk? This affects all people with a lower income or middle income. I have referred to this unfortunate rule in budgetary policy, the closure of the burden framework, earlier. The Council of State is critical of the justification for amending the budgetary rules, but it seems that the Council is calling for an adjustment here. I'd like a response. And then there's the taxes on power. I agree that we wanted a solution for savers, because the capital efficiency tax is unfair, but the current proposal is not a fundamental choice for a tax on real capital gains and does not start until 2022. Why not a quick temporary solution for savers and for the next cabinet period a real plan for taxing wealthy people? 'Cause the power inequality is big. Of all developed countries, this is even greater only in the United States. And let's take a fundamental look at the free power build-up in box 2. Mr. Chairman. We have often talked about burden-sharing between companies and households. Here too, the cabinet has taken a small step to the left. I do not think we should reduce the tax on profits, but the ratio has become somewhat fairer. This has to do, among other things, with the reduction of the energy bill in the mix of green taxes. I'm happy about that. The cuts in the energy discount last year were not sensible. We remember the debates and the attempts to restore some of them. This is where the cabinet turned the Stevens 180 degrees. That's good. Let us look at this with delay as a profit from a democratic debate. It is also a good thing that this cabinet, together with this Secretary of State, is for the first time really working on tackling tax avoidance and basic erosion in large companies. But there is still much to do, internationally and in our own system. Recent research by the IMF shows that 40% of foreign investment worldwide is ghost capital and has nothing to do with real investment, but fiscally motivated. A very large proportion of them fly by Luxembourg and the Netherlands. One of the things we have to do is to limit the regime for liquidation losses, which means that a company like Shell will also pay a profit tax in the Netherlands. I was therefore pleased to be surprised by the fact that the Cabinet intends to take over my proposal for a reduction of the liquidation loss regime. The law had already been co-signed by the SP and the Labour Party, by Mrs Leijten and Mr Nijboer, but that the cabinet now takes over this law is very nice. Large companies are now also going to pay income tax in the Netherlands. I've worked on it with great pleasure. I would like to thank the staff of our Bureau of Legislation. I thank my expert advisor, Professor Jan van de Streek, who was the intellectual driver of this project. I was also very pleased with the expert and creative cooperation of the State Secretary's officials. I've been fascinated by the discussions between them and science. They do not speak in plain language, they speak in judgments of the Court of Justice. I have said it before, but it also appears in this section: the Ministry of Finance remains the best in The Hague. Mr. Chairman. I am pleased to hand over the draft law to the Secretary of State through you. I wish him as much pleasure in bringing this law to the parliamentary conclusion as I have had in preparing the draft. Please.

Then I come to Mrs Beckerman's concerns about energy poverty. I said earlier that we are focusing on purchasing power and that we recognise poverty. I don't see specific energy poverty. But first let me focus on the number of 650,000. It is a number from 2014; it comes from a TNO report. More recently, we come up with smaller numbers of people who pay a very large part of their income in energy and who have a payment risk. In the 650,000 there are also people who have a very spacious lifestyle, have a lot of money, open the doors and windows wide open and set them loose. But that is not energy poverty; that may be behavioral poverty at the most. But that is not energy poverty. Mrs Beckerman's implied suggestion is that the energy bill is also rising. That's not true. Indeed, the amount, adjusted for inflation, of the energy account of an average household with average consumption does not increase at all over recent years. There'll be all kinds of households that have different ways... Very large houses that are very poorly isolated, rise considerably. We have just made an ODE shift that has benefited small households in particular and significantly less. So there are all kinds of deviations from that, but it is not right that we have an ever-increasing energy bill for average use, quite the contrary. The suggestion is also that the ODE would be a very important part of the energy bill and completely blown up. In 2005, we had the forerunner of that, the MEP. Now we have the ODE. It's not a big source of rise at all. It could have happened, but for that we have shifted those proportions. We have reduced the taxes on the energy bill of a household with an average consumption by €100. The following year these taxes increased by €0 and next year this increase is very limited, probably a few euros. Nevertheless, it is important to keep thinking about the energy bill, if only because the energy bill is also paying for energy that you may not want to use at all. An important part of the target group referred to by Mrs Beckerman could become part of that start-up engine, in which the corporations play a role. I said once that I would not be surprised if the average corporation house was preserved before the average private house. I hope that doesn't happen, but we brought it in as a starter engine. What could be the solution for households that pay a lot of energy? So what is the purchasing power issue? It's a cliché. Mrs Beckerman already knows the answer, but I fully support it. Every year we have income policies. Every year we do this in the August decision-making process. Energy is part of that and all the other burdens a household has are part of that. That's how we do it. I must therefore discourage the amendment, but that is what she thought. This isn't the way to do it. There are a lot of schemes for households. A limited proportion of households are now able to deal with house charges neutrally, but with this gas price that is only the demand. That means we have to keep an eye on that. That's all true, but cutting off 20% of the SDE is not the way.

There has been quite a lot of work on this climate agreement by a lot of people. That was just wiped off the table in one go: we are against this climate agreement. Now we already have a bit more nuance around the CO levy: that might work out well. But there are more elements in it. If you are against the Climate Agreement, are you opposed to the ODE tax, the storage on your energy bill, to a third citizen, two thirds of companies instead of 50% citizens, 50% companies? Or does that go off the table with the same speed?

Since municipalities play such an important role in achieving this energy transition, they also have an interest in ensuring that projects they need for regional energy strategies are not made impossible by stacking. That is certainly an aspect to be taken into account. In these cases, moreover, there is no obligation to provide a cost story, but an opportunity to ask for a financial contribution. If municipalities are of the opinion that this makes the project itself impossible, because, for example, it has been chosen to involve the environment very widely, so that there is little room left in the business case to allow a project to continue, with support of the environment, they are not obliged to go into cost stories. That's a choice. Can cost stories also be used in large infrastructure projects? That's the point of Kornwerderzand. Cost story is possible under the Environmental Law under private law and public law. If infrastructure involves building, costs can be recovered. How this works exactly in the case-Kornwerderzand I did not have any sharpness, but in my promise just now I said that we are going to see how the current system is working out on this kind of specific projects, whether there is a gap there and what the solutions are. Wider, namely in the context of the construction of infrastructure, is the question of how to make this possible with one another. In fact, Mr Crone's question is somewhat in that context. Those were the answers to questions about the cost story. Then I come to questions about lot exchange and then to expropriation. The redevelopment of urban areas may be hampered by fragmented ownership. The urban lot exchange creates an additional opportunity to deal with this. At least three owners can exchange land and/or stables independently and after mutual consultation. This will improve the layout of the area. For two and a half years, together with the Kadaster and a wide-scale sounding board group, the possibilities of urban lot exchange have been tested through the Urban Lot Exchange Stimulation Programme. As the programme's annual report shows, the experience is positive. Urban lot exchange has potential in areas where ownership is fragmented. The programme has fostered awareness and application of lot exchange. A good example, to make it concrete, is the Merwedekanaanzone in Utrecht, where municipalities and owners prepare a new plan, regardless of the limits of ownership. In the meantime, an intention agreement has been signed as a basis for further cooperation and exchange of property. The housing crisis was a good example where a very large number of new homes are realized within the city. The Christian Union asked about the letter from the KNB and my response to it. The letter is known to me. About the boundary between rural and urban areas the following. The notary checks a lot exchange against its description in the bill and against the criteria laid down for the lot exchange rural area. If lots with an urban function are involved in the exchange, there is no lot exchange rural area. The municipality defines what belongs to urban area and the notary is simply going to check which lots it concerns and where they fall under: under the definition of the lot exchange urban area or not. Actually, that's how it is. In the programme Getting started with the Environment Act, particular attention will be paid to lot exchange, and a practical manual will also be published to remove any uncertainties here. The question then was whether registration of the lot exchange agreement was an obligation. The draft law explicitly stipulates that the lot exchange agreement is to be entered in the public registers. As a result, it will have the desired business effect, which means that any successors under special titles will be bound to the lot exchange agreement. It is also stipulated that the subsequent action, resulting in the acquisition of property ownership rights in immovable property, shall be entered in the public registers. The explanatory memorandum to the legislative proposal also makes it clear that the parties have no choice as to the registration in the registers. Then there was the question as to whether it was clear to the notary that he had to investigate in the processing of a re-arrest document. The notary has an obligation to investigate the Land Registry and investigates the legal status of the real estate listed in the Relandings Act. That is, of course, one of the core tasks of the notary. The search for a notary at a re-arrestation certificate is similar to the investigation that takes place during a regular transfer. D66 asked whether the Minister considered it possible for the government to actually make this instrument possible in the event of positive research results regarding the introduction of mandatory urban land consolidation. Yes, the government has an open attitude towards urban land consolidation. It has advantages and disadvantages, but that is why we should also consider what a mandatory urban land consolidation scheme could look like and what its effects would be. If that research is available, we will be happy to discuss it. Then there is the need for improvement in the case of voluntary lot exchange, on which the SGP asked a question. Why is the specific improvement requirement not deleted or the legal text clarifies that the specific improvement requirement does not need to be assessed independently? The improvement requirement for lot exchange is an important requirement in relation to the efficient use of public funds. That requirement is important for exemption from transfer tax. That is why this demand is made for improvement. The exemption therefore applies only to a lot exchange rural area which aims at an improvement. Otherwise, that exemption will not apply. The Tax Administration also checks whether these conditions for exemption from transfer tax are met. Moreover, this improvement requirement is not a new requirement, it is already covered by the current legislation.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. At the end of last year, the Supreme Court dismissed the state's appeal against Urgenda and thus the previous judgment became final. The VVD Group would have preferred a different outcome, especially in view of the fact that many measures have been taken to reduce CO emissions in the Netherlands in the coming decades and to reduce them to the Paris target. That transition has now really been deployed, supported by many companies and institutions in the Climate Agreement. But within the Dutch rule of law we accept this judgment. Hence the cabinet's efforts to comply with the verdict. And if that is the case, we also think that it is a good idea that the cabinet has also looked at measures taken to give economic impetus to sectors that are currently struggling as a result of the corona crisis. The same crisis is currently causing a temporary reduction in CO emissions, mainly due to a change in electricity demand. This gives extra importance to the adaptive strategy which the Minister intends to pursue with regard to the reduction of production in coal-fired power stations. This measure is the biggest blow in this package of measures and therefore an inevitable part, but it is important to measure it. After all, even if we do nothing, coal plants will be closed by 2030 anyway. So in order to reduce CO emissions more quickly, the government has to put a fee on the table. I therefore believe that the measure should not go beyond what is necessary to comply with the judgment. So there are just a few more questions about that. The measure will be announced temporarily for a few years. Does the Minister have a picture of how many years that will have to be? What does the intended weighing moment look like? On the basis of what information will the measure be adjusted if it so wishes? The corresponding law is due to enter into force at the end of this year, but now the PBL has published several scenarios, depending on how long the corona crisis lasts. Is there also a possibility of flexibility, for fine-tuning, following the entry into force of the law, depending on CO2 emissions and expectations in 2021 and later? I have a question for the effect, so the answer does not have to be given today. The Minister announced that he would inform the Chamber before the summer. How's it going for the summer? Could he then take the next thought with him? It points out that this measure may also have a nitrogen effect. It is of its nature that this measure is temporary. The government's nitrogen approach has now indicated that the temporary nitrogen reduction may be used for projects, such as sustainability projects, which have only a temporary nitrogen effect. I would ask the Minister to answer the question as to whether this measure can be added to the coal-fired power plant, so that the temporary nitrogen effect can be temporarily used again. Mr. Chairman. The other measures focus not only on being feasible in the short term, but also on seducing people and businesses to reduce CO emissions. That's what got us out of the heart. In our view, it can stimulate people if we take measures that will also have a positive effect on themselves, for example energy savings, which you will find in your energy bill. The goal we support is CO reduction, but in a way that doesn't have to change the way of life for people. A few more questions and comments on the rest of the package of measures. When is the outcome of the exploration for specific measures in industry known? For greenhouse horticulture additional support has now been announced in the form of LED lighting in greenhouses. A good thing, but it is without prejudice to the fact that the cabinet is still engaged in a broader investigation into the impact of the Climate Agreement and the ODE increase on greenhouse horticulture. My question is when it will be ready. Then there is the SDE spring round, which we discussed earlier in a previous Urgenda debate. It was raised in view of the Urgendavonnis. Will the applications that receive a grant on the basis of this round also be subject to the extended implementation period due to the corona crisis? Finally, it is a good thing that funds are available for SMEs. Mrs Mulder and I have already made a commitment to this in the budget debate. It is precisely in these difficult times that the money to invest in renewable energy evaporates or evaporates there, and SMEs would have to face up to the wall if they had to comply with an information requirement for energy saving but then have no chance of taking any action to actually invest and take measures. Apart from the package, I would also like to inform the Minister that this is something he must constantly take into account in the future. Thank you.

I fully agree with Mr Sjoerdsma. That is why, in my first reply, I indicated that there are alternatives, such as those from Algeria. Mr Sjoerdsma indicated that himself. So that's what we're agreed on. I'm trying to point out that maybe I'm repeating a little bit that in times of crisis we're sometimes inclined, with some kind of tunnel vision, to go the way of the least resistance. The path of the least resistance is: back to unsustainable energy. This means, for example, the reopening of coal-fired power stations. I believe that Mr Sjoerdsma and I agree that we do not want that. At the moment when there would be an energy shortage that's already going on and scenarios are already being written for it, Volt says: bet on sustainable alternatives. So instead of opening a coal power plant, go, for example, for unsustainable but better gas from Algeria. That is the short term, but at the same time keep the instruments we have, like those two directives I mentioned, on hand and do not go back to what you already know in a time of crisis.

Mr. Chairman. The Netherlands has traditionally had a reputation of solidity, economy and thrift, wary of wild business adventures, throwing money over the bar or administrative sloppyness. Well, the state's accounts wouldn't be too bad for a third-rate collection agency by now. Year after year, the General Court has turned a finger on the government. Successive ministers promised to get better: "Next time we'll do our best to get a good school report from the Court's accountants." And then it goes wrong again. The ministers remain seated; the same is true of pupils who have not understood the lesson. With the knowledge of today, I would like to ask what the Minister or perhaps the Prime Minister would have done differently. BVNL wants a smaller government and lower taxes. That goes hand in hand. The government costs money and does not generate money. The bigger the government, the bigger the waste. That's what we're seeing for the third year in a row. The ordinary hardworking Dutchman may pay the bill of that spilliness in the form of higher taxes. The growth of the almighty government, which wishes to interfere with every step of the citizen and which determines what is good for the people, continues unbridled. I hold my heart on climate and nitrogen funds, together EUR 60 billion. BVNL is also in favour of climate: a favourable location climate, a friendly tax environment and a fair business environment in which working pays and saving is not penalised. In short, a smaller government, lower charges. Mr. Chairman. The good hardworking citizen is plagued by inflation, housing shortage and towering energy bills and sees Schiphol turn into a day camping. He should not get it in his brain to fill out a form error once or to make an administrative mistake in SMEs, because the distrustful state apparatus will put him in the official meat grinder. But the state continues with flawed accounting, including unlawful obligations. That's about 5% of the total or about 15 billion over 2021. With unlawful income, the State does not have so many problems, but fortunately the Supreme Court has more or less prevented tax robbery in box 3. The fact that the accounts are not correct again cannot be surprising. The government does not have a complete overview of all its assets either. Its value is about 350 billion, as the Court of Auditors reported to us at the end of last year. All of us own ports, real estate, roads, bridges, barracks and so on. All these things add up to about EUR 350 billion, but how this is administered is not entirely clear. Mr. Chairman. If the State were a company, the CFO would have been nail-biting under the valium to await the opinion of the shareholders and the supervisory board. The Commissioners would then first check their liability insurance before giving a judgment. But maybe I'm too strict. Management taking the measure is always easier than self-driving. I would therefore like to repeat the message of the President of the General Court: a paper reality is emerging that is independent of real reality, and this problem is in danger of getting worse. "On paper, we approve what is not really acceptable," the Court of Auditors rightly said. The implementation by the government in relation to its citizens and the provision of public goods are more and more unsatisfactory. Society is changing faster and is becoming more complex. Both the Court of Auditors, the Council of State, the National Ombudsman and senior officials warn time and time again that policy and implementation are increasingly wringing. That is a problem for all of us, including politics. By always demanding exceptions, additions, modifications and adjustments with the best intentions, rules become increasingly complicated and sometimes impossible to implement and enforce. At a bank, the golden rule is that the back office, say the operations, should never lag behind the front office, the commerce, to avoid foreseeable disasters. That's what the government should do. I should like to hear from the cabinet that the feasibility and not necessarily the political will prevails on new proposals. Can the Cabinet undertake to do this? Finally. Too often I read that loyal officials write that it is feasible, provided there are no other priorities, the occupation is improved qualitatively and quantitatively within three months, the absenteeism is halves, the Prime Minister learns Chinese in one week and the Minister of Finance places himself in front of the semi-final mixed double on Wimbledon. The Frisians then say "I apologize to the Frisian colleagues for my statement it's just pouring. And that's something different than most people think. Thank you.

Yes. I'm not much of a campaign strategist either. The biggest dialogue you have with people and which is by far the most decisive factor when it comes to your home, you don't do with a campaign. That dialogue is about the moment you say: the gas is really going off; there must be a different solution in the years to come, but we are starting now. You don't do that with a campaign. Maybe we agree with each other. That's a very special moment. That goes from kitchen table to good information up to and including funding. That's not what the campaign's about. The campaign isn't about buying the refrigerator or the mixer either, because that's what you do when you buy something. It's about the underlying awareness that something's going on. I am aware that Mrs Dik-Faber thinks that this is not very convincing, if I may put it that way. I will pass that on to the people who are thinking about such a campaign, but I do not have the illusion that a campaign is the most important contribution to support. For example, if you speak or go with those who consult with people in Purmerend door on the other heating of their home, including insulation, the hot water solution, the cooking solution and so on, you will see that there is no alternative but to gain support in this way. I refer to Purmerend, because when I came from there, I was very impressed by the person who does. That's, I think, pure support. There's no campaign against that.

The billing, or the explanation of how we get at least 1,000 billion, is extended on our site. You'll find that in no time. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The European Union has experienced crisis in recent years: Brexit, the corona pandemic and now the war in Ukraine. Time and time again we see European integration and we see a Europe that works together and acts decisively. That makes sense, because together you stand stronger and the European Union faces challenges that can only be tackled cross-border. But as soon as the crisis is less urgent, we can see that national interests are regained and ambitions are weakened, which does not make full use of the strength of the EU. For a strong Union, we need a European vision and we need to ask ourselves what Europe we want to be. This applies to the reaction to the war in Ukraine, to security and defence policy, to our energy policy and to our economy. The war has a human face in the millions of refugees who come to Europe and are taken care of here. We therefore understand that funds must be available for the border countries that are hit hardest. At the same time, we see how in Poland and Hungary Arab and African refugees are being pushed back and violations of the rule of law continue. How credible is it, then, if Europe claims to stand up for democratic values, if it allows those values to be violated in its own Member States? I ask the Prime Minister not to overlook the crisis of the European rule of law and to ensure that funds in countries such as Poland and Hungary reach the local authorities and aid organisations, while ensuring that independent media can do their work in safety. Mr. Chairman. Our reaction to Ukraine is and must also be valued, because war concerns us all. The EU indicates that it is ready to deploy further coordinated sanctions rapidly. There are several proposals for this, such as the imposition of a full embargo on energy imports, a trade embargo and pressure from third countries to impose sanctions. Can the Prime Minister indicate how the Netherlands relates to these proposals? Mr. Chairman. There is a limit to how economic sanctions can influence the progress of the war. That is why I ask the Prime Minister whether he can write back what the effect of the current and proposed sanctions will be, and what impact they will have on the continuation of the war. The sanctions we impose also have a major impact on third countries. For example, sanctions and the ongoing war are causing famine in South Asia, Africa and Latin America. That is why I am asking the Prime Minister: is there any idea of which banks are handling payments for Russian grain, and are they, like the Russian gas and oil banks, excluded from SWIFT sanctions? And what is the Netherlands' position on the recommendations of the Committee on World Food Security, as set out yesterday in the European Parliament? Then there's our energy dependence. This crisis has made it even clearer that we need to diversify our energy supply as quickly as possible, but we now see that Europe and the Netherlands are focusing on unsustainable alternatives, such as American LNG and biogas, and that they are even talking about reopening coal plants. The situation demands real ambition and accelerating the green transition. That is why I ask the Prime Minister: is the Netherlands prepared to increase the ambitions of the Renewable Energy Directive and the Energy Efficiency Directive, and take a leading role in the Council? If the Netherlands is not prepared to do so, why not?

Mr. Chairman. Where some parties will say today that it is embarrassing that the Netherlands is so late in presenting and discussing this plan, the SP actually finds it embarrassing that a plan is needed at all to get some of our own money back from Brussels. That's what the interrupting debate was about just now. Solidarity and emergency aid, especially between friendly countries, is of course important when it comes to a crisis situation, but not in this way. Not through Brussels, where a significant part of the money is hanging. Not only on the condition that the political demands of the EU are met and not long after the crisis is over. However, we are here today because this fund was set up. There is therefore no point in constantly holding such a fundamental debate. Now there's a plan. Then it is also logical that we should discuss this plan in the Dutch Parliament. In doing so, I would like to distinguish between the investments that are being proposed and the reforms that the cabinet intends to undertake, whether under Brussels pressure or not. On the investment side, there are good things to do. These are things that should be done in any case and should be done anyway, such as the sustainability and improvement of our inland waterways, wind energy at sea and the improvement of our railways. These are all useful and necessary investments in our own future. My question to the cabinet is whether these investments would have been different, in terms of size or form, if it had not been for the European Corona Restoration Fund. What is the added value of this fund for the Netherlands? How have these investments been adapted, if that is the case, to meet the requirements of Brussels? In addition, the SP wonders whether consideration has also been given to setting the VAT rate for public transport at zero, as recently made possible by the revision of the VAT Directive. Mr. Chairman. The money to invest in this kind of useful and necessary business, which is really just our own money, is not just from Brussels. To do so, we must meet their political demands and implement the reforms they consider desirable. Fortunately, there are also useful and necessary things, for example when it comes to curbing the unhindered housing market in our country. Thanks to the motion of the SP, for example, the jubelton is reduced more quickly and eventually abolished, as stated in the coalition agreement. In this respect, the Cabinet can therefore count on our support. But the cabinet also wants to triple the flight tax, regardless of whether you fly twenty times a year or only once for a well-deserved holiday. The SP doesn't think that's fair. We have said that several times. But what is completely bizarre is that people who switch to Schiphol, who make a transit, and thus add nothing to our society other than pollution and nuisance, do not have to pay the flight tax. Is the Cabinet prepared to make the flight tax fairer by making the transferrs pay as well? Is it willing to include that in this plan? And is the cabinet prepared to investigate whether every Dutchman can fly once a year without paying that flight tax, so an exemption for a well-deserved holiday for everyone? Mr. Chairman. But in fact, I fear that it will not stop at the flight tax, at the cost of driving or at any of the other unpleasant demands that Brussels imposes on us through this cabinet plan. The EU bureaucracy will not easily give up this new power in the form of the Recovery Fund, the SP fears. Is the government therefore prepared to reiterate in the plan that this fund is temporary and exceptional and that the Netherlands will never, but never, support it again in the future? Thank you.

I have just given an example of the fact that the three owners of coal power stations are completely overcompensated. If we can believe the NRC, it happened with nearly 1.5 billion to stop the coal plants. But we won't get that letter until next week. 800,000 households have to do with less than half of that. On the one hand a great over-compensation, on the other hand a CPB that says 1.1 million households are sinking through the ice. Does the government not see the possibility of ensuring that there is no overcompensation for the decommissioning of coal plants? No one makes as much profit as the owners of stationary coal plants in this country. Doesn't the government see any possibility of doing something for those people?
